title: Google Home MCP lets Antigravity, Claude, OpenClaw, & more control your smart home
snippet: Google today announced “Home MCP” to let your personal AI agent interact with your smart home devices via the Model Context Protocol. more…
fullText:
Google today announced “Home MCP” to let your personal AI agent interact with your smart home devices via the Model Context Protocol.

This allows Google Antigravity, Claude, Hermes, OpenClaw, and any other agent that supports calling MCP tools to “interact with all of the devices and event history in the Google Home ecosystem.” 

This includes Google Nest cameras and doorbells, Nest Thermostats, Matter light bulbs, and beyond. Example use cases include:

Cross-Camera Analysis: Ask your agent what the kids did when they got home from school, and it will provide a summary across all of your cameras of what they did and show you the clips

Analyze home history: Your agent can use your device state history to track how many loads of laundry were done in a week, or how long the lights were left on.

Interact with you via voice: If your agent is completing an asynchronous or proactive task,  it can send you an audio message over your Google Home speaker when it’s finished.

Build a dashboard: Your agent can build you a custom dashboard that provides a view of your smart home tailored just to you.

Google frames this as giving your agent “real-world physical context—allowing it to analyze and answer questions about home activity, summarize camera footage across rooms, manage devices on your behalf, or even create your own smart home dashboards using everyday language.”

	

On the security and privacy front, Home MCP “enforces rate limits and safety protections, such as prohibiting sensitive actions like unlocking doors.” Google cautions about how:

However, depending on your agent, connecting it to Home MCP can result in unexpected or even undesired behavior. Carefully review developer policies and terms of service.

As of today, Home MCP is rolling out for Google Home Premium Advanced users in US English. The setup process involves creating a Google Cloud project and then configuring it to use Home MCP. 

…simply provide the MCP configuration details to your agent and ask it to set it up. Your agent will ask you to sign in and grant permissions. After that, you’re ready to go. For complete setup guides, visit the Google Home Developer Center.

title: WhatsApp may soon let iPhone users add a third account
snippet: After recently letting iPhone users add a second account to the same app, WhatsApp is now working on expanding support to up to three accounts. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
After recently letting iPhone users add a second account to the same app, WhatsApp is now working on expanding support to up to three accounts. Here are the details.

WhatsApp to support up to three accounts

Last June, WhatsApp officially rolled out support for multiple accounts on iPhone, allowing users to add a second account to the same app.

The move came after the feature had spent several months in beta testing, giving users an alternative to relying on WhatsApp Business as a workaround for managing a second account.

Now, as spotted by WABetaInfo, the app appears to be working on expanding the feature to let users switch between up to three accounts without logging out.

Image: WABetaInfo

From WABetaInfo:

The attached image shows the account selector when multi-account supports up to three profiles. The left screen shows the option to add a second account at the bottom of the interface. The right screen shows the interface when users log into their third profile. The layout is the same as before, so accounts appear with their name, profile photo, and phone number, and the active one has a green checkmark. When this feature becomes available, users will see the “Add account” option even when they have two active profiles in the same app. Note that WhatsApp may support even more than three accounts in the future.

The report adds that each account will keep its own chat history, notifications, privacy settings, backups, and media.

WABetaInfo notes that while two accounts may be enough for many users, the feature could come in handy for those who have different combinations of work and personal phone numbers.

That said, the feature is still under development and isn’t available to beta testers yet, suggesting there may still be some time before a wider rollout.

title: Apple releases first iOS 27.2 developer beta for iPhone
snippet: Apple has released the first iOS 27.2 developer beta for iPhone. The update follows the release of iOS 27 to everyone on Monday. It also leaps over iOS 27.1, which Apple has shown as an iPhone Duo-focused release. more…
fullText:
Apple has released the first iOS 27.2 developer beta for iPhone. The update follows the release of iOS 27 to everyone on Monday. It also leaps over iOS 27.1, which Apple has shown as an iPhone Duo-focused release. 

iOS 27.2 beta 1 arrives before iOS 27.1 beta

Today’s beta release follows the official launch of iOS 27 on September 14. The new version comes as a sizable 22GB update.

Apple has already detailed how the iOS 27.1 SDK will let developers take full advantage of the iPhone Duo display. You can see how apps will appear on iPhone Duo based on which iOS version they target here.

But today’s iOS 27.2 developer beta 1 release skips over iOS 27.1 for now.

Apple presumably wants to save iPhone Duo-specific code until closer to the new hardware’s release in October. However, developers will still need to prepare their apps for the new device. Apple has said to expect the tools for this to be ready by the end of September.

Apple has already pointed to other changes for all iPhones coming next month. This includes the redesigned Apple Health app as well as expanded Siri AI support.

“A more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding, broad world knowledge, onscreen awareness, and even more systemwide app actions, Siri AI is now rolling out as a beta in English, with support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish coming in October,” Apple confirmed this week.

This likely gives us an idea of when to expect the official release.

We’ll know more about what Apple has included in this first release once we have it running.

We’ll cover new features and other changes in a separate roundup as we explore today’s new beta update. Stay tuned for our ongoing iOS 27.2 beta coverage.

title: How Bain Capital Ventures plans to deploy its fresh $1.6B fund
snippet: BCV's latest fund targets early-stage founders harnessing AGI and building the infrastructure to run it efficiently.
fullText:
Bain Capital Ventures (BCV), the venture division of private equity firm Bain Capital, has raised a new, $1.6 billion fund, which is 14% larger than its previous $1.4 billion fund the firm announced three years ago.

Like many other venture investors, BCV says it will use the fresh funds to back startups primarily focused on AI. The firm believes artificial general intelligence (AGI), which it defines as agents performing many tasks as well as humans can, has already arrived, and the next wave of startups will not only harness its power, but also build the infrastructure needed to make it run efficiently.

Some of the main themes that will be the most relevant in what the firm calls “the post-AGI era” include infrastructure, healthcare, physical AI, and security, said partner Kevin Zhang. 

He said BCV aims to fund compute infrastructure until intelligence becomes “too cheap to meter,” meaning that the cost of running AI drops to nearly zero. He pointed to one company in BCV’s portfolio that can help with this mission: data center developer Crusoe, which is reportedly valued at $30 billion and viewed as a near-term IPO candidate. BCV originally led Crusoe’s Series A in 2019, back when it focused on crypto mining.

The firm wants to focus on healthcare because it believes the sector may be vastly transformed by AI. Security, meanwhile, has recently become a matter of national debate after AI agents went rogue during training, and BCV believes there’s much potential to bet on in this space. Some of the firm’s significant investments in these sectors include Loyal, a longevity startup aimed at pets, and Dream, an AI-powered defender of national infrastructure.

BCV stands apart from other VC firms, according to Zhang, thanks to its affiliation with Bain Capital, which provides deep expertise and financial products across credit, real estate, insurance, and private equity. “BCV can support founders not just with equity capital, but with debt facilities, infrastructure partnerships, and real-economy relationships,” he said.

From the new fund, the firm’s 11th, BCV intends to invest in 30 to 40 companies, primarily at the seed through Series B stages.  Unlike most VC firms where a single partner champions a deal, BCV’s partners often team up in pairs or trios to back a specific investment, Zhang said.

“We need to have enough mind space and time to really be thoughtful partners to every team we work with,” he said.

title: Meta Reportedly Creating Glasses Without Cameras After ‘Pervert’ Uproar
snippet: The new glasses would focus on audio capabilities and ditch the cameras, according to a news report.
fullText:
The backlash has spoken. Meta reportedly is developing smart glasses without cameras amid a general anxiety about the wearable technology’s potential for privacy violations and following incidents of people using what have been dubbed “pervert glasses” to record videos of women without their permission or knowledge.

According to reporting from The Information, Meta wants to begin selling the new glasses — called Luna — in October and could introduce the new devices at its Connect developer conference next week. Meta Connect is scheduled for Sept. 23-24 and will be livestreamed.

The Information said Luna will have two styles, Clubmaster and Burbank. The smart glasses will have six microphones, along with speakers directed at the user’s ears. Wearers can speak to and listen to the Meta AI chatbot by pressing a button on the side of the glasses, The Information reported.

A representative for Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Read more: Smart Glasses Are Putting Cameras on People’s Faces. Here’s How to Spot Them

Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses have gained an unfortunate reputation. News reports have cited men using the device’s cameras to record women  — for instance asking to go out on a date while secretly recording the encounter — and then posting the videos on social media. The smart glasses have also been used to film pranks and harassment interactions.

One woman told CNN she had a conversation with a man at an airport and later discovered that he had posted several videos on social media of interactions he had with other women. Despite being asked by the woman at the airport not to post their conversation online, he did it anyway.

Read more: Meta Explained Its Smart Glasses AI Privacy Policies to Me. I’m Still Worried

Although there is a small LED light that turns on and blinks during recording, some people have removed the light or found ways to camouflage the LED so that people would not know they were being recorded. Meta rolled out a software update in late July that would deactivate the camera if the LED light was tampered with in any way.

But as CNET’s Scott Stein writes, it is difficult to spot the white LED light in bright daylight, and the Meta glasses look almost identical to the non-smart Ray-Ban glasses that have been around for decades. Stein also reported in June that Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth had indicated the company’s interest in releasing a less-expensive, camera-free version of its smart glasses that would focus on audio capabilities.

Austin Evans, a YouTube tech reviewer with nearly 6 million subscribers, said he rarely wears the Meta Ray-Bans anymore because of the bad vibes associated with them. He said he’s talked with folks at Meta about why glasses without cameras would be a good idea.

“It’s pretty simple technically, I would assume,” Evans told CNET. “It probably would allow them to slim the glasses down a bit. But most importantly it will be a really strong step toward removing the stigma around wearing them.”

title: SmartGym 8 brings natural-language workout creation, Siri AI integration, more
snippet: SmartGym is out with a massive update today that introduces AI-powered workout creation, management, deeper Siri integration, and several features that leverage the new possibilities of iOS 27, iPadOS, and watchOS 27. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
SmartGym is out with a massive update today that introduces AI-powered workout creation, management, deeper Siri integration, and several features that leverage the new possibilities of iOS 27, iPadOS, and watchOS 27. Here are the details.

I’ve written before about how much I like using SmartGym to track my exercise routine.

SmartGym is an Apple Design Award winner, and it doesn’t take long to see why. Developer Matt Abras is constantly changing, updating, and tweaking the app to make it easier and more streamlined to manage, track, and log gym sessions, improving on what has long been one of the most mature and useful gym-tracking apps on the App Store.

Today, SmartGym is getting one of its biggest updates ever. SmartGym 8 introduces SmartGym Intelligence, which is, in essence, the app’s own take on Private Cloud Compute.

SmartGym introduces its own Private Cloud Compute alternative

As Abras explains, SmartGym is currently not eligible to use Apple’s Private Cloud Compute through the new Foundation Models framework. So, he decided to build his own.

SmartGym Intelligence is private by design. Every request sent to a model is anonymous and disconnected from the user’s identity. Prompts and responses are never logged, cached, or retained by SmartGym.

SmartGym 8 relies on Apple’s new Language Model APIs to extend the Foundation Models framework to frontier models running on SmartGym’s own private cloud infrastructure, while keeping requests anonymous and disconnected from the user’s identity.

SmartGym never connects directly to an AI lab. The labs behind these frontier models never receive users’ prompts, and nothing users submit is used to train their models.

With today’s update, users can now create workout routines with natural language. This means they can type something like “create a push-pull-legs workout with 10 exercises per day. Avoid bench press. Include 2 warm-up exercises per day,” and the app’s new framework will handle the rest.

Once the workout is created, users can send new prompts such as “move leg day to Friday,” “remove the barbell squat,” or “make Wednesday a rest day,” to tweak it even further.

To try the new SmartGym Intelligence, users can go to the Routines tab in SmartGym 8 on iPhone and iPad, tap the + button, and type in what they need. On the Apple Watch, they can just open the app, scroll down down on the main screen, tap “Add Workout”, choose “just say it,” and describe what they want.

SmartGym + Siri AI

SmartGym 8 also leverages the new Siri AI, introduced in today’s 2027 OS updates. Here’s Abras:

SmartGym now integrates more deeply with Siri, making routines, exercises, equipment, muscle groups, schedules, and other training information accessible through natural voice requests. Siri can surface relevant SmartGym information directly and take you to the corresponding content when needed.

Users can now also start SmartGym workout sessions directly from Siri, in addition to controlling an active workout with commands such as “Next exercise in SmartGym,” or “Log set in SmartGym.”

With SmartGym’s data accessible to Siri, users can also ask questions such as “Which routines do I have in SmartGym this week?” or “Show me my dumbbell workouts in SmartGym,” and the app’s integration will not only surface the relevant information but also provide rich visual results right from the Siri interface.

This integration also works for specific session information, such as “Show my Heart Rates in SmartGym,” and even for exercise creation.

Users can also use the new Siri AI to create entirely new sessions by typing in or dictating a workout plan in natural language. Then, Siri AI and SmartGym will handle the rest, creating and organizing a new training routine based on the prompt.

Finally, SmartGym 8 also leverages Siri’s new on-screen awareness feature, which can be really helpful during gym sessions. Users can simply ask Siri to identify something on the screen, answer questions about it, or “Open the third routine on the screen,” and they can jump in without touching their device. Users can also start from an image, which is great for when they receive a written plan from their personal trainers.

Other tidbits

There’s plenty more in SmartGym 8. That includes:

Exercise Questions with images: SmartGym can now feed exercise execution images into Apple’s on-device Foundation Models to provide better and more descriptive answers about individual movements.

Resizable UI: The app’s interface now adapts more dynamically across different window sizes, orientations, and display shapes, getting the app ready for the new iPhone Duo.

More Liquid Glass: SmartGym has expanded its Liquid Glass design across more parts of the app, including its segmented controls, muscle group picker, alerts, and duration timer.

title: iOS 27.2 will help users move data and settings from an old app to its replacement
snippet: Starting with iOS 27.2, developers will be able to offer users a way to move their data and settings from an existing app to its designated replacement. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Starting with iOS 27.2, developers will be able to offer users a way to move their data and settings from an existing app to its designated replacement. Here are the details.

iOS to make app replacement easier

While uncommon, developers occasionally retire an existing app and launch a new one in its place, requiring users to move over to a separate app.

Even though most developers try to make that transition as seamless as possible, migrating can still require some work from the user, particularly when it involves data that isn’t stored in the cloud.

With iOS 27.2, Apple will address this with a new system-managed migration flow that can move an app’s data and supported settings to its designated replacement before deleting the old app.

Based on existing code in iOS 27.2 beta 1, users will be presented with an alert that says:

The developer recommends moving your existing “%1$@” app data and settings to the new “%2$@” app.

iPhone can do this for you now, before you start using your new app. Afterwards, the old app will be deleted from this iPhone.

Users will then be able to choose either “Move App Data and Settings” or “Don’t Move Anything.” If the user rejects the migration, iOS will present a second confirmation warning that some preferences, including notification and location settings, may need to be configured again.

To be clear, the feature appears to be limited to cases where a developer replaces one of its own apps with a designated successor, rather than migrating data between apps from different developers.

Based on the current implementation, iOS can migrate a range of system-level settings and permissions, including:

Privacy, location, and Health authorization decisions

Notification settings, including accessory notification settings

Per-app Do Not Disturb and Focus settings

App locking and protection settings

CarPlay icon order and compatible widget layouts

Live Activities and accessory Live Activities

Access to associated accessories

LaunchServices preferences, fonts, capture-related defaults, telephony data, and Secure Element services

We will keep an eye out for changes to this framework during the iOS 27.2 beta cycle and report back if we learn more about how developers will be able to implement it.

title: iOS 27.2 introduces Apple Health app overhaul, here’s what’s new
snippet: Today Apple released iOS 27.2 beta 1, skipping over 27.1 entirely in the testing cycle. And among other changes, the new iOS 27.2 update includes the previously announced all-new Health app. more…
fullText:
Today Apple released iOS 27.2 beta 1, skipping over 27.1 entirely in the testing cycle. And among other changes, the new iOS 27.2 update includes the previously announced all-new Health app.

All-new Apple Health app debuts in iOS 27.2 beta 1

Last week during its September event, Apple unveiled an all-new Health app that would be coming to iPhone later this year.

Now today, beta testers have received the first access to the Health app redesign via iOS 27.2 beta 1.

When Apple introduced the new Health app, it emphasized how Apple Intelligence would be used to help users better understand their health. Here’s what the company said:

The Health app has been redesigned to dynamically respond to a user’s data using Apple Intelligence, with a new Insights tab that surfaces timely health information and a new Longevity tab that analyzes a user’s longitudinal health data for deeper insights. The Longevity tab includes Health Age, an Apple Watch feature that shows users how certain metrics are tracking relative to their actual age. The Health app also includes movement evaluations that measure flexibility, strength, balance, and more using vision-based AI models on iPhone and heart rate data from Apple Watch.

Now today with iOS 27.2 beta 1, the new Insights tab and Longevity tab are both available for testing if you’re a developer.

Because the new Health app relies on Apple Intelligence, you’ll need an AI-compatible iPhone to try it out. Certain features require a paired Apple Watch too. And your device must be set to US English.

So if your iPhone is less powerful than an iPhone 15 Pro, or you don’t have a compatible Apple Watch, the Health app upgrades will be missing. But for everyone else, iOS 27.2 provides a first glimpse at Apple’s expanded vision for the Health app.

Note: Apple says additional Health features will roll out in future betas, like the ability to order labs from Quest and personalized recommendations. Also, despite its availability in the beta, Apple says the new Health app won’t actually ship in iOS 27.2 but instead is coming later in the year.

title: Apple planning to sell AI servers powered by M8 Ultra chips, says report
snippet: Apple is working on plans to make enterprise servers powered by M8 Ultra chips, according to a new report. The report specifically says that the company plans to offer the AI-focused servers for sale, not just use them internally. Two versions are said to be in development, with Apple considering incorporating Nvidia networking tech in the machines … more…
fullText:
Apple is working on plans to make enterprise servers powered by M8 Ultra chips, according to a new report. The report specifically says that the company plans to offer the AI-focused servers for sale, not just use them internally.

Two versions are said to be in development, with Apple considering incorporating Nvidia networking tech in the machines … 

The Information reports that plans have not yet been finalized and that the servers are not expected to go on sale until 2029.

Apple has been developing the server with plans to sell it to AI developers, other businesses and governments, the people said. The product under consideration would come in two versions—a smaller one with two of Apple’s planned M8 Ultra chips clustered together, and a bigger one with four M8 Ultra chips.

Apple has considered connecting the M8 chips in the server using an Nvidia set of products called NVLink Fusion, which includes switches, chiplets and software that help chips communicate with each other in data centers.

Apple is said to have been working on the project for around a year, with CEO John Ternus in favor.

9to5Mac’s Take

While 2029 is some way off, and the report acknowledges that the project could be canceled before then, it does make a great deal of sense. People are already using clusters of Mac Studios to run AI models locally, so it seems clear there would be a market for more powerful Apple servers. The only question is whether this is a big enough priority for Apple to say yes to launching it.

title: iOS 27.2 lets developers use an alternative App Tracking Transparency prompt in the EU
snippet: Starting with iOS 27.2, developers will have the option to use an alternative App Tracking Transparency system prompt in the EU, as part of Apple’s recent deal with the bloc. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Starting with iOS 27.2, developers will have the option to use an alternative App Tracking Transparency system prompt in the EU, as part of Apple’s recent deal with the bloc. Here are the details.

New prompt is mandatory in select European countries

A few weeks ago, Apple confirmed it would comply with “fairer” App Tracking Transparency rules in the EU, following an investigation by Germany’s Federal Cartel Office.

The deal concluded a years-long antitrust probe into whether Apple’s ATT rules unfairly disadvantaged third-party apps compared with its own services. Apple has always denied the allegations, claiming that it applies the same strict privacy principles to its own apps from the ground up. German regulators, however, remained unconvinced.

As a result, Apple agreed to eight changes in the ATT framework in Europe, and you can read more about that here.

That said, Apple confirmed today that iOS 27 will let developers choose whether they want to “use an alternative version of the App Tracking Transparency system prompt in the EU,” and added that “due to legal requirements, only the alternative version of the system prompt is available for apps distributed in Germany, France, Italy, Poland, and Romania.”

In an update to the “User privacy and data use” developer support page, Apple elaborates on the alternative version of this system prompt:

The alternative version of the App Tracking Transparency system prompt has modified formatting and language and provides you the option to use a text button labeled “Additional Information.” This allows you to surface additional information about your request to link user or device data collected from your app with user or device data collected from other companies’ apps, websites, or offline properties for targeted advertising or advertising measurement purposes, or to share user or device data with a data broker.

The company adds that EU developers will also be able to re-prompt users one year after their previous ATT choice, regardless of whether they initially accepted or declined tracking.

title: OmniFocus adds Siri AI support as Omni Group updates its apps for iOS 27, macOS 27, more
snippet: Unsurprisingly, the Omni Group worked all summer to get its suite of apps ready for Apple’s 2027 system updates from day one. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
Unsurprisingly, the Omni Group worked all summer to get its suite of apps ready for Apple’s 2027 system updates from day one. Here’s what’s new.

OmniGroup updates its suite of apps for Apple’s 2027 system releases

As the Omni Group’s CEO, Ken Case shared in a fun blog post titled “Hey Siri, We’re Ready!” the teams behind OmniGraffle, OmniOutliner, OmniPlan, and OmniFocus worked hard to get all of the company’s apps “ready for all of Apple’s platform updates, compatible universally across the board.”

Here’s Case:

This is no small juggling act, with OmniGraffle supporting three platforms, OmniOutliner and OmniPlan supporting four platforms, and OmniFocus supporting five platforms—especially while we’re simultaneously pushing forward on new major features of our own for each product.

Chief among the updates is OmniFocus 4.9, which is fully compatible with macOS 27 Golden Gate, iOS 27, iPadOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27. That includes Siri AI support, optional Apple Intelligence-powered date parsing, “a range of new and updated App Intents exposed as Shortcuts actions,” and design refinements to better match Apple’s 2027 system updates.

OmniFocus users can now ask Siri to assign and edit due dates, flags, notes, and even repeat schedules. The app can also take advantage of broader Siri AI capabilities, such as onscreen awareness and Visual Intelligence, to help users get things into OmniFocus more quickly:

For example, you can pick up a note with hand-written action items and ask Siri to add those items to OmniFocus. Or you can take a picture of a whiteboard and ask Siri to do things with that input.

Siri AI can now also leverage the user’s personal context, which in practice means it can answer questions based on the user’s OmniFocus database, summarize actions, suggest items to work on, turn follow-up items from meeting notes into reminders, and more.

Other tidbits from the Omni Group’s round of updates this week include:

OmniOutliner 6.3 has also been updated with Liquid Glass refinements across Apple’s platforms.

OmniFocus and OmniOutliner now include a new API that lets users and tools search the Omni Automation API, which should make it easier to pull up the documentation needed to write scripts.

The Omni Group says that work is also part of its effort toward implementing the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

Finally, Case also noted that, following last week’s iPhone Duo announcement, the team is already working to get its apps ready for the foldable’s launch.

title: iOS 27.2’s First Developer Beta Brings These Features to Some iPhones
snippet: The developer beta includes updates to apps like Facetime and Podcasts.
fullText:
Just two days after Apple released iOS 27 to the general public, the tech giant released the first developer beta for iOS 27.2. While iOS 27 brought Siri AI and more to your device, this early look at iOS 27.2 shows Siri AI expanding to other languages and a few upgrades in other apps, like Facetime.

If you’re wondering what happened to iOS 27.1, Apple has said the foldable iPhone Duo will launch on 27.1 next month, and all devices will be able to update to 27.2 sometime later.

Since this is a beta, I recommend downloading it only on something other than your primary device. This isn’t the final version of iOS 27.2, so the update might be buggy and battery life may be short — it’s best to keep those troubles on a secondary device.

Also, since this isn’t the final version, more features could end up landing on your iPhone when Apple releases iOS 27.2. 

Here are some features developers can try now in the first iOS 27.2 developer beta.

Siri AI in more languages

In iOS 27, Siri AI is only available in English. But the first developer beta of iOS 27.2 expands Siri AI to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish.

Apple previously said Siri AI would expand to these additional languages, so this shows the company moving quickly on that promise.

Use front and rear cameras simultaneously in Facetime

In the first developer beta of iOS 27.2, you can use your front and rear facing cameras at the same time in Facetime calls. This allows you to Facetime call with a larger group of people — you don’t have to squeeze everyone into a single frame in order to see the person on the other end of the call. However, everyone on the call needs to be on iOS 27 or later for this feature to work.

Refreshed Podcasts options

The Podcasts app also gets an update in the first iOS 27.2 developer beta. The beta introduces two rows to the top of the Home tab within the app: New Episodes and Continue Playing. This can help you keep track of what podcasts are new and what podcasts you still have to finish. 

It’s a small, pleasant addition to the interface, and I appreciate how it helps keep my podcasts organized.

Apple TV profile expansion

In the first developer beta of iOS 27.2, you can create TV Profiles in your Apple TV app. You can assign a profile to your child or someone else and ensure your preferences aren’t messed with. 

So if you’re tired of being recommended kids shows after letting your child watch the series Shape Island, you can create a profile for your child and let them watch those quirky little shapes all they want. (But also, it’s possible that I like Shape Island more than my son does, so you should check it out.)

Apple TV multiview on iOS

Another Apple TV update in the iOS 27.2 developer beta is Multiview. Developers who subscribe to Apple TV can watch up to four live sports streams, including streams from Major League Soccer and Formula 1, at once. That way, you don’t miss an important game, or you can look at a map of the racecourse while watching feeds from driver-view cameras.

Updated Health app

Developers can see a redesigned Health app in the first developer beta of iOS 27.2. However, the redesign is expected to launch sometime later this year, despite being featured in this beta.

Those are a few of the new features developers can try now with the first developer beta of iOS 27.2. There will likely be more betas before the OS is released to the public. Apple has not said when exactly it will release iOS 27.2 to the general public, but we expect it to land on devices in October.

For more, here’s what to know about iOS 27 and why your battery might be draining faster after updating. You can also check out why the iPhone Duo will launch with iOS 27.1.

title: SwiftKey ‘AI voice’ is Pixel 11’s Rambler voice-to-text for other Android phones, works offline
snippet: Rambler in Gboard is perhaps one of the best Pixel 11 features, delivering powerful voice-to-text backed up by AI models. Once you’ve used it, it’s hard to switch back to anything else, but the Microsoft-owned SwiftKey is testing out a new “AI voice” feature that brings the core functionality of Pixel 11’s Rambler to basically any other Android phone. more…
fullText:
Rambler in Gboard is perhaps one of the best Pixel 11 features, delivering powerful voice-to-text backed up by AI models. Once you’ve used it, it’s hard to switch back to anything else, but the Microsoft-owned SwiftKey is testing out a new “AI voice” feature that brings the core functionality of Pixel 11’s Rambler to basically any other Android phone.

Available in the latest SwiftKey for Android beta release (v9.13.16.4), “AI voice” is an enhanced voice-to-text feature that allows you to speak and then let the AI step in to clean up filler words, format text, and more. In other words, it’s Pixel 11 Rambler, just without the exclusivity.

You tap a microphone icon to get started, with no live preview showing (the one thing we don’t love about Rambler) and a checkmark button ending the session, leaving the AI to process the result. 

Android Central notes that you’ll need to download an offline language model for “AI voice” to work, which is one big difference – it works offline, no servers required. The publication says that testing the feature on a Fold 8 required only 163MB of storage and worked with the device fully offline, something you can’t do with Rambler on the Pixel 11 series. Droid-Life also tested it out, finding that you can’t use voice commands to edit the test as Rambler allows, but it gets the job done.

	

While it initially seemed like Rambler might not be a Pixel exclusive, that’s where we’re at right now, so “AI voice” in SwiftKey is probably a good alternative for many. Wispr Flow is also available, as we previously covered, though its lack of keyboard integration can be a bit annoying at times.

You can download the SwiftKey for Android beta through the Play Store.

Available in the latest SwiftKey for Android beta release (v9.13.16.4), “AI voice” is an enhanced voice-to-text feature that allows you to speak and then let the AI step in to clean up filler words, format text, and more. In other words, it’s Pixel 11 Rambler, just without the exclusivity.

title: Gentler Streak and The Outsiders’ iOS 27 updates add Siri AI, onscreen awareness support, more
snippet: The unstoppable team at Gentler Stories is out today with updates to both of its exercise-tracking apps, taking advantage of the new Siri AI and other capabilities introduced with iOS 27. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
The unstoppable team at Gentler Stories is out today with updates to both of its exercise-tracking apps, taking advantage of the new Siri AI and other capabilities introduced with iOS 27. Here are the details.

Gentler Streak and The Outsiders get iOS 27 updates

Gentler Streak is without a doubt the app I’ve used most to track my performance, exercises, and especially recovery since I took up running and working out a few years ago.

Since joining 9to5Mac, I’ve had the opportunity of getting to know the people behind Gentler Stories, and it quickly became clear why Gentler Streak and its younger sibling, The Outsiders, are among the best fitness apps out there. The amount of love and care that goes into both apps is inspiring, and it quickly shows when you use them.

So it came as no surprise that both apps were updated today, allowing users to take advantage of some of the new features introduced with iOS 27 from day one.

With iOS 27 now available, Gentler Streak 5.13 and The Outsiders 1.8 can take advantage of the new App Intents capabilities, letting users ask the new Siri AI for health and fitness information from either app without having to open it first.

Additionally, both apps now support Siri’s new onscreen awareness capabilities, allowing the assistant to understand what users are looking at in the app and provide additional context about things like workout summaries, health charts, and other training data.

Here’s Gentler Stories’ CEO Katarina Lotrič on today’s updates:

Ask Siri for your daily health and fitness update (no need to open the app): check your training and health stats by asking Siri a question related to your health and fitness. Always make sure to include the app’s name to your prompt.

Gentler Streak: You can ask about today’s workouts, activity status, Go Gentler daily workout suggestions, daily body metrics, or last night’s sleep. (e.g., “Show today’s workouts in Gentler Streak”)

The Outsiders: You can ask about your training readiness, today’s workouts, daily body metrics, or last night’s sleep data. (e.g., “Training Readiness in The Outsiders?”)

Ask Siri for more context (when in the app): Open either of our two apps, go to a workout summary, a health chart, or a feature that’s unclear, and ask Siri to explain what’s on your screen. On-screen awareness turns Siri into an always available guide that can help you understand the app and your training better.

The update also introduces a new on-device, AI-powered workout title suggestion feature, which offers more descriptive names for recorded workouts while still letting users choose their own.

They also include a refreshed set of app icons, which, alongside the app’s own interfaces, further adopt the Liquid Glass look on both Gentler Streak and the Outsiders.

Finally, both apps now “automatically adjust to fit any screen size or position,” making them iPhone Duo-ready and better adapting to different iPad window sizes.

To learn more about Gentler Streak and The Outsiders, follow this link.

title: The Apple Watch Series 12 is the start of a new wearable era
snippet: This time, heart rate monitoring is truly continuous. You wouldn't know that the Apple Watch Series 12 is a big deal just by looking at it. It has the same design, buttons, sizes, and sensor types as generations of Apple Watches before it. But under the hood, the Series 12 builds in major changes that lay the groundwork for big ideas about the future of health and wearables. These ideas - and this year's updates - can be divided into two parts: catching up to the recent boom in AI health and leading the way in AI wearables that surface helpful information based on your entire day. When it comes to the former, Apple is catching up to the rest of the wearable space, which has eagerly embraced AI … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
You wouldn’t know that the Apple Watch Series 12 is a big deal just by looking at it. It has the same design, buttons, sizes, and sensor types as generations of Apple Watches before it. But under the hood, the Series 12 builds in major changes that lay the groundwork for big ideas about the future of health and wearables.

These ideas — and this year’s updates — can be divided into two parts: catching up to the recent boom in AI health and leading the way in AI wearables that surface helpful information based on your entire day. When it comes to the former, Apple is catching up to the rest of the wearable space, which has eagerly embraced AI as a way to make sense of all your health data. With the latter, Apple is potentially kicking the door down on what’s been a niche, nascent, and recently problematic market. (Either way you slice it, AI is part of the equation.) Most of the ideas explored with the Series 12 aren’t novel, but they haven’t been implemented by a company with Apple’s scale or reputation.

8

Verge Score

$399

The Good

Faster charging

Redesigned sensor array 

Ceramic is back

Thoughtful privacy structure for Audio Intelligence

Siri on the wrist is more useful

The Bad

Thoughtful privacy may not change how laypeople feel

Many of the new features aren’t available at launch

After a week with the Series 12, I can’t say I have a complete picture. Several of the most interesting health and AI features aren’t launching until later this year and weren’t available for review. But even without them, the revamped internals provide some meaningful upgrades. So for now, this is a look at the health features that’ll be available at launch — and a preview of the wild AI ideas to come.

New hardware

Two key hardware updates separate the Series 12 (and the Ultra 4) from previous Apple Watches. The first is the new S11 chip, which features a secure exclave for microphone data processing on top of a faster CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine. There’s also a completely redesigned health sensor array. This new array doesn’t necessarily capture new data, but it enables the watch to measure health metrics in a more frequent, accurate, and power-efficient way. The electrodes that enable the EKG feature are larger to ensure better skin contact, the photodiodes have been reconfigured to capture reflected light more efficiently, and larger, less power-hungry optical LEDs are in place to shine light into the skin.

This is a significant hardware redesign compared to previous Apple Watches.

Together, these hardware upgrades enable a host of new software features, including more frequent heart rate sampling, a new readiness score, and a brave new world of Audio Intelligence, which is what Apple is calling its upcoming suite of AI-powered ambient listening features.

Most notably, the redesigned sensors mean the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are now capable of truly continuous heart rate monitoring. Previously, to preserve charge, Apple Watches only sampled heart rate once every five minutes when you weren’t working out. Now, the Series 12 measures heart rate every five seconds, both at rest and during activities. Other wearable companies have been able to do this for ages, but this is a genuinely helpful update for folks who might need to monitor heart rate due to chronic illnesses.

Siri AI is more front and center in watchOS 27.

Apple put out a white paper comparing how accurate its continuous heart rate monitoring is to a gold-standard Polar H10 chest strap, as well as competitors like the Pixel Watch 4, Samsung Galaxy Watch 8, Oura Ring 5, and Whoop across several types of workouts and at rest. (It’s an interesting read for wearable nerds!) I’d need roughly eight arms and legs to replicate this study in a week, and alas, I’m not an octopus. However, I did wear an H10 chest strap during two runs (one steady state and one interval run), a walk, and while at rest. At all times, the Series 12 was within five beats per minute of the H10. There was a slight lag compared to the H10, but in regular use, you’re not going to notice that four-second difference.

I’ll continue testing the Series 12 and Ultra 4 against other devices and across activity types, but I’m pretty confident the Apple Watch is now in line with many other popular wearables.

The S11’s impact was also noticeable in testing. Siri AI queries are faster on the Series 12 than my Ultra 3. You still might run into latency as Siri “thinks,” but not as much. If you want more in-depth thoughts about Siri on the wrist, my opinion hasn’t changed from my watchOS 27 preview. In a nutshell, this is the most capable wrist computer Apple’s made, and adding a single pinch gesture to select items makes one-handed control the best it’s ever been.

I didn’t notice a negative impact to battery life from continuous heart rate tracking. People will gripe that the Series 12 doesn’t have multi-day battery and sticks to the Series 11’s 24-hour battery estimate. But like last year, I maintain that faster charging is a fine enough solution. In a 20-minute charging test, I went from 20 to 64 percent battery. Yes, that does mean charging daily in little spurts, but I’ve yet to have the watch die on me. I vehemently believe everyone needs to let their wrists breathe daily, and showering is the perfect time to go watchless. You’ll survive 20 to 30 minutes of no data.

Are you ready?

All this new hardware paves the way for a much more robust health tracking experience. That’s probably why, later this fall, we’re getting a new, redesigned Health app. From the demos I’ve seen, it’s going to be a dramatic change. There’ll be AI-powered insights, a longevity tab that includes a Health Age score, VO2 max assessment tests using your phone’s camera, and even the ability to order a blood panel through Quest Diagnostics for $119. The redesigned app is currently available in the latest iOS 27 developer beta, and I’ll give my early impressions on that soon. However, in this review I’m only going to talk about what’s available to everyone at launch.

The big update ready today is Apple’s take on a readiness score. Readiness scores were popularized ages ago by Fitbit, Oura, and Whoop and are meant to be a digestible gauge of how well you’ve recovered from physiological stress. In essence, how “ready” you are to work out again.

It takes seven days to populate the readiness score, but the Vitals app now includes extra information about your overnight vitals.

Apple assesses “readiness” through a combination of overnight, daytime, and weekly metrics like activity, sleep score, and overnight vitals encompassing resting heart rate, respiratory rate, wrist temperature, and a new metric called recovery heart rate variability (HRV). You might think — wait, my Apple Watch has been able to measure HRV for years. You’d be correct. This new recovery HRV metric uses a different formula and is enabled by the fact that the watch’s updated sensor array can now take any HRV measurement much more frequently. Whereas “regular” HRV is meant to be a longitudinal look at your overall stress and cardiovascular health, Apple uses recovery HRV as a gauge of your daily, short-term strain. (And because this is enabled by the new array, it does mean readiness requires at least a Series 12 or Ultra 4.)

It takes a hot minute to generate the score — seven nights of sleep in which you get at least four hours of rest. On the eighth day, you wake up with a score from 0 to 10. A 0 to 1 means you should recover, a 2 to 4 means “pace yourself,” 5 to 7 is a benign “ready,” and anything 8 and above is a signal to “go for it.” My week of serious sleeping and accuracy testing culminated in a readiness score of 7.

Radiant gold up top, dark bronze on the bottom.

I’m of the opinion that people intuitively know whether they feel like working out or not. This is a feature that’s most useful for stubborn athletes who overtrain and need a reminder to not burn themselves out. I appreciate this isn’t a static score. A powerful nap or an extra hard workout could cause your readiness score to rise or fall during the day. For the Garmin nerds, I’d say it’s like a combination of Body Battery (which estimates your energy levels in real time) and traditional readiness scores. Given that wearable companies keep pumping out new metrics, I appreciate that Apple’s chosen to consolidate what could’ve been multiple data points into one.

After WWDC, I wrote that I was relieved Apple wasn’t diving full-on into AI health coaching features. I have to eat my words a teeny bit, considering Apple is clearly starting to incorporate some — though not all — of the AI health trends I’ve seen cropping up over the past two years. So far, I think Apple is carefully weighing what trends to hop on and which ones to avoid. That’s a smart long-term move. But I’m still relieved Siri AI isn’t playing a larger part just yet.

Audio Intelligence, part one

Aside from faster, more power-efficient performance, the S11 chip also enables the most surprising update to the Series 12: ambient listening. That ability is what enables Audio Intelligence, a suite of four features that essentially turn the microphone into a potentially powerful AI tool.

The two flashiest features are Live Rewind and Siri Recap. The former lets you read a short transcript on your wrist of the past 15 seconds, while the latter is a high-level summary of conversations you’ve had during the day. In this summer of public backlash against so-called pervert glasses and Flock cameras, these two features understandably stirred up a lot of concern and emotion on social media. That said, I wasn’t able to test these features because they’re not available yet. They’ll arrive later this year via a software update.

What was available to test was faster Shazam for identifying songs and sound recognition for alerting you of potentially urgent nearby noises. Both of these features require you to opt in and are not turned on by default. If you do turn on music detection, it is extremely fast. You can just pinchy pinch to bring up the Smart Stack, AI will surface the Shazam widget, and boom — there’s the song, correctly identified. (I did trip it up a teensy bit by rapidly switching between songs, but that’s not likely to happen in an organic Shazam experience.)

The improved Shazam works in the Smart Stack. Here, Shazam is battling against ambient noise from a helicopter. Shazam did not win.

Testing sound recognition, which is an accessibility feature for the deaf or hard of hearing, was less conclusive. It’s designed to flag on the wrist when sounds like doorbells, alarms, or sirens go off. Ironically, I haven’t had my doorbell ring this past week, but I did pull up several YouTube videos of doorbell chimes at various volumes. None triggered the feature. I think that’s a good thing. In my previous tests with other ambient listening AI wearables, they struggled to distinguish between “real” sounds and TV shows. The last thing you want is a fictional doorbell triggering an annoying, real-life alert. A blaring truck horn also didn’t trigger the feature, as it wasn’t a siren. I’ve asked Apple whether there’s specific tuning to minimize false positives, but I haven’t heard back yet.

I’ll do a deeper dive into Audio Intelligence once the whole suite of features is available. But to me, it’s clear that Apple has been taking notes about the burgeoning AI wearable space. It’s a deliberate choice to introduce these features on the Apple Watch, an already familiar and beloved device. As other tech companies deal with surveillance and harassment concerns, Apple’s published a privacy white paper and support documents to position itself as a leader trying to set a new standard. If successful with the public, it’s not a stretch to see how Apple might include these kinds of features on a pair of smart glasses or, perhaps, AirPods with camera sensors. If not, it’s no big miss. The Apple Watch is already a useful, sometimes lifesaving device without Audio Intelligence.

The most interesting, and perhaps consequential, piece of this rollout is that it comes from Apple, a wildly successful tech company with the strongest privacy reputation in Silicon Valley. If it can’t make this category of device work, that certainly doesn’t bode well for AI wearables as a whole.

Testing the waters

In many ways, this is an incomplete Series 12 review. Judging solely on what’s available today, this is a straightforward hardware upgrade that closes the gap between Apple and the standout perks of more niche rivals like Whoop and Oura.

For those pondering upgrades, Apple has laid a strong foundation with its hardware for some ambitious features down the road. I’d understand if you have qualms about Audio Intelligence and privacy, and to those folks: I’ll remind you that last year’s models are still great, probably available on sale, and don’t come with as many privacy questions.

I’ll be back to test everything once it’s all available, but even now you can see where Apple is heading.

Otherwise, the Series 12 is a worthy upgrade if you’re sporting a Series 6 or earlier. Series 7 and 8 users should weigh how much they care about AI features versus their device’s current battery life, as watchOS 26 will continue to get security updates. Series 9 and later don’t need to upgrade unless, perhaps, they have a chronic illness that could benefit from the improved continuous heart rate monitoring. The excellent SE 3 remains my recommendation for smartwatch newbies who just want a basic fitness tracker. I’ll have an Ultra 4-specific review out soon, but I can already tell you that’s for folks who like big screens, better battery life, and aspire to the outdoor life.

If the Series 12 only had a new sensor array, updated Health app, and a more useful Siri on the wrist, that’d be a significant update and win on its own. But there’s a lot more here that’s going to change this product in some fundamental ways over the next few months. I have a feeling that Apple’s ambitions for the watch don’t end with health tracking.

Agree to Continue: Apple Watch Series 12

Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them, since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate.

You can only use the Apple Watch Series 12 with an iPhone. That means you’ll have already agreed to the iPhone’s terms of service and privacy agreements. Optional services, like Apple Pay, Apple Music, or Fitness Plus, will also come with their own agreements. Using the Health app also comes with its own terms and conditions. Audio Intelligence features are opt-in and are not turned on by default.

If you choose to enable cellular service, you’ll also have to agree to your carrier’s terms. I activated cellular on T-Mobile and was asked to agree to one mandatory agreement. If you add any third-party apps or integrations, you must also agree to those individual terms and privacy policies.

Specific to the Apple Watch, you must agree to the following:

Some features, like hypertension notifications, EKG, sleep apnea, or blood oxygen monitoring, may also require you to disclose your location data, as it depends on local regulatory clearances.

Final tally: One mandatory agreement plus any mandatory agreements for your iPhone. Several, several optional agreements.

Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

title: Apple releases iOS 27 with Siri AI and these new iPhone features
snippet: iOS 27 is officially here. After a summer of beta testing, the free software update has arrived for everyone. It brings Siri AI, new Apple Intelligence features, more control over Liquid Glass, and improvements throughout the system. Here’s what’s new, which iPhones support it, and how to update. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 is officially here. After a summer of beta testing, the free software update has arrived for everyone. It brings Siri AI, new Apple Intelligence features, more control over Liquid Glass, and improvements throughout the system. Here’s what’s new, which iPhones support it, and how to update.

How to install iOS 27

You can download iOS 27 by opening Settings → General → Software Update on your iPhone. Select the iOS 27 upgrade, then follow the onscreen instructions.

Before installing, back up your iPhone using iCloud or a computer. Apple also provides installation instructions if you need help.

You may need to swipe down on the page to reveal the iOS 27 update option.

Siri AI is the biggest new feature

With iOS 27, Apple introduces a more conversational assistant called Siri AI.

The new Siri can use personal context to find information across your messages, emails, photos, and other content.

It also understands onscreen information and supports more actions across apps. That means you can ask follow-up questions or request help with what you’re viewing.

A dedicated Siri app lets you revisit conversations and continue them across supported Apple devices. Meanwhile, Siri mode in Camera brings Visual Intelligence into the viewfinder so you can ask about things around you.

Write with Siri also helps you draft and revise text. In Messages and Mail, it can adapt to your writing style.

Which iPhones support Siri AI?

Siri AI and the new Apple Intelligence features require iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, or an iPhone 16 model or later. iPhone Air and iPhone Duo also support Siri AI.

Liquid Glass gets more controls

iOS 27 adds a slider in Settings that lets you adjust Liquid Glass from clear to fully tinted. Apple also refines app icons and the system’s appearance.

Performance is another focus. Apple reports faster app launches, quicker loading of newly captured photos, and faster AirDrop transfers in its testing. Search improvements also aim to make results more useful in Spotlight, Photos, and Mail.

Photos and Safari gain new AI tools

On supported iPhones, Photos adds several editing options:

Spatial Reframing: Adjust a photo’s composition by virtually changing the camera position.

Extend: Expand an image beyond its original edges.

Clean Up: Remove larger objects with improved results.

Safari also gains automatic tab grouping by topic. In addition, Notify Me can monitor a webpage for changes, such as a price drop or an item returning to stock.

More iOS 27 features worth trying

	

Apple also detail several practical additions:

AirPods Custom EQ: Adjust audio to suit your preferences.

Separate alarm and timer volume: Set independent volume levels for alarms and timers.

Expanded parental controls: Approve new websites with Ask to Browse, set app schedules, and manage daily time allowances.

Communication Safety updates: Extend protections to images and videos containing gore or violence.

Call Context: Surface relevant information, such as a reservation number, during supported business calls.

Accessibility improvements: Expand capabilities in VoiceOver, Magnifier, Accessibility Reader, and Voice Control.

Read Apple’s full release notes for the detailed breakdown.

Which iOS 27 feature are you trying first? Let us know in the comments.

title: Nintendo Urges Switch Owners to Update Their Firmware After Security Exploit Discovered
snippet: The problem does not affect the Nintendo Switch 2.
fullText:
Owners of the original Nintendo Switch should patch a security exploit immediately, especially if they use the game console in public. Nintendo announced the vulnerability on Sept. 10, shortly after the company released its latest 23.0.0 firmware update.

The vulnerability applies only to original Nintendo Switch owners who use the Send to Smartphone feature. This feature generates a QR code on the Switch that users can scan with a smartphone, letting them transfer game captures and screenshots directly to a phone. 

The exploit also affects people playing Super Mario Kart: Home Circuit on the physical cartridge, as the game uses a QR code to establish a wireless link with nearby players. 

Should someone else scan the QR code before you, they can connect their device to your Switch and use the connection to run unauthorized code on your Switch or steal information stored on the game console. Since your account information is stored on your Switch, that’s information you don’t want in the hands of someone else. 

A Nintendo representative did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.

The exploit does not affect the Nintendo Switch 2. 

How to fix the problem

The fix is simple. Nintendo released update 23.0.0 on Sept. 9, which fixes the exploit. It’s recorded as CVE-2026-82079, which is “a stock-based buffer overflow vulnerability” that lets attackers within wireless range execute code. It only affects the original Switch on firmware versions older than 23.0.0.

To update your Nintendo Switch, head to System Settings > System > System Update to apply the update. Follow any additional on-screen prompts to install the update. 

Nintendo says that those who can’t immediately update their firmware can avoid the issue by only using the Send to Smartphone feature at home, where attackers can’t see them, or by not playing Super Mario Kart: Home Circuit in public. The gaming giant also recommends not scanning any QR codes with any device that isn’t yours. 

People who only play games at home are protected from this exploit and don’t have to worry about it.

title: Al Gore says the real AI risk isn’t data centers
snippet: In an interview with TechCrunch, Al Gore suggested he isn't losing sleep over AI data center emissions — he's more worried about the AI industry's own warnings about where the technology is headed.
fullText:
Al Gore has spent more than two decades as one of the most recognizable voices in the climate movement, so when he talks about AI, it’s worth paying attention to what he considers truly scary. And it isn’t what has people protesting data centers in the streets.

In an interview with TechCrunch this week alongside Lila Preston, head of growth equity at their investment firm Generation Investment Management, Gore said emissions from AI data centers aren’t what should keep people up at night, despite the mounting opposition over their environmental impacts. What should concern people more, in his view, are the warnings coming from inside the AI industry itself, and he takes them seriously.  

It’s not a new position for Gore. This past May, for example, he described AI data centers to another outlet as a “cause for deep concern, but not panic,” and in our conversation this week, his central point about emissions was about scale.

“If you look at the emissions of all of the AI data centers put together, it’s only a fraction of the emissions from uncovered landfills in the world,” he said, adding that a comparable build-out is tied to something that gets far less attention: air conditioning.

It’s a valid observation (and one the AI labs should be using in their discussions with cities and states if they aren’t already). The International Energy Agency estimates that global air conditioning already consumes more electricity annually than the entire European Union, and with ownership still under 15% across the hottest, fastest-growing parts of the world, that demand is expected to triple by 2050, putting far more pressure on the grid than AI data centers over the same period.

Gore isn’t dismissive of concerns about how these data centers are being powered. “It is a matter of deep concern that some of the hyperscalers are jumping into new methane turbines,” he said.

But what worries him about methane turbines isn’t the AI workload driving demand so much as the prospect that building new gas plants to meet that demand locks in decades more of fossil fuel generation. 

“I much prefer those that are supplying their energy needs with renewables and batteries,” he continued, saying he expects more companies to move inexorably in that direction simply because renewables are increasingly the cheapest option available.

In fact, Gore thinks the public backlash at planning-commission meetings has less to do with carbon emissions than with anxiety over automation upending society in the not-too-distant future. 

“I think that part of the reason for the growing bipartisan opposition to data centers in so many parts of the U.S. is being driven by the underlying concerns about job losses and some of the other threats that experts inside OpenAI and inside Anthropic have been trying to alert the public to,” he said.

We also pressed Gore on the wave of warnings from AI industry leaders that has dominated headlines over the last week. Though President Trump and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang shared a laugh at their expense on Monday during a conference in Los Angeles (Trump suggested that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s public call to slow the pace of capability gains, quickly seconded by Sam Altman and Elon Musk, was a “hoax”), Gore said he takes the warnings at face value.

“I think we went through a phase where some cynically suspected that the apocalyptic warnings were some kind of bizarre marketing strategy. If that was ever the case, I don’t think it is now,” he said. “I do think that Dario Amodei is very sincere, and I think that Sam Altman and Elon Musk were sincere in seconding [Amodei’s] warning of a few days ago.” 

Gore being Gore (he often reaches for literature, Scripture, and pop philosophy to make a point), he invoked Maya Angelou’s well-known line: “When someone tells you who they are, believe them the first time.”

Part of what’s changed his calculus, he said, is recent, concrete behavior from AI systems themselves — pointing to “the recent example of models escaping confinement, collaborating secretly, covering their tracks, engaging in deceptive behavior,” and noting that Anthropic has said it stopped instances of Claude being used to help develop biological weapons in different countries. 

That said, Gore doesn’t treat AI risk and AI’s climate potential as being in opposition. He cited a recent study from economist Nicholas Stern of the London School of Economics projecting that AI applications aimed at efficiency and waste elimination could drive global emissions down by 6% to 9% per year starting next decade. 

If Gore’s focus was risk, Preston’s was where capital is already moving in response. She pointed to several fronts where the AI build-out itself is generating investable opportunities, not just consuming energy.

Among these, the firm is focused on opportunities to decouple compute from energy intensity at every layer of the stack, from the power supply down to green cement and green steel used in construction, storage optimization software, and database design. The firm is also focused on grid resilience and flexibility, as the mix of power sources grows more complex. Here, Preston noted, Generation has invested in Volue, a European company helping utilities pull more renewables into the grid, and Gridware, which places sensors on utility poles to monitor and help protect the grid from wildfire risk.

Gore tied the AI moment to a broader argument made in Generation’s 10th annual Sustainability Trends Report: This year marks the second time in four years the world has been “brutally reminded” that fossil fuels are a volatile source of energy, first with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and now with the disruption to the Strait of Hormuz.

But unlike past years, when Gore’s exasperation with the pace of the clean energy transition was obvious, he doesn’t see these events as a setback but instead as reasons for countries to embrace it at long last. 

Indeed, Gore noted that globally, clean energy investment now runs at roughly twice the level of fossil fuel investment. Of all new electricity generation capacity added worldwide last year, 86% came from renewables, and in the U.S. specifically, that figure was even higher, at 91%, “in spite of Donald Trump’s best efforts to slow it down,” he said.

China, in particular, received high marks from Gore, who, among other things, applauded Beijing for wanting to be measured on emissions reductions rather than improvements in carbon intensity.

Asked what’s changed more than he expected a decade into publishing this report, Gore immediately pointed to solar power. 

“For me personally, the scope and scale of the solar revolution is the breakout star of the sustainability transition,” he said. After observing that it’s at, or near, the cost floor for new electricity generation right now — roughly tied with wind and meaningfully cheaper than gas, coal, or nuclear — he closed with a line from a friend in Tennessee that had stuck with him:

“If God had intended us to have a limitless supply of cheap, clean energy, he — or she — would have put a fusion reactor in the sky,” Gore said with a chuckle. “The joke makes itself.”

Al Gore has spent more than two decades as one of the most recognizable voices in the climate movement, so when he talks about AI, it’s worth paying attention to what he considers truly scary. And it isn’t what has people protesting data centers in the streets.

In an interview with TechCrunch this week alongside Lila Preston, head of growth equity at their investment firm Generation Investment Management, Gore said emissions from AI data centers aren’t what should keep people up at night, despite the mounting opposition over their environmental impacts. What should concern people more, in his view, are the warnings coming from inside the AI industry itself, and he takes them seriously.

Meta’s camera-equipped smart glasses have proven more successful than other entrants into the market, but they have also deeply disturbed certain consumers who see them as invasive emblems of a dystopian surveillance society run amok. Now, as the company weathers complaints that it’s selling “pervert glasses,” it has reportedly decided to sell a pair that doesn’t come with integrated spy equipment.

The Information reports that Meta is developing a new smart glasses model, dubbed Luna, that, sans cameras, comes equipped with a convenient system to communicate with the company’s AI chatbot and Muse, its AI consumer agent. The glasses include six built-in microphones so users can communicate with the chatbot, as well as a button on the side of the glasses that, when pressed, activates the AI system.

Luna may be unveiled as soon as Meta Connect, Meta’s annual hardware/developer event happening in Menlo Park next week, the outlet notes.

TechCrunch reached out to Meta for more information. 

The smart glasses industry has grown over the past few years, with Meta positioned near the front of the pack of providers. However, concerns over usability, cost, and privacy have dogged the business, with many consumers still unsure of how, why, or if they should use the devices. Meta’s Reality Labs, which is responsible for developing its smart glasses line, is still losing a gargantuan amount of money, as its earnings report from April revealed.

title: Interest Rates Just Went Up. Here’s Why Consumer Tech Might Cost Even More
snippet: The Federal Reserve hiked interest rates. Now, if you want to finance a tech upgrade, you’ll pay more in interest.
fullText:
The Federal Reserve on Wednesday raised interest rates for the first time since 2023. For the average US household, that means the cost of borrowing money — whether through a loan, a mortgage or a credit card — is about to become more expensive. But that’s just the first layer of the onion: The cost of everything, from rent and groceries to household devices and electronics, has already been climbing steadily over the last 18 months. 

The Fed’s policy move is intended to cool inflation: One of the central bank’s primary objectives is to promote price stability and keep inflation growth at 2% year over year. 

But even after the Fed carried out a series of aggressive interest rate hikes between 2022 and 2023 to control record-high inflation after the COVID pandemic, prices didn’t return to normal. Inflation is the speed at which prices are rising, not the actual sticker price you pay. So if inflation were to fall from 3.4% (the current rate) to 2%, prices would still be rising, albeit more slowly. 

Getting inflation down won’t actually lower prices, said Kathryn Anne Edwards, an independent economist and policy consultant. The higher price level is already out of the bag. What’s hurting is the cumulative increase in prices over several years, and that won’t be resolved anytime soon, she told CNET by email. 

There’s also policy inflation, i.e., the increase in prices caused by the Trump administration’s tariffs and trade policy, war in Iran, fiscal stimulus and other factors. “Unless inflation can drop quickly now, we are likely in for a long haul of small rate increases,” Edwards said. 

The AI tax is hurting us all 

A big reason gadget prices are rising is the AI boom. Data centers that power AI services are gobbling up memory chips, storage and electricity, which pushes up costs for everyone else. Apple recently hiked prices on its devices (including its new phones), as did Samsung, Amazon and other tech and gaming companies. 

Higher interest rates make that worse. When the Fed raises rates, credit card APRs, store cards and buy-now-pay-later plans tend to go up too, so the monthly payment on a $1,200 laptop or a $600 phone ends up costing more over time. Retailers and device makers also borrow to stock inventory and fund production, so as financing costs rise, they have less room to offer discounts or promotions, keeping sticker prices elevated. 

Senior Economics Writer Jeff Horwich of the Minneapolis Fed wrote in a recent article that AI is “moderately heating up today’s economy,” exerting upward pressure on inflation and interest rates through two main channels. The first is a near-term demand shock amid rising supply chain costs for key AI inputs like electricity, metals and computer components. The other is the “wealth effect,” in which soaring AI-driven stock market gains drive consumer spending among the wealthiest households. 

Horwich’s article also pointed to the counterargument that AI could eventually make things cheaper by raising productivity. But he noted that the Fed’s own economists say those benefits are years away and “not yet meaningfully apparent at a macroeconomic level.”

In the near term, if you’re upgrading a work-from-home setup, buying a back-to-school laptop or financing a holiday gadget, you’re likely to see higher prices and higher interest charges — two headwinds hitting all of us, all at once.

title: The 2.5-hour AI-generated Odyssey movie is 2.5 hours too long
snippet: Christopher Nolan's engrossing take on The Odyssey dominated at the box office and spurred a newfound interest in classic literature among filmgoers. But a new retelling of the story made entirely with AI is so bad that it might just make viewers hate the original tale altogether.
