fullText:
Christopher Nolan’s engrossing take on The Odyssey dominated at the box office and spurred a newfound interest in classic literature among filmgoers. But a new retelling of the story made entirely with AI is so bad that it might just make viewers hate the original tale altogether.

The new film, called Odysseus: The Fall, comes via AI firm Fountain 0 and is written and directed by company cofounder Ash Koosha, who also lent his likeness to the title character and created all of the music. (The film’s credits are very short.) The studio’s only previous work is an AI film called Dreams of Violets that made it into Tribeca earlier this year. The Fall is, on its face, a much more ambitious project, billed as “the first completely AI generated film produced at the level of a Hollywood blockbuster.” In reality, it’s nothing close to “the level of a Hollywood blockbuster.” That may not necessarily be surprising, but after watching the entire 2.5-hour production I nonetheless found myself constantly surprised by just how much worse things could get. The Fall is the opposite of a glimpse at the future of AI filmmaking — it’ll make you wonder if there’s really any future in it at all.

The movie is available to rent now for $9.99 and, as far as I can tell, you can only watch it via a web browser. In order to view it on my living room TV I had to mirror the screen from my phone, which is not exactly IMAX in 70mm. Things didn’t get much better once I pressed play.

The Fall is plagued by two main issues. The first is consistency. The world of the film is constantly morphing, to the point that it’s incredibly distracting. The height of the cyclops that traps Odysseus and his men changes from shot to shot, waves move in the opposite direction of the wind, mouths don’t match the words spoken (and sometimes they move without producing a sound at all), and oars bend and twist as sailors row. In one scene a huge fleet of boats is racing through the ocean and one of them is inexplicably moving sideways. The AI-produced voice-overs can be incomprehensible, and at various points the names of both Odysseus and Zeus are pronounced wrong.

If it were just the odd hiccup it might be understandable, but there are so many faults in The Fall that it can be hard to focus on anything else. I watched the movie with my 13-year-old kid and it basically became a game of finding the weirdest mistakes. I noticed that a sword magically turned into a dagger, and then she one-upped me by spotting an alien carcass roasting over a spit. The Fall seems like a film designed to prove why script supervisors exist.

The thing is, while all of the AI-induced errors are distracting, they’re also the most entertaining part of the movie. There isn’t really much to distract from in The Fall because it is so dull. Because current AI models are really only capable of generating scenes that last a few seconds, the movie feels like a disjointed collection of moments from the odyssey that have been stitched together with little rhyme or reason. If you didn’t already know the story going into this, I don’t think you’d have any idea of what was going on, because the film explains very little. You don’t even learn about Penelope’s suitors until the movie is almost over.

I also can’t think of a single aspect of The Fall that feels improved because of AI. The “acting” is bafflingly bad, with characters pausing for seconds at a time for no apparent reason and bursts of laughter that jolt you out of nowhere. There’s no weight to the action, as if this takes place in a world where things like physics and gravity are suggestions rather than constants. Similarly, there aren’t any cool or impressive effects that wouldn’t be possible without the technology. The monsters look like shabby stop-motion creatures from the 1930s, which is all the weirder when they’re put beside the smooth, hyperreal human characters that AI spews out. It’s not just jarring, it’s boring and ugly.

Koosha claims that he adapted this story because he “always felt passionately about Homer’s epic tale since [he] originally read it years ago.” It seems much more likely that he’s trying to skate by on the hype and energy created by Nolan’s film, turning AI slop into a modern-day iteration of direct-to-video cash grabs. But this also puts the film at an incredible disadvantage from the very beginning, inviting comparisons to one of the most critically and commercially successful movies of the last few years, one that was especially beloved because of the director’s insistence on human craftsmanship. Nolan is someone who cares deeply about film, and his passion and enthusiasm is why stars want to work with him and viewers flock the theaters to see his movies.

The existence of The Fall, meanwhile, shows utter contempt for the medium, attempting to boil the work of hundreds of skilled workers into slop produced by a tiny team. It’s so terrible it’ll make you appreciate human-made art all the more.

title: iPhone Duo could be very hard to get at launch, per report
snippet: iPhone Duo pre-orders open next month, and a new analyst report indicates the device could be in even shorter supply at launch than expected. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
iPhone Duo pre-orders open next month, and a new analyst report indicates the device could be in even shorter supply at launch than expected. Here are the details.

‘Hinge constraints’ will reportedly limit iPhone Duo supply at launch

Following months of rumors about Apple’s first foldable iPhone, last week Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo.

Unlike the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, iPhone Duo won’t ship in the typical September timeframe. Instead, pre-orders will open Friday, October 16 ahead of the first deliveries October 23.

We’ve seen reports before saying that supply could be very constrained. And the latest update from analyst Jeff Pu adds further corroboration to that claim.

In a research note seen by 9to5Mac, Pu writes that iPhone Duo units shipped in 2026 are now expected to be only 6 million, down from his previous 7 million estimate.

The reason isn’t a lack of demand, but rather “hinge constraints” that are causing production slowdowns.

	

For context, Pu estimates 72 million iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max models will ship by the end of the year—about 12x the iPhone Duo estimate.

So if you’re hoping to get an iPhone Duo at launch, it might be quite the challenge despite having the highest-ever $1,999 starting price for an iPhone.

title: iOS 27 adds scam-prevention feature to iPhone, here’s how to enable it
snippet: iOS 27 introduces a new security feature called ‘Impersonation Risk Detection’ that helps protect you against scams, but it’s off by default. Here’s what the feature does, and how to enable it. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 introduces a new security feature called ‘Impersonation Risk Detection’ that helps protect you against scams, but it’s off by default. Here’s what the feature does, and how to enable it.

Impersonation Risk Detection in iOS 27 can detect suspicious activity in real time to prevent scams

Every day around the world, people get tricked into sharing sensitive information like bank details or other financial info with bad actors.

This commonly happens via text messages, emails, or phone calls to iPhone or Android devices. And while iOS has built-in tools like call and message screening, those tools can’t prevent a scam if you choose to take action on it.

But iOS 27 introduces a new level of scam-prevention with a security feature called ‘Impersonation Risk Detection.’

Here’s what it does, per Apple’s website:

Impersonation Risk Detection helps protect against active social engineering scams. In these scams, an attacker might pose as a bank, government agency, or someone you trust to pressure or guide you into making a payment or changing your account details. Traditional security measures like two-factor authentication can’t always detect this kind of scam. That’s because you’re taking the action, even though you’ve been tricked or pressured.

Impersonation Risk Detection analyzes information about your device and Apple Account to help detect signs of an active scam. Based on this analysis, it returns a risk level to the app. The app receives only the risk level, not the underlying information used to generate it. The app decides what to do next. For example, it might ask you to verify your identity, add a delay, or show a warning.

You can turn Impersonation Risk Detection on in iOS 27 by going to Settings ⇾ Privacy & Security ⇾ Impersonation Risk Detection then toggling on ‘Share with App Developers.’

Impersonation Risk Detection is only available in supported apps, and Apple hasn’t published a list of those apps at the moment. But once enabled, it provides the app with a “risk level” while omitting the underlying information driving it. Risk levels include:

Unknown: No evidence of suspicious activity was detected

Medium: Some signs of suspicious activity were detected

High: Significant signs of suspicious activity were detected

Once the app has this risk level, it decides what action to take. For example, it may prompt you to offer additional authentication, or show a warning message related to scams.

For more details on how the feature works using ‘Trust Insights,’ see our coverage here.

title: The new Boox e-ink devices get Android 16 out of the box, including Palma 3
snippet: Boox just announced three new e-ink devices on Android 16; the largest tablet is available now, but you’ll have to wait a little longer for the updated Palma 3. more…
fullText:
Boox just announced three new e-ink devices on Android 16; the largest tablet is available now, but you’ll have to wait a little longer for the updated Palma 3.

E-ink devices have taken off in the last couple of years for a couple of reasons. The main reasoning that comes to mind is the natural disconnect that comes from using an e-ink device instead of a traditional modern OLED smartphone or tablet. Another likely has something to do with the universal appeal of an e-reader or note-taking device that lets you access apps from the Google Play Store.

Boox announced three new additions to its lineup of Android e-ink devices:

Boox Note Air6 C

Boox Note Mini C

Boox Palma 3

All three will run Android 16 out of the box, which is notable because the latest public version of Android is only one generation ahead of that. It wouldn’t have been a surprise if these devices were still a generation or two behind that. Two could be considered tablets, while the Palma is a generational upgrade to the company’s beloved compact e-reader that looks like an Android phone, at first glance.

	

The Note Air6 C is the only model Boox says is available starting today. It’s the workhorse of the three, with a new internal processor and a reasonable 3,700mAh battery. The new processor boosts the Note Air6 C’s performance with features like Dual Notes that let you annotate two documents in split-screen mode.

Boox mentions the large Android tablet also has new AI features for transcripts and document scanning. But the real improvement might just be an upgraded refresh rate that increases performance by up to 40%. Refresh rates have always been a sore point for e-ink tablets, but it’s always come with the territory for a paper-like display.

The 10.3-inch tablet has a color display that works with the included Pen3 stylus. It also wouldn’t be a Boox tablet without a front-light with temperature controls for any-time viewing.

The Note Mini C isn’t available to order just yet. It’s an 8.52-inch Android e-ink tablet aimed at users who need a little more portability from Boox devices. Similar to the Note Air6 C, it has a Kaleido 3 color e-ink display with a front light, as well as an octa-core processor. It has a little less battery power at 3,150mAh. On an e-ink tablet, that still goes a long way.

We’re also getting an upgraded model in the Palma series with the Palma 3. The form factor has grown more popular since Boox began teasing the Picco. The Palma 3 is slightly bigger and has a 6.13-inch display.

This version has a “refined anodized aluminum frame” instead of the plastic exterior seen on the previous models. The rear panel is made from fiberglass that has a “paper-textured” feel. Under that panel sits a 3,950mAh battery, which hasn’t changed from even the original Palma.

Boox hasn’t announced a release date for the Note Mini C or the Palma 3, but the Note Air6 C is available now. The Note Air6 C starts at $579. Boox’s Note Mini C is priced at $579, too, and the Palma 3 will be $339 at launch.

title: Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking powers Gemini Live, Gmail, & Keep
snippet: Google today announced Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking as its “most advanced live dialogue models yet.” more…
fullText:
Google today announced Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking as its “most advanced live dialogue models yet.”

Following the launch of 3.1 Flash Live in March, the new models aim to “make conversing with AI feel more intuitive and intelligent.” 

As the name suggests, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking offers “increased intelligence and multi-step reasoning.” It’s meant for high-complexity tasks like the recently launched Gmail Live (conversational search), Docs Live (draft generation and editing), and Keep Live (note creation). The model is also beginning to roll out to Gemini Live today.

3.8 Live Extended Thinking “reasons and speaks simultaneously.”

	

It delivers increased intelligence for complex workflows while maintaining an uninterrupted conversational flow — using early verbal cues like “Let me check that…” to acknowledge prompts naturally, and live progress narration to walk users through multi-step background tasks as they progress.

In terms of benchmarks: 

“…the #1 overall spot on Artificial Analysis’ Speech to Speech Quality Index (82.6)”

“…leads in agentic task completion with 68.6% on τ-Voice”

“…35.1% on Sierra’s τ-Voice-banking benchmark”

“…strong reasoning capabilities, scoring 97.7% on Big Bench Audio, while maintaining a highly competitive price point compared to other frontier models.”

Meanwhile, the Gemini 3.8 Live base model offers “conversational intelligence with fluid dialogue and visual grounding.” The model can process “visual inputs in near real-time,” with tools and API calls executing in the background while the conversation continues. 

Users can expect the model to “acknowledge requests and keep chatting while tasks finish in the background.” Additionally, it can detect and transition between 97 supported languages mid-conversation. 

It’s “built for scale and cost efficiency” with a “second place in the Speech Agent Arena.” Gemini 3.8 Live will power AI Mode’s Search Live experience.

title: iOS 27 gives Camera app on iPhone three powerful new features
snippet: iOS 27 brings powerful upgrades to the iPhone’s Camera app, especially for users who have AI-compatible models or the iPhone 18 Pro. Here’s what’s new for Camera in iOS 27. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 brings powerful upgrades to the iPhone’s Camera app, especially for users who have AI-compatible models or the iPhone 18 Pro. Here’s what’s new for Camera in iOS 27.

#1: Siri mode

iOS 27 adds a brand new ‘Siri’ mode to the Camera app on all AI-compatible iPhones. It requires enabling Siri AI support first.

Siri mode essentially brings the visual intelligence features previously tied to Camera Control directly into the iPhone’s full Camera app. But it adds to it new capabilities thanks to Siri AI.

You can use Siri mode to capture and take action on anything your iPhone sees. For example, you can snap an image of text in another language to quickly translate it, or capture an event flyer to add the details to your calendar, or get care instructions for a plant, nutritional info for food, and a lot more.

#2: Customizable controls

Apple has made the controls in each Camera app mode fully customizable in iOS 27.

When in modes like Photo, Video, Portrait, and more, you can open the controls panel by tapping the icon with six dots in the bottom-right. iOS 27 adds a new ‘Edit’ button to the top-left corner when viewing this panel.

After hitting ‘Edit,’ you’ll see options for additional controls and can tap to add them to your default controls at the top of the screen. It’s a great way to remove controls you never use, and make your favorites easier to access.

#3: iPhone 18 Pro exclusives: Pro controls, Photographic Styles 3, Apple Reference Mode

iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max users will get even more new Camera app features in iOS 27.

Pro controls is a new set of options that are iPhone 18 Pro-exclusive. They include:

lens aperture

shutter speed

white balance

histogram viewer

Photographic Styles have been upgraded for owners of the latest iPhones. ‘Photographic Styles 3’ adds new texture and grain controls so that users can further dial in their favorite looks.

Finally, Apple Reference Image lets you “capture, view, and share reference images, which are like digital negatives, so you can verify exactly what the camera originally captured.”

AirPlay improvements may sound like a minor change, but in practice they can make a big difference in connecting quicker than ever to your HomePod. Using the iOS 27 beta, I’ve been pleasantly surprised by how fast and easy it is now to switch playback to and from my iPhone and HomePod.

title: Iceland-based Treble raises $18 million for its voice simulation platform
snippet: Treble's voice simulation platform is used by voice AI model developers and AI wearable and robotics companies,
fullText:
Voice AI has emerged as one of the hottest sectors in AI, with investors pouring in billions of dollars to serve use cases ranging from automating customer support and sales calls to creating meeting notetakers and developing AI smart glasses that use voice as the primary interaction surface. 

Meanwhile, AI labs are quickly releasing models, and hardware makers are trying to create the best experience for consumers to interact with devices. 

All of this new technology needs testing and a feedback loop for improvement. An Iceland-based startup, Treble, is positioning itself to be at the center of the voice AI industry by creating a simulation platform that can cater to model makers, robotics companies, and consumer hardware makers.

The company, founded in 2020 by acoustic engineers Finnur Pind and Jesper Pedersen, has raised $18 million in an extension of its Series A funding led by Paladin Capital Group, with participation from existing investors KOMPAS VC, Frumtak Ventures, EIC, and Omega ehf. It received an investment of $12 million in 2024, bringing its total raise to date to over $40 million. The startup counts Amazon and Logitech as customers.

Treble co-founder Finnur Pind Image Credits:Treble

Treble has a few verticals related to simulation and data. For voice AI companies, it has a synthetic data generation platform that could be used for speech enhancement, noise suppression, and model training. It also evaluates voice AI models in different conditions to provide feedback to labs. Earlier this year, it partnered with Hugging Face to launch a benchmark for speech recognition models across different realistic conditions.

“Audio AI is really a data challenge, and this is where the most opportunities to enable next-generation models and hardware lie. To date, pretty much all sound-related AI has been made from recordings and data scraped from the internet. We believe that accurate physics simulation can be an alternative way to create data for sound,” Pind told TechCrunch. 

The startup also focuses on hardware design and testing from a voice perspective. For instance, it works with headphone and speaker companies for virtual prototyping to help them understand how their product might sound. It could also test how a smart speaker can understand commands based on the positioning of the speaker. Lately, Treble has ventured into providing simulation testing for smart glasses and AI devices.

Pind said that the company is excited to work on wearables that could enhance hearing for users. 

“I’m really excited about the next generation of these devices like headphones and smart glasses that can enable [a feature like] superhuman hearing. That’s an area where you can really just hear better in challenging acoustic environments. Maybe you are in a restaurant, and you only want to hear people within two meters of range, or you are in a seminar, and want to mute people around you,” he said.

Treble aims to increase its focus in the physical AI space, including robotics, automotive, and drone companies, to enable sound-based functions for them through testing and simulation.

Francois Ruether, VP of Paladin Capital Group, told TechCrunch that Treble’s platform, which simulates different models and devices, stands out; the platform’s importance will increase as it gets involved in more areas.

“Our thesis is that, as more products depend on understanding sound, this infrastructure becomes increasingly valuable across voice AI, wearables, robotics, and physical AI. Customers retain ownership of their models, products, and development workflows, while benefiting from a shared foundation of a simulation-native acoustic infrastructure layer,” Ruether said.

title: X will now let US users trade via Cashtags
snippet: The move closes the gap between the market discussions taking place on the timeline, and the market itself.
fullText:
X will now allow users to trade from their timelines. The Elon Musk-owned social network on Wednesday launched a feature called Cashtag that will let U.S. users on X place stock trades via participating brokerages. Initial partners in the effort include Interactive Brokers, Moomoo, Gemini, Kraken, and Coinbase.

The move takes advantage of what users on X have been doing for years: talking about stocks and, in more recent years, crypto. In 2008, the financial platform Stocktwits even came up with the idea for X-precursor Twitter’s Cashtags, which placed a dollar sign ($) in front of stock ticker symbols to make market conversations easy to find and reference.

However, those Cashtags were about tracking the conversations around a particular stock, not actually trading them. Now that X has moved into the financial space with X Money, that’s changed.

Now, Cashtags, which turn ticker symbols for stocks, ETFs, and cryptocurrencies into interactive destinations, will give X users the option to trade stocks.

“Cashtags close the gap between a ticker on the timeline and the market itself. When you post or tap a ticker, you’re taken right to the asset, where you have seamless access to the live chart, the conversation around it, and now the ability to trade with one of our brokerage partners,” said Mridul Singhai, X Product Engineering lead, in a statement shared with TechCrunch.

To use the new feature, users who tap on a supported Cashtag will be able to view the asset’s price chart and related posts on X. They can then tap “Trade” to continue at a participating brokerage. There, they’ll sign in and complete their trade. Users can also tap on a brokerage partner to reach their mobile app or website to log in to their existing account or sign up for a new one, X notes.

“With our Cashtag partners, we’re connecting the financial conversation to action. People come to X to discover what’s happening, shape the conversation, and act in real-time on what matters to them,” Monique Pintarelli, SpaceXAI’s head of Global Advertising, said in a statement. “Our Cashtag partners make it possible to move seamlessly from discovery and conversation to a brokerage, without breaking the moment.”

However, the feature could spur more market manipulation by the way of AI-controlled bots, spammers, and other bad actors, who could attempt to shift the conversation in one direction or another. But one could argue that this is already happening on X today, even without the direct connection to brokerages.

title: Noise wants to help everyday people become paid content creators
snippet: Marketing platform Noise is on a mission to help anyone with a smart phone make money from their content.
fullText:
Marketing platform Noise aims to connect brands with content creators at a much lower cost than hiring traditional influencers or running standard ad campaigns. 

That’s because many creators on the Noise platform are everyday people — anyone can download the app, regardless of follower count — and Noise presents them with campaigns they can join and create content for on their platforms of choice (TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, YouTube). It then pays them per view rather than a flat fee. Brands, meanwhile, sign up for Noise to share their content brief requests and budget. From there, Noise makes it easy to handle the rest, so brands can scale without the operational headaches of sourcing content creators, managing client relationships one by one, or managing payments. Noise lets them run campaigns simultaneously across thousands of content creators. 

On Wednesday, Noise announced a $5.5 million seed led by Capital Midwest, M25, and Grishin Robotics, bringing its total raise to $7.2 million. Others in the round include Capitalize VC and operators from companies like DoorDash.

The startup is tapping into the ever-expanding influencer market, in which 57% of young people and just a little over 40% of U.S. adults overall now want to take part. It joins other content creator infrastructure companies like Billo and JoinBrands.

Diego Kafie, Stu Feldt, and Nic Weber launched Noise in 2025 after spending two years building a mobile game app called Playbite, and it now touts 1.5 million creators on the platform. 

CEO Kafie said the company’s top creators make more than six figures a year, and the platform takes a fee from what brands pay creators once views are delivered.

“Our top brands work with several thousand creators on autopilot,” he said. Right now, many of its customers are mobile apps, those working with startup budgets that want to employ influencer marketers. The goal is to one day work with companies of all sizes.

“They are the most interested in reaching a really wide range of potential customers, making them the prime users for something like Noise, where they can easily recruit a small army of people to become their biggest users and advocates,” Kafie said. “This gives brands unprecedented level of content diversity and reach at a fraction of the cost of other traditional marketing playbooks.” 

Kafie, Feldt, and Weber came to this idea from their experiences at Playbite. “We tried a bunch of different creative marketing strategies,” Kafie said of how they tried to scale Playbite. For example, they attempted to recruit their own gamers and teach them how to create social content that promoted the app. “We started with five, ten, 25, then 100 people,” he continued. “Before we knew it, our installs were skyrocketing as this small army of people went to places like TikTok and posted engaging content daily about mobile games and our app specifically.”

Most importantly, he noted, this happened “at a fraction of the cost of traditional marketing playbooks,” because they were teaching regular people how to be content creators from scratch. “Had we gone to established creators with big followings and clout, their rates would’ve been cost-prohibitive for our scrappy startup budget.” 

That gave them the idea for Noise. The fresh capital will be used to expand product capabilities and to hire. Noise also just launched its Organic-to-Ads program, letting brands take the videos that Noise creators make and run them as paid ads on Meta and TikTok, in addition to the creators’ posts. 

“The creators still post to platforms,” he said. “But in addition, the brands can now put paid ads spend behind those creatives to reach more people.” 

He pushed back when asked if this was a way to pay creators less than they could make on their own if a brand approached them. He said that brands will name their rates and creators can decide whether to say yes or no. He also emphasized that the platform specializes in working with “everyday people and turning them into brand-new creators.”

It’s harder to become an influencer these days, so this, Kafie believes, could be a way for many people to get around the stress, time, and money it takes to make it big in content creation on their own. 

He said when a user first joins the platform, they take Noise creator training modules that teach them how to create content for brands. Those early creators can access only certain campaigns, but as they do more training and get hired for more work, higher-paid opportunities can come to them, Kafie said. 

“By democratizing ‘becoming a creator’ to literally anyone with a smartphone,” he said, “we’re bringing costs down for brands, but enabling millions of people to make their first dollar on the internet.”

fullText:
It’s iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate launch day, and Fantastical is here for it. The new version released today includes support for Apple’s major new operating systems. This includes Siri integration, a new widget size, and some nice Liquid Glass updates.

title: Comu’s Action Pro is a great meeting recorder that struggles to justify its AI premium
snippet: As my house becomes increasingly strewn with the detritus of parenting, I’ve made the inverse effort to eliminate excess, physical and digital, from my life. As much as it is about control, it’s also about mental health; I already use my phone too much, so adding yet another thing to the backpack, to the pocket, feels anything but additive. more…
fullText:
As my house becomes increasingly strewn with the detritus of parenting, I’ve made the inverse effort to eliminate excess, physical and digital, from my life. As much as it is about control, it’s also about mental health; I already use my phone too much, so adding yet another thing to the backpack, to the pocket, feels anything but additive.

But I’m also aware of the single-use gadget’s pull, increasingly powerful precisely because people are relying too much on their phones. Digicams to augment overly-processed smartphone photos. Writing tablets that feel like paper without the waste. Smart rings and health trackers to reduce notification overload.

And so it is with a product like the Comu Action Pro, a standalone note-taking gadget that attempts to turn a simple idea into something indispensable.

Pixel owners are likely well aware of the superlative built-in Recorder app that’s been around for years, adding features like real-time transcription and translation as it’s matured. The current app is about all you could want from a piece of software that leverages a phone’s built-in microphones.

	

It was with this framing that I undertook the review of a novel gadget category: the AI voice recorder. I’m not entirely unfamiliar with it: I’ve used early versions of Plaud’s NotePin and Note devices in the past, but never for long enough to feel acquainted with them. In response, I wanted to spend enough time with the Comu Action Pro to understand where and how it fits into my life, and why one may feel justified in spending the $180 it currently costs instead of just using the phone they already have in their pocket.

First, the basics: at a thickness of 7mm, it’s a svelte mixture of aluminum and plastic that’s designed to stick magnetically to the back of a compatible phone, like an iPhone or Pixel. (The box comes with a couple of circular magnetic stickers for devices without built-in MagSafe support.) That said, it’s nowhere close to the 3mm dimensions of the Plaud Note and Note Pro. But that additional girth comes with a few benefits: it fits a USB-C port, so you’re not forced to charge it with a proprietary magnetic cable that will almost certainly be missing when you need it most. And it carries a larger battery that pushes recording time to 70 hours, double that of the Plaud Note Pro.

The primary question I ask myself, and am asked by others, when I use the Comu Action Pro is, “Why?” Why do you need a separate piece of hardware when your phone will suffice, particularly in a world of inexpensive or free AI transcription services that can do most of the job? In short, it’s the passivity of it all; you can just leave the Action Pro running in the background whenever you’re going about your day to collect snippets of conversations, or covertly place it on a boardroom table to record a meeting.

The Action Pro has six far-field microphones that pick up voices from distances that phones are just not tuned for. That omnidirectional nature means the actual recordings sound thin and tinny, but the product is not the audio — it’s the data from the audio. Placing the Action Pro on the table in front of me next to my phone and recording the deliberately subdued tones of a conversation I was having showed the form factor’s inherent compromise; it picked up voices from the tables next to me, leading to audio that was basically unusable to listen to. Conversely, my Pixel 11 Pro did a great job isolating our two voices in the recording itself.

I was surprised, then, to discover the Action Pro transcribed our conversation with minimal errors. The company works with a number of AI vendors, including OpenAI and Google, and while it’s usually accurate, it made more errors than the competition.

It’s the “Action” in Comu’s Action Pro the company really wants to emphasize, and it’s what I believe has the largest potential — and the longest way to go to reach it. If you’ve ever used a cloud-based meeting recorder like Granola you’ll know that its primary job is to synthesize what it records into something compelling and useful, a summary that can lead to identifiable action items. From there you can ask it questions about the content or have it draft a follow-up email.

Comu’s Action Pro tries to go one step further by integrating with foundation models like Claude Opus 5 or GPT-5.6 Terra to turn those summaries into more than just emails; you can ask it to create a summary document or even a presentation, choosing from a number of predefined templates. All of this is done through the app, which is poorly designed, making for an awkward experience.

I’ll give you a small example: I had the Comu Action Pro record all 20 minutes of a YouTube video that was playing at a pretty comfortable volume from my Mac Mini’s thin but capable internal speaker. It was a video I watched doing research for this review, attempting to grasp the scope of the AI note taking market, since I’d really only ever heard of and used Plaud’s products.

As a baseline, I also used my Pixel 11 Pro’s Recorder app alongside a Plaud Note. All three were sitting four or so inches from the speaker and there was little ambient noise in the room. After the recording was finished, I compared the transcripts of each recorder for accuracy, and then delved into the post-production aspects of each product. For full transparency, here are links to both Comu’s and Plaud’s outputs from that recording:

Summaries are good on both, but Plaud’s are neater and better organized.

Plaud’s transcript is slightly more accurate.

Ironically, the Action Pro kept referring to Plaud as “Plot” throughout, though that can be traced to the word’s pronunciation by the host.

Plaud’s output included a mind map and a summary image, whereas Comu’s was text-only.

Comu’s custom documents and presentations are basic, hard to read, and rarely useful as standalone assets.

The Comu app is buggy and, in places, poorly translated into English.

The Comu web app is basically unusable in its current state.

The issue I keep returning to is that the Action Pro really only solves a real-world problem. While you can attach it to the back of the phone to record both sides of a conversation (with consent, of course), there’s no mechanism to record or sync web-based meetings. Plaud, being the more mature product, boasts a much better app, a usable web interface, and a desktop app that records and transcribes video calls, usage of which is included even in the free Starter plan.

Comu’s best features are also gated behind a subscription. Unlike Plaud, which provides access to most features for free but limits transcription minutes to 300 on the free Starter tier, Comulytic goes the other way, offering unlimited transcriptions indefinitely and putting its AI workflows, including translation and document generation, behind a $10/month paywall. Access to Anthropic’s Claude model is also limited to paid subscriptions.

Those are the actions meant to be solved by the dedicated AI button that sits above the record button which, when pressed, acts like a voice-powered agent for your work needs. Anything recorded when the button is pressed goes into a general ChatGPT-like stream, where the data source is the transcribed meeting notes. Unfortunately, that’s where the “Action” part of the Action Pro breaks down: the Comu agent is brittle, and doesn’t interface with other parts of the phone. 

For instance, there’s a “Schedule Tasks” prompt that Comu invites you to use, and tapping it pre-fills a number of templates, including “Schedule a deep work block for this week.” I completed the prompt and wrote “Schedule a deep work block for this Friday from 1 to 5 PM,” but at the moment the model isn’t able to connect to my external calendar. 

In fact, as of writing, every calendar- and task-based connection is listed as “Coming soon.” Once these connections are added, Comu’s offering may be more competitive, but given the proliferation of similar services like Gemini Spark, Meta Muse, Town, Poke, and many others, I’m doubtful that most users will be willing to shell out the monthly fee that Comu is asking for.

At its core, the Action Pro is a competent meeting transcriber with some impressive hardware and lackluster software that, at least right now, doesn’t justify its asking price. If you’re looking for something from the company that’s thinner, lighter, and cheaper, and still has some AI capabilities, Comu’s own Note Pro is a decent alternative at under $120. If you need something a bit more full-featured, including better web and desktop support, I’d go with something from Plaud.

					

A competent meeting recorder and digital note taker whose ambitions to be an AI project manager don’t quite work.

					

				

Pros

				

											

Great audio transcription quality

											

Good build quality

									

			

					

				

Cons

				

											

App is a mess

											

AI features are half-baked or missing entirely

											

AI features require a minimum $10/month subscription

title: Google confirms Pixel phones were exploited in ‘targeted’ attack related to modem
snippet: Google has confirmed that a “limited” number of Pixel phones were attacked by a vulnerability related to the modem on the device. more…
fullText:
Google has confirmed that a “limited” number of Pixel phones were attacked by a vulnerability related to the modem on the device.

As part of the September 2026 security update, Google patched over 200 security vulnerabilities, but specifically calls out that one of those was actively exploited in the wild.

Note: There are indications that CVE-2026-58704 may be under limited, targeted exploitation.

The issue is related to the modem, with a bypass that requires no user interaction. CVE-2026-58704 is described as follows:

In Cellular Modem, there is a possible permission bypass due to a logic error in the code. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

Exact details of how the vulnerability was exploited are unclear – as well as which models were affected – but CISA (via The Hacker News) says that it was exploited on Pixel phones, explaining that “Google Pixel devices contain an improper authorization vulnerability in the cellular modem.” Combined with Google’s announcement, this was used in the wild, apparently to hack “targeted” devices. CISA issued a notice that this is a “known exploited vulnerability,” explaining that “this type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.” TechCrunch notes that this is called a “zero-click” attack, adding that Google hadn’t replied to a request for comment around the vulnerability being exploited and who was exploiting it.

	

If you’re on a Pixel phone, updating to the September 2026 patch, rolling out now, fixes the issue.

title: Another Intel iMac has joined Apple’s vintage products list
snippet: After adding three MacBook models to its obsolete products list last month, Apple today updated its vintage products list to include the 2019 21.5-inch iMac with Retina 4K display. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
After adding three MacBook models to its obsolete products list last month, Apple today updated its vintage products list to include the 2019 21.5-inch iMac with Retina 4K display. Here are the details.

iMac (Retina 4K, 21.5-inch, 2019) now vintage worldwide

Apple maintains a list of vintage and obsolete products, which lets users know whether older devices are still eligible for hardware service and replacement parts.

The company considers a product vintage once it has been off the market for more than five but less than seven years. Products may become obsolete once Apple has stopped distributing them for more than seven years.

Apple doesn’t necessarily move products to the obsolete list as soon as they cross that threshold, as service and parts availability can vary by product. That said, once a product is classified as obsolete, Apple and its authorized service providers generally stop offering hardware service for it, and parts can no longer be ordered.

Today, the company added the iMac (Retina 4K, 21.5-inch, 2019) to its vintage products list, which means it may still be eligible for hardware service and replacement parts, but they’re subject to availability.

In practice, if you own this iMac and have been putting off a repair, it might be a good idea to get it serviced sooner rather than later.

title: Samsung Gallery is adding Google Photos backup to replace OneDrive
snippet: New updates are starting to roll out that will let Samsung Gallery replace its OneDrive integration with Google Photos support. more…
fullText:
New updates are starting to roll out that will let Samsung Gallery replace its OneDrive integration with Google Photos support.

Earlier this year, Samsung Gallery removed integration with OneDrive and, in turn, also removed native cloud backup for Galaxy users. Users could, of course, use apps from Microsoft, Google, Amazon, or any other number of providers, but there was nothing built into Samsung’s own Gallery app anymore.

Now, Samsung is confirming its replacement.

In an update to the “Gallery Cloud Sync” app on Samsung devices, the company says:

	

Gallery Cloud Sync is a service that safely backs up your precious memories to Google Cloud, allowing you to enjoy them seamlessly on all your devices at any time. View photos taken on your smartphone right away on your tablet.

Easy and secure backup: Safely store your Gallery photos, videos, and albums in the Cloud.

Seamless multi-device sync: No matter which device you use, your Gallery is always kept identical and up to date.

Google Cloud-based reliability: Provides a fast and stable environment through Google’s trusted cloud storage.

Edited for formatting

The mention of “Google Cloud” here is a bit misleading, as Samsung Gallery is adopting direct Google Photos integration, as shown by an early preview of this functionality by @WigettaGaming and SammyGuru writer “That Josh Guy” on Twitter/X. It’s not live just yet – at least in our testing – but Samsung Gallery will offer support for “Sync with Google,” including the ability to see available storage via the Gallery app, choosing which albums to sync, and what data conditions must be met to sync.

Samsung requires the “Gallery Cloud Sync” app and “Samsung Cloud” to both be updated, but it seems a Gallery app update or perhaps even a full system update will be required to get this working fully.

Google Photos integration like this has existed for a few years now, previously being added to the OnePlus Gallery app in 2024 and on devices from Xiaomi and select other brands. Google’s support page on the topic does not yet mention Samsung.

Samsung Gallery will still let existing OneDrive users sync their photos through September 30, but it’s great to see a replacement lined up.

title: Android Canary 2609 adds ‘Require unlock for Quick Settings’ on Pixel
snippet: Google today is rolling out Android Canary 2609 with another update to Quick Settings that lets you require an unlock before making changes. more…
fullText:
Google today is rolling out Android Canary 2609 with another update to Quick Settings that lets you require an unlock before making changes.

ZP11.260821.010 with the September 2026 security patch is available for the Pixel 10a, Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro XL, Pixel 10 Pro Fold, Pixel 9a, Pixel 9, Pixel 9 Pro, Pixel 9 Pro XL, Pixel 9 Pro Fold, Pixel 8a, Pixel 8, Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel 7a, Pixel 7 Pro, Pixel 7, Pixel 6a, Pixel Fold, and Pixel Tablet.

Google notes that “support for Pixel 11 devices will be added with the next Canary release. Additionally, Google has dropped support for the Pixel 6 and 6 Pro.

As always, “Canary builds are highly experimental and are NOT recommended for general use.”

	

Require unlock for Quick Settings

Go to Settings > Display & touch > Lock screen for the new “Require unlock for Quick Settings” toggle that is off by default: “To prevent unauthorized changes, you must unlock your device to use Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Mobile Data, and Airplane Mode.”

When enabled, you can still open the Quick Settings panel from the lockscreen, but tapping on those key Tiles will prompt you to fingerprint or PIN unlock. The flashlight, rotation, dark theme, etc. don’t require authorization.

Audio streams Quick Settings Tile

Additionally, the “Voice broadcast” Tile moves from system apps to Connectivity.

Notification Intelligence 

Appearing on older devices (Pixel 8) with just the existing Notification cooldown feature.

title: Spotify’s newest feature has been on my Apple Music wishlist for years
snippet: Today Spotify announced a feature every parent has probably asked for: the ability to exclude kids and family music from their algorithm. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Today Spotify announced a feature every parent has probably asked for: the ability to exclude kids and family music from their algorithm. Here are the details.

Parents can use new toggle so Spotify Wrapped and recommendations don’t include children’s music

A core feature of modern music streaming services is their ability to recommend music you’ll love.

But if you’re a parent, you know that children’s music has long been a blind spot for Spotify and Apple Music.

I have a toddler, so much of my Apple Music activity these days consists of Mickey Mouse Clubhouse and other children’s songs. Thus, my recommendations and Apple Music Replay are more tailored to my child than me.

But Spotify just launched the solution, and I really hope Apple follows suit soon. Per Spotify:

Starting today, we’re rolling out a new toggle in your settings that lets you exclude kids and family music from your taste profile, so those streams no longer shape your recommendations. This includes, for example, the songs you play on repeat from your kids’ favorite animated movies, theme songs from family TV shows, nursery rhymes, and more.

When you turn this setting off, you can still search for, listen to, and build playlists of kids and family music, but those streams won’t affect what Spotify suggests for you. That means experiences like Discover Weekly, Daily Mix, and Wrapped more accurately reflect your taste. And yes, it applies retroactively, so kids music you’ve already listened to won’t count toward your Wrapped top song or artist, for example.

I’m shocked at how long it took for a feature like this to arrive. But I’m thrilled that it’s finally here.

To use the new toggle, go to ‘Settings and privacy’ in the Spotify app, then ‘Content and display,’ and switch off the toggle labeled ‘Include kids and family music in taste profile.’

If you’re an Apple Music user, one alternative workaround is to use Focus modes to toggle listening history on and off. But I imagine most parents won’t have the mental bandwidth to remember to switch modes back and forth constantly, so it’s not a great solution.

How do you handle streaming children’s music as a parent? Let us know in the comments.

title: US automakers could soon be forced to include AM radio for free
snippet: The House of Representatives, in rare bipartisan support, overwhelmingly approved legislation that would require new vehicles to include AM radio.
fullText:
It turns out that the one thing that can apparently bridge Washington’s partisan divide is AM radio. U.S. automakers may be forced to build AM radio into new vehicles within the next year.

The House of Representatives, in a rare instance of bipartisan support, overwhelmingly approved legislation on Wednesday that would require new cars, trucks, and SUVs to be built with AM radio at no additional charge to consumers. The AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act, which would direct the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to require automakers to include AM radio in new passenger vehicles as standard equipment, will now head to the Senate.

Until recently, proponents of AM radio have waged an unsuccessful lobbying effort for a mandate, arguing that it offers critical information during emergencies because its signal can travel long distances. But a groundswell of support from Democrats and Republicans, the broadcast industry, emergency responder organizations, and even former administrators of the Federal Emergency Management Agency is pushing this legislation closer to becoming law.

And there is reason to believe the Senate will follow the House’s lead on the bill, which was co-sponsored by Senators Ed Markey (D-Mass.) and Ted Cruz (R-Texas). Earlier this year, the senators secured 60 co-sponsors for their version of the bill, a critical threshold to overcoming a filibuster.

Cruz, who chairs the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, and Markey hailed the decision in a joint statement Wednesday.

“This vote sends a clear message to car manufacturers that AM Radio is a lifeline that must be protected in new vehicles. From emergency response to sports, entertainment, and news, AM radio is an essential communication tool for tens of millions of Americans. It is now time for the Senate to pass the AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act and for this legislation to become law so AM radio remains a trusted and essential resource for commuters and communities across the country.”

A growing number of automakers, including BMW, Rivian, Tesla, and Volvo, have moved away from the century-old broadcast band in favor of software-defined vehicles that offer streaming services like TuneIn and SiriusXM. Ford had also removed AM radio from some vehicles but has since reversed course. 

Tesla couldn’t be reached for comment; Rivian declined to comment for this story.

EV makers have led the charge because the electromagnetic interference generated by electric motors can affect the frequencies used by AM radio. Automakers have argued that this interference degrades the AM signal and audio quality.

Tesla doesn’t have AM receivers in the base versions of its Model 3 and Model Y vehicles. Rivian’s new R2 SUV doesn’t have an FM or AM receiver; however, the vehicle model offers AM/FM radio through the digital radio platform iHeartRadio for free. The Rivian R1S and R1T models allow customers to access FM content digitally or via built‐in receiver.

		Kirsten Korosec is a reporter and editor who has covered the future of transportation from EVs and autonomous vehicles to urban air mobility and in-car tech for more than a decade. She is currently the transportation editor at TechCrunch and co-host of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast. She is also co-founder and co-host of the podcast, “The Autonocast.” She previously wrote for Fortune, The Verge, Bloomberg, MIT Technology Review and CBS Interactive.

title: Galaxy S26 series reportedly getting a price hike imminently, could be as much as $100
snippet: In the era of RAMageddon, the price hikes just keep coming. Samsung has left its Galaxy S26 untouched thus far, but a new report suggest prices hikes of around $100 could be on the way. more…
fullText:
In the era of RAMageddon, the price hikes just keep coming. Samsung has left its Galaxy S26 untouched thus far, but a new report suggest prices hikes of around $100 could be on the way.

The Galaxy S26 series launched in February with the base S26 and S26+ seeing slight price bumps from their predecessors, and the Ultra unchanged – $899, $1,099, and $1,299, respectively. But a lot has changed in the time since, and it seems Samsung may be bumping those prices further up.

Hans Economy reports that, at least in Korea, Galaxy S26 prices “will be abruptly raised starting October 1.” The planned price hikes (and their converted pricing in USD) follow:

Galaxy S26: 1,254,000 won > 1,403,600 won ($930~ > $1,040)

Galaxy S26+: 1,452,000 won > 1,601,600 won ($1,077~ > $1,188~)

Galaxy S26 Ultra: 1,797,400 won > 1,947,000 won ($1,334~ > $1,444~)

Apparently, Samsung is making this move based on two factors; the continual rise of component costs, and the fact that Apple also just hiked its iPhone prices. The latest iPhone 18 Pro launches are more expensive while the iPhone 17 also saw a $100 price hike in the US (more on 9to5Mac), with the lineup now starting at $899 in the US and 1,450,000 won in South Korea.

	

With that comparison in mind, it’s harder to imagine Samsung plans to bring these price hikes to the US, as they’d make Galaxy flagships $100 more expensive than iPhones across the board, but anything’s possible. 

Samsung, commenting on the report, says that “nothing has been finalized” yet (translated):

We have not sent out any official notice regarding a price increase for the Galaxy S26 series… While it is true that we are internally reviewing whether to adjust prices in consideration of cost burdens, such as the recent rise in component prices, nothing has been finalized as of now.

title: Google Maps rolling out Android Auto speed limits and speedometer that show even without navigation
snippet: While the speedometer has been hit or miss for some Android Auto users as of late, Google Maps is now confirmed to be rolling out speed limits and a speedometer that show at all times, even when you don’t have a destination selected. more…
fullText:
While the speedometer has been hit or miss for some Android Auto users as of late, Google Maps is now confirmed to be rolling out speed limits and a speedometer that show at all times, even when you don’t have a destination selected.

Speed limits in Google Maps launched back in 2019, with the live speedometer appearing later and only starting to show up on Android Auto a few months ago. Earlier this month, though, the speedometer vanished for some users. 

Google is now confirming two things.

First, the disappearing speedometer is being investigated by the Android Auto team. In other words, it appears to be a bug of some kind rather than an intentional removal or rollback of the feature.

	
	

More interesting, though, is that Google is rolling out the ability to see the speed limit of the current road as well as the live speedometer on Maps via Android Auto even when a destination is not set. There have been intermittent reports of this for a few weeks now, but Google is confirming that it’s actually rolling out.

…the ability to have the speedometer, speed limit, and traffic signals/stop signs showing without a destination set is still rolling out. Thus, not everyone will have this particular feature yet.

The exact timeline for when this will be widely available remains to be seen, but it’s great to see nonetheless. Drivers are very often using Google Maps navigation, but shorter or more familiar trips don’t always require setting a destination – but it’s still nice to see speed limits and the speedometer at those times.

title: Android Auto update lets you customize your Google Maps ‘driving avatar’ via car display
snippet: Google is rolling out an update for Maps on Android Auto that gives users the ability to edit their “driving avatar” directly from the car’s display. more…
fullText:
Google is rolling out an update for Maps on Android Auto that gives users the ability to edit their “driving avatar” directly from the car’s display.

The ability to change the classic blue arrow navigation icon in Google Maps itself is not new, but it’s only been available on car displays for about a year. In May 2025, Google Maps rolled out support for showing your chosen icon on Android Auto and CarPlay, but it needed to be set on the phone itself. 

Now, Google is rolling out an on-car picker for your Google Maps “driving avatar” on Android Auto.

The change is rather simple. Through Google Maps on Android Auto, a new “driving avatar” setting appears alongside settings for home/work and alerts. Tapping it gives you the option to pick your avatar and change it to the color of your choice. It’s the same functionality found on your phone, just now accessible directly via the car’s display.

	

This appears to be going live with a server-side update. Android Authority spotted the change with Android Auto 17.8.163744 and Google Maps 26.38.01.980791571 but, despite using those same versions, we’re not seeing the option just yet. Sound off in the comments below if you have it.

In our teardown of Android Auto 17.8, we also noticed that Google has removed the neat little “Jimothy” Easter egg which, as we predicted, was clearly never meant for a public-facing rollout.

title: Pulley, a Carta rival, is shutting down
snippet: Cap table management platform Pulley, backed by General Catalyst, Stripe, and Founders Fund, announced that it's closing shop in December.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

2:23 PM PDT · September 16, 2026

Image Credits:Royalty-free / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Cap table management platform Pulley announced this week on its website that it was shutting down, and its final day of operations and services will be December 8. In a twist, it said it has partnered with its rival, Carta, to offload customers; it’s also redirecting prospective clients to Carta. 

Yin Wu, a serial founder and ex-Microsoftie, started building Pulley in 2020 and went on to raise over $50 million from top investors, including General Catalyst, Stripe, and Founders Fund.

Pulley didn’t offer a reason for the shutdown (we’ve reached out to Wu for comment, but she didn’t immediately respond). However, a former employee speculated online that Pulley wasn’t so much competing with Carta as it was with spreadsheets. And these days, startups can easily use AI to keep, improve, and maintain their spreadsheets.

In a statement posted to LinkedIn, Wu thanked her team and backers, writing that “though this is the closing of one chapter, I, along with many of our strongest team members, have no intention of riding off quietly into the night.” 

“There has never been a better time to solve big problems,” she continued. “Thank you again to everyone who supported us over the years.”

title: Lucid Motors has a potential robotaxi partner for Europe
snippet: The company is partnering with mobility platform Bolt -- but no vehicle orders have been placed just yet.
fullText:
Lucid Motors has entered into a partnership with European mobility platform Bolt that could bring robotaxis made by the California company to the continent.

The two companies announced Thursday that Bolt “aims to deploy at least 25,000 fully autonomous vehicles” built on Lucid’s upcoming mid-size EV architecture, which is supposed to be smaller and cheaper than its current offerings.

The announcement follows a major restructuring at Lucid Motors under its new CEO, Silvio Napoli, who recently laid off nearly 20% of the company’s workforce and delayed the launch of the first vehicle to be built on the mid-size platform by almost a year to the second half of 2027.

Lucid Motors has yet to deploy a commercial robotaxi version of either of its two existing vehicles. The company has spent the last year working in partnership with Uber and autonomous vehicle firm Nuro to launch a robotaxi version of its Gravity SUV. That is supposed to happen by the end of 2026.

Napoli has said he believes the business of becoming a robotaxi provider would have margins that “vastly” exceed those of “the traditional retail model.” 

Bolt intends to own and operate the fleet, according to a press release. The two companies “will work together from the product-development stage on an autonomous driving system (ADS)-ready vehicle platform,” it says.

The vehicles will use Nvidia’s autonomous vehicle compute and sensing architecture (called Hyperion), but the companies did not say which company (or companies) will provide the autonomous driving software. Lucid declined to offer any more information beyond what was in the press release.

No money has changed hands, and Bolt has not placed an order for the vehicles. There is also no public timeline for deployment — only that Bolt considers this a “major step toward” its “ambition of 100,000 autonomous vehicles on its platform by 2035.” 

“Autonomous driving in Europe requires data, software, vehicles, and operations to work as one system built for European roads and regulation,” Markus Villig, founder and CEO of Bolt, said in a statement. “Lucid brings a world-class platform, and together, we will co-design the vehicle and software based on our data and more than a decade of operating experience across more than 850 cities. No one is better placed to operate autonomous mobility services efficiently at scale.”

Napoli, in a statement, said, “Bolt’s reach and operating expertise make it an ideal partner to scale autonomous mobility across Europe.” 

.

title: Musk’s long-time backer is giving SpaceX stock to its investors
snippet: Valor Equity Partners is handing out stock to its LPs instead of cash returns.
fullText:
VC firm Valor Equity Partners, founded by Antonio Gracias, a long-time Elon Musk backer and current SpaceX board member, has opted to simply give away a chunk of its SpaceX stock to its limited partner investors, according to an SEC filing spotted by Bloomberg.

Valor made a killing on SpaceX after investing in it over decades, with entities controlled by Gracias owning more than 500 million shares at the time of the IPO. This was second only to Musk (who owned over 6 billion shares at the time). But instead of cashing out and issuing returns to LPs, Valor handed over 8.5% of its holdings to them, worth about $8.5 billion, Bloomberg estimates. Valor will still own more than 460 million shares after the giveaway, the SEC disclosure form says.

Transferring ownership of the shares could give those Valor limited partners a tax advantage. More importantly, it avoids dumping a giant tranche of shares into the open market. Such a dump could cause a glut of available shares and a corresponding dip in price. SpaceX is already down about 10% since its blockbuster IPO day.

fullText:
tvOS 27 is the latest software update for Apple TV 4K, and it’s rolling out now to all users. Here’s what’s new in tvOS 27.

tvOS 27 adds revamped Apple Podcasts app, new Apple Music features, custom text sizes, more

tvOS 27 is now available to install via the Settings app on your Apple TV. The software is compatible with all Apple TV 4K models except the first generation; Apple TV HD is not supported.

Apple’s new tvOS 27 update adds the following features and changes:

Podcasts: Apple Podcasts gets a revamp on tvOS that follows a similar iOS update earlier this year. The new tvOS Podcasts app fully supports Apple’s new video features, making it a great place to watch video podcasts. And there’s a fresh design with sidebar navigation and more.

Software Updates via iPhone: One convenient tvOS 27 change is that you can now update your Apple TV 4K’s software directly from your iPhone. Using iOS 27’s Home app, you’ll be able to install tvOS 27 and subsequent updates without actually booting up your Apple TV.

Apple Music upgrades: Apple Music gets two new features in tvOS 27. AutoMix is coming to Apple TV as a fresh option for song transitions that are more DJ-like and could fit in well at a party. Hi-Res Lossless Audio is another addition, available for users with compatible external speaker outputs.

Larger text sizes: You can now use Dynamic Type in the Settings app to customize the size of text systemwide, letting you make it larger to better suit your needs and viewing setup.

Finally, Apple says that tvOS 27 supports faster AirPlay connections, smoother animations and app launches, and makes Control Center more responsive.

Notably missing from tvOS 27 is the new Siri AI assistant. Only the old Siri is offered. Rumors indicate that’s because a new Apple TV 4K is about to launch with hardware upgrades that can power Siri AI.

Another missing upgrade is a “Smart downloads” feature that Apple mentioned at WWDC. tvOS has never previously supported downloads for TV content, so it was a surprising announcement. title: Automattic’s interim CEO and legal chief signed reciprocal severance deals during Mullenweg’s brief ouster
snippet: CFO Mark Davies and legal chief Andy Missan signed each other’s severance agreements while Matt Mullenweg was on leave, providing a year of salary and additional equity vesting if their departures qualify for the benefits.
fullText:
Last week, on September 9, Automattic’s board voted to put CEO Matt Mullenweg on paid leave, a decision the board still hasn’t explained publicly. Mullenweg, in a company-wide Slack message, accused CFO Mark Davies of “conspiring” with three board members behind his back to force the vote through, saying he was given only 50 minutes’ notice and was denied time to have the resolution reviewed by outside legal counsel. He returned to the role roughly 33 hours later, and the same board members who voted him out have since departed the company.

They didn’t just walk out the door, though. In the 33-hour window between Mullenweg being put on leave and his return, two key executives at the company signed off on generous exit packages for each other. Davies, who became interim CEO during that window, and Chief Legal Officer Andy Missan, each signed the other’s severance agreement, effective September 10.

These agreements, effectively golden parachutes, provide each of them with 12 months of base salary paid out as a lump sum, an accelerated vesting schedule for their equity, the ability to exercise their vested stock options, and another year of health coverage, according to the severance documents reviewed by TechCrunch.

Between the two of them, the full package — accelerated equity plus a year of salary — comes out to $8.15 million that Automattic would now owe both executives, since Mullenweg fired them upon his return. 

Automattic’s legal team is working to determine what the next steps are: pay out these sums or fight them by challenging their legal validity. (The company replaced its earlier counsel, Gibson Dunn, with Stephen Shackelford and Shawn J. Rabin of Susman Godfrey LLP, the company and Mullenweg jointly announced on Wednesday. Automattic’s general counsel, Jordan Hinkes, also had his company account deactivated, sources told us. Mullenweg has since stated on X that this move had been in the works for weeks, as Hinkes is joining an AI startup.)

Want to correct the record: Jordan Hinkes, with my support and encouragement, is joining an exciting AI startup as General Counsel. We've been planning this for weeks before anything started; he's still fully @automattic through Friday. :)

— Matt Mullenweg (@photomatt) September 16, 2026

Under the agreements, the executives only get their benefits if they sign a broad release of claims and continue to comply with confidentiality, nonsolicitation, and other legally binding post-employment restrictions.

The agreements are also written in a way that favors the executives when it comes to how “cause” — the legal standard a company must meet to fire someone without owing severance — is defined. Under these terms, the company must notify the executive in writing within 60 days of learning about the conduct, give them 30 days to cure the conduct if curable, then get a majority of the board to agree that cause exists.

“Cause” itself is narrowly defined in the agreements as gross negligence that materially harms the company; knowing dishonesty, fraud, or misrepresentation causing material harm; a material legal violation causing material harm; a material confidentiality or IP breach; or a felony or crime involving “moral turpitude” (a legal term for conduct considered inherently dishonest or morally reprehensible).

In Davies’ case, the agreement also specifies that his removal from the interim CEO role won’t count as “Good Reason” — a legal term that normally lets an executive resign and still collect severance, on the grounds that their job conditions changed for the worse — as long as he remains CFO. While that clause itself is not strange for a legal agreement, it suggests the document was drafted with Davies’ precise circumstances in mind —becoming interim CEO — effectively ensuring Automattic won’t owe him severance once his temporary CEO stint ends, as he can’t claim that alone as a reason to resign.

While it’s not necessarily improper that the executives signed each other’s agreements, in the context of a governance struggle at Automattic, it is noteworthy. 

Another factor that has recently come to light is that Davies held no Automattic stock at the time of his departure, according to an HR document viewed by TechCrunch. (One source at the company said Davies sold the stock a “few months ago,” but TechCrunch cannot confirm the time of the sale. Davies did, however, still hold a large number of outstanding vested options, the HR document showed.)

These events can be interpreted in two very different ways. In one scenario, Automattic’s board is responding to an internal leadership crisis, voted to put Mullenweg on leave, and then established protections for the executives who could face adverse consequences if the intervention failed (as it now has).

Automattic’s legal battle with hosting provider WP Engine could come into play here. In July, WP Engine accused Mullenweg of destroying evidence in legal filings, specifically text through messaging apps like Signal, WhatsApp, and Telegram. If the directors believed Mullenweg’s behavior had become a serious corporate risk, putting him on leave and changing management could help demonstrate to the court that the board took the concerns seriously. This could potentially help reduce any possible sanctions or fines or improve settlement terms. (Mullenweg’s X post on September 10, which referenced the alleged destruction, or “spoliation,” of evidence right after the board action, could support this theory.)

Image Credits:Screenshot from X
Image Credits:Screenshot from X

In another scenario, it could appear that Automattic’s board was trying to create a window of control for some other reason — perhaps a strategic transaction — by putting Mullenweg on leave and taking the reins. According to sources, this is the theory Mullenweg suspects — though by his own account, the board never gave him a stated reason for the vote to begin with, leaving him, like outside observers, largely to speculate about the underlying motive. That absence of explanation, combined with the CFO’s stock sale, appears to have fed his suspicions and factored into his decision to retake the CEO role and remove the board and other executives.

Automattic has been asked for comment. Attempts to reach Missan and Davies have not been successful.

This article was updated after its publication to include further context about Hinkes’ departure and embed an X post.

fullText:
A new post on Apple’s Security Research blog details the fascinating tech, architecture, and thinking behind the iPhone 18 Pro’s new Reference Image camera mode. Here are the details

Apple explains why it developed the new Reference Image camera mode

In a blog post titled “Apple Reference Image: A New Approach for Verified Photography,” Apple goes in-depth into how its new photographic authenticity system works.

The post confirms that the company’s motivation to build Apple Reference Image was the ever-lowering barrier to creating or adjusting images synthetically.

Apple explains that while industry standards such as C2PA help address the problem, they remain vulnerable to compromise at points in the editing chain.

For this reason, Apple developed a fascinatingly creative chain-of-verification system that is private, secure, and, to the company’s knowledge, “the only image provenance system that provides quantum-secure defenses.”

‘A new standard for verifiable digital photography’

In its explanation, Apple uses classic photography terms, such as a secure digital negative, which contains the raw captured pixels along with information such as signed metadata and timestamps, and is developed in a secure, private, and verifiable environment within the company’s Private Cloud Compute structure.

This semantic authenticity is just one of the three core requirements Apple says a high-assurance photographic provenance system must meet, the other two being resilience to compromise and privacy preservation.

If Apple’s confidence scoring system identifies a sensor as low-scoring and that sensor is revoked, Private Cloud Compute will no longer sign Reference Images captured by it.

Likewise, individual Reference Images can be revoked if later determined to be fraudulent, with Apple devices regularly fetching updated revocation lists.

Another interesting aspect of the Apple Reference Image chain of trust is that it begins once a camera sensor is first initialized, during the iPhone’s manufacturing process.

The sensor generates a signing key pair, keeping the private key to itself while sharing the public verification key with the factory recording station, which then signs it with a factory certificate authority and records it in the device’s hardware manifest.

That private key will later be used to sign every photo taken in Reference Image mode, binding the captured pixel data and sensor metadata to that specific camera sensor before the image ever reaches iOS for further processing.

Apple also uses cryptographic timestamps to establish a verifiable window for when each photo was taken. Instead of relying on a timestamp provided by the device’s general operating system, which the company says can be compromised, the iPhone periodically receives a secure timestamp token that serves as a lower bound.

It then requests another after capture to establish an upper bound, allowing Apple to verify that the image was captured sometime between the two.

The Secure Enclave also plays a role by signing metadata that originates outside the camera sensor. Private Cloud Compute later verifies those signatures, confirms that the sensor and Secure Enclave belong to the same iPhone, and checks the timestamps before developing the secure digital negative.

Once those checks pass, Private Cloud Compute processes the negative into the final JPEG Reference Image and signs it using a combination of traditional and post-quantum cryptography, which Apple says is designed to keep the image verifiable even against future quantum attacks.

Apple goes on to explain that the Reference Image framework was designed so that an outside observer cannot determine the identity of the photographer, which device took a given photo, or whether the same device captured two Reference Images.

This is particularly important, Apple notes, for photographers working in sensitive environments, such as conflict zones, where proving an image is authentic should not require giving up anonymity.
