title: Google rolling out Android 17 QPR1 for Pixel
snippet: Following an extended beta period, Android 17 QPR1 is rolling out to Google Pixel devices with the September 2026 Feature Drop and security patch. more…
fullText:
Following an extended beta period, Android 17 QPR1 is rolling out to Google Pixel devices with the September 2026 Feature Drop and security patch.

There are a number of interface changes in Android 17 QPR1, starting with more blur effects across the system UI. The volume panel is where you’ll most likely notice the Dynamic Color-themed translucency, with the full bottom sheet also updated. The Power menu has also been refreshed and is joined by a background blur. This matches the updates that the widgets picker received in the initial Android 17 June release.

The system media player has a new Material 3 carousel-based interface when there are multiple apps. Instead of dots at the bottom, you now see a preview of other open applications, with your current card shrinking to make room.

When opening Quick Settings, you’ll notice a new bouncy animation, while there’s a new icon in the bottom-right corner for making edits.

	

The Mobile Data Tile has been updated with a “Don’t ask me again” toggle. There’s also a new QS Tile for “Keyboard” that lets you access the system switcher. The Screen recording tool now defaults to the last-used application.

When long-pressing on homescreen apps, the menu has been split into app Shortcuts and system Actions (like Bubble and Widgets).

Meanwhile, holding down on an empty homescreen spot reveals an updated fast wallpaper switcher that has more pronounced corner rounding, while the gaps between menu items have been removed. Other changes include:

There’s a new M3 Expressive Settings app icon that was first introduced on the Pixel Watch.

New animation when launching the camera from lockscreen with power button double-tap.

Health Connect on phones can now track distance and calories burned in addition to step count.

Android 17 QPR1 is rolling out starting today for the Pixel 6, Pixel 6 Pro, Pixel 6a, Pixel 7, Pixel 7 Pro, Pixel 7a, Pixel Tablet, Pixel Fold, Pixel 8, Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel 8a, Pixel 9, Pixel 9 Pro, Pixel 9 Pro XL, Pixel 9 Pro Fold, Pixel 9a, Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro XL, Pixel 10 Pro Fold, Pixel 10a, Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold.

Visit Settings > System > System update and click the “Check for update” button if the OTA hasn’t already appeared on your device. Android 17 QPR1 Beta 9 users will get a small update to this final release.

The Android Beta Program will remain open and continue testing QPRs and feature drops. 

To get the stable version, those running the Android 17 QPR1 Beta have to opt out first. Devices will not be wiped by the stable OTA once that becomes widely available.

title: Amazon fixes bug that caused problems with Fire TV app sideloading [U]
snippet: Fire TV hardware will be able to freely sideload apps again without issue after an upcoming Android software update for Amazon’s streaming hardware. more…
fullText:
Fire TV hardware will be able to freely sideload apps again without issue after an upcoming Android software update for Amazon’s streaming hardware.

Late last year, Amazon rolled out a series of software patches to its Fire TV hardware. On the surface, the Android update for the streaming devices contained the usual security patches and performance updates. It was later discovered that the update also seemed to disable sideloading on certain Fire TV devices, preventing third-party apps from being installed if they didn’t come from certified app stores.

Amazon recently commented on that aspect of its previous Android updates in a response to AFTV News. Amazon says sideload prevention was due to a bug in the update and wasn’t an intentional part of the patch.

If users attempted to install a third-party app, the Fire TV device would list an error and block the process in some instances. It didn’t appear to affect all Fire TV devices, though the issue was widespread enough to be considered intentional. According to Amazon, it wasn’t.

	

There was a bug in a recent Fire TV Settings update that caused the “Install unknown apps” list to appear incomplete or empty on some Fire TV devices. We have identified the cause and a fix will roll out in an upcoming Fire TV Settings update, installed automatically on affected devices over the coming week.

This comes as the company recently announced its latest Fire TV Stick, which runs on Vega OS – not Android. It also confirmed that all future Fire TV Stick devices would run Linux-based software in lieu of Google’s OS to achieve a better performance-to-power ratio.

In essence, existing Fire TV devices will seemingly be able to sideload apps again, but that likely won’t be the case for streaming hardware Amazon launches in the future. Amazon says the patch will roll out to affected devices “over the coming week.”

title: YouTube’s login-breaking bug is getting a fix on TVs and consoles
snippet: Users met with an error at login, preventing them from accessing their YouTube account on TVs, and some consoles will be happy to know Google is rolling out a fix. more…
fullText:
Users met with an error at login, preventing them from accessing their YouTube account on TVs, and some consoles will be happy to know Google is rolling out a fix.

An issue began popping up for some users in the last couple of days, preventing a successful login on the TV or console app. Even with the proper password, some users were reporting they were unable to log back in after being kicked out. The issue seemed to persist on Xbox, PlayStation consoles, smart TVs, and streaming hardware – what YouTube classifies as “licing room devices.”

According to YouTube, the login bug that logged users out and blocked them from re-entry has been fixed. YouTube says the issue has been investigated and is now “fully fixed” in a community post separate from existing threads.

It’s unclear when this issue truly began, but there have been several new threads posted on Reddit within the last 24 hours, suggesting the bug affected a wide number of users worldwide.

	

The community post didn’t suggest an app update was needed. It was likely a server-side bug blocking Google Accounts from access, and in some cases, guest accounts.

Good morning. Today I’m wondering if I should revisit Diablo IV in light of the Diablo V announcement, what I would possibly do with a Steam Frame if I could justify its $1,059 price, and whether I missed any major features by reading as many iOS 27 and macOS 27 reviews as I can stomach.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

We’ve known for years that Apple was building a foldable phone, which means that Samsung, the company that popularized the format, also knew. So in July, when the company unveiled the Galaxy Z Fold 8, a wide foldable with proportions similar to the rumored iPhone Duo, it was seen largely as a preemptive move to claim, once again, that Samsung was ahead of the curve.

	

And thankfully the phone was a success; it sold better than expected, and Samsung has been left scrambling for components from next year’s model to satisfy demand today.

But Samsung, as it is wont to do, couldn’t let the phone’s success just speak. It had to inject itself into the conversation around the iPhone Duo in a series of posts that can only be described as cringe. To me, it’s another case of this “I don’t think about you at all” meme.

Of course, this is just silly stuff, but it speaks to the perception that even when Samsung leads, it follows. The good news is that, as Samsung points out in this funny but awkward ad called “Switchers,” it’s now much easier to move from iPhone to Android since Apple and Google collaborated on a new framework.

Samsung appears to be taking the Duo’s release in stride, doubling down on its commitment to foldables by reportedly moving up the release of its second-generation TriFold.

Apple on wide Android foldables beating iPhone Duo; ‘They got the aspect ratio’

✉️ Inbox

Android rolling out passkey transfers between password managers. It’s no longer difficult to transfer credentials between password managers, but passkeys have always been another matter. This system-level change is more than welcome.

Samsung’s first Android XR glasses with a color display may launch in late 2027. We’re only a month or so away from Samsung’s first smart glasses released in collaboration with Google, Warby Parker, and Gentle Monster, so it’s no surprise that by the end of next year there will be an option with a display.

Google brings Gemini for desktop app to Windows. It feels like it’s been forever since Google announced a Windows version of its popular Gemini app, but it’s now available and appears fully featured.

Google details ADB Wi-Fi 2.0 for more reliable wireless Android debugging

YouTube details NFL Sunday Ticket pricing & availability for 2026 season, including a 50% discount. The absolute disaster that is watching NFL games in one place with one subscription doesn’t appear to be any better for the 26/27 season. 

NFL Sunday Ticket is $204/year for YouTube Premium subscribers, nearly 60% off

Google’s hyper-personalized ‘Dreambeans’ feed is now free to test. I still have no idea what this is; I just know that it has the worst possible name for an app.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 needs battery banks that actually fit; iPhone Duo might help. One benefit of Apple launching a similarly sized foldable is that accessory makers may unintentionally make things better on the Android side.

Possible Google device at FCC could be Wear OS-powered fitness tracker. It would not surprise me if Google is working on more fitness trackers after the runaway success of the Fitbit Air. Hope this one lacks a screen, too.

Oppo confirms Find X10 series details ahead of September 22 launch. The next Find X flagships are coming soon, and they’re just as ambitious as previous generations.

Welcome to a new project I’m calling Cc:, where I ask interesting people in the community about what’s making them happy both inside and outside the world of tech. This week, I’m speaking with my friend and former colleague, Nicholas Sutrich.

Who are you?

Nicholas Sutrich

What do you do for work?

I’m the Senior Content Producer at Android Central. This is a fancy title that really means I test a lot of devices every week and write about them.

What do you do for fun?

I reviewed devices for 10 years on the side before going full-time, so I still like to think of my job as being a fun hobby I just so happen to get paid for. Other than work, I love video gaming with my wife and son, reading novels, gardening and chicken tending, CrossFit, and the occasional hike when I can squeeze it in.

What is your relationship like with technology these days?

I spend less time on my phone now than maybe ever. I’ve deleted all social media off my phone (otherwise, I find I work too much for my own good), and I don’t generally play games on my phone unless I’m doing it for a review. My goal is to get off my devices when work is over and spend more quality time with friends and family in person, instead. 

What are a few apps you can’t live without and why?

eMeals: A meal planning service I subscribe to. It’s $5 a month and has a boatload of recipes on there, plus new recipes each week and plans for specific dietary restrictions, stores, or budgets.

Zepp: This is the app for Amazfit smartwatches. I use it for food logging and for workout logging. The food logging portion is particularly fantastic because it’s LLM-driven, so you can tell it you had “2 eggs fried in coconut oil with 2 slices of avocado toast and a glass of orange juice for breakfast” and it’ll log all that crap instantly. No more scrolling through tedious lists.

Discord: Everyone probably uses this, but it’s my main chat app with friends. We bounced between apps for years until it came out and haven’t switched since. 

What is a gadget that you love right now?

Motorola Razr Fold. This phone is just such a joy to use. Excellent camera and displays, never have to worry about battery life. Software is snappy and has great features (double-chop for flashlight, woot!). Oh, and the sides are CURVED, not friggin’ flat. I hate stupid phones with flat sides, especially foldables.

What’s a recent TV show you loved?

Gotta be Pursuit of Jade on Netflix. It’s a time period drama/romance/kung-fu show set in ancient China. We randomly tried it after The Algorithm™️ recommended it to us and haven’t stopped since. We only watch like 20-30 mins of TV a day tops, so it’s taken a while to get through all 40 episodes, especially since they’re usually 45 minutes or so apiece.

What’s a recent book you loved?

Jurassic Park by Michael Crichton. I somehow never read these books (although I love the OG movie). It was fun reading the original content and seeing the author’s direction for the story versus the films. Also fascinating to see what parts of the book the films stripped out and randomly slapped into other movies.

What’s a recent movie you loved?

Project Hail Mary. I read this book twice (one of which was out loud to my family) and was so happy that they were making a movie. It’s such an excellent mix of science reality and science fiction in a unique end-of-times scenario. If aliens exist, I hope they’re like Rocky.

What’s a recent game you loved?

Orbitals for the Nintendo Switch 2. I’ve played many co-op games in my time, but few are as well produced and executed as Orbitals. The visuals are beyond stunning and make you feel like you’re playing a Studio Ghibli movie. It’s basically impossible to describe the gameplay other than a wild mix of adventure, puzzle, and platforming.

What’s something offline you do every day that brings you joy?

Family reading time. We’ve done this since our son was little and it never ceases to be wonderful. At the end of most days (I wish we did it every day), we’ll curl up in bed or on the couch and read together. Sometimes, it’s reading manga; other times, it’s an audiobook or reading aloud to each other. We’ve gone through a lot of books this way, and it’s a great way to spend quality time together, drink some tea, have snacks, and start conversations.

Thank you, Nick, for being awesome as always. See you on the putting green.

Over the weekend, American AI titans, including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, xAI’s Elon Musk, and Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis, came out in support of “pacing the frontier,” a term popularized by a letter released in July by nearly 1,400 employees of large American AI companies.

In fact, Amodei wrote his own 3,000+ word paean called “We Must Pace the Frontier,” in which he posits that the industry needs to slow down its frenetic work on improving AI model capabilities in order to prioritize alignment and safety.

“Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails.”

This self-policed slowdown comes as the US government continues to distance itself from regulation, despite entreaties from both sides of the aisle, as well as countries around the world. In a Truth Social post, President Trump said that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades! There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so.”

fullText:
Terrence O'Brien

 

is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Getting added to Spotify’s Fresh Finds playlists can be a huge break for artists trying to cut through the noise on streaming. Now Spotify is launching a program called Fresh Finds Forward, which aims to give artists the tools to capitalize on that exposure. Artists added to any Fresh Finds playlist after January 1st, 2026, can join the program and get 12 months of additional resources, the most extravagant of which is free studio time for US-based artists at Electric Lady Studios in NYC, The Lighthouse at Ocean Way Nashville, or Spotify Studios in LA.

Beyond that, artists will get early access to Spotify tools and features, priority access to tour and music video partnerships, as well as 12 months of Landr Studio Pro and Splice’s Creator Plan. Spotify is also offering artists six months of free therapy through BetterHelp, because we all know trying to make it as a musician is stressful and potentially soul-crushing, as scoring a Fresh Finds placement doesn’t guarantee there won’t be further rejections and failures.

Unlike with the so-called Discovery Mode, where artists were paid a “promotional royalty rate,” in exchange for higher algorithmic promotion, Spotify says the Fresh Finds Forward program doesn’t change royalty rates, and is provided completely free of charge to participating artists.

fullText:
Andrew Liszewski

 

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Bose announced a new version of its Ultra Open Earbuds that helped kick off the industry trend of clip-on wireless earbuds nearly two-and-a-half years ago. The new Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) feature a subtle redesign with improved performance in both sound quality and battery life. They’re also joined by a new cheaper alternative called the Bose Sport Open Earbuds designed to provide a more secure and stable fit during physical activities.

The Bose Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) will be available for preorder on September 19th for $299 with availability starting on October 1st. Color options include black, white smoke, cherry chocolate, olive green, and sky pink. Preorders and availability for the Bose Sport Open Earbuds are the same, but they’re $100 cheaper at $199. Colors include black, white smoke, and eucalyptus green.

Like the original version, the new Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) feature a design that clips to your outer ear with a transducer that directs audio into your ear canal with “minimal sound leakage,” Bose claims. There’s still no ANC because these are designed to do the exact opposite and let you hear what’s going on around you while enjoying music or a podcast.

In addition to a refreshed design with a new beveled finish on each earbud’s metal cap, the 2nd Gen feature a new driver delivering higher volume with automatic adjustments and deeper bass. A new Cinema Mode simulates a “wider, more immersive soundstage” using Bose’s TrueSpatial technology while keeping dialogue clear and centered. Battery life with the buds alone has been boosted to up to nine hours (from seven hours) with an additional 19.5 hours of playback from the redesigned case that can now stand upright for use on a wireless charger.

The Bose Sport Open Earbuds take a similar approach with a design that clips to your ear to project sounds inward, but they feature a thinner cuff with a “soft silicone matte finish” providing more grip to keep them in place. Bose says the Sport version will stay secure during head shakes, cartwheels, and running. They also feature automatic volume adjustments that adapt to ambient noise levels to ensure what you’re listening to isn’t drowned out, and the customizable shortcut button on the end of each battery barrel has an added texture, so they’re easier to find while working out. Battery life is rated at up to seven hours of playback plus an additional 22 hours with the wireless charging case.

fullText:
Google today is rolling out the September 2026 Pixel Drop. This is a smaller update, with Android 17 QPR1 bringing the bulk of new features and changes. That said, recent weeks have seen updates for Pixel Journal, Now Playing, Recorder, Screenshots, and Weather.

Phones

title: Here’s what’s new with parental control features in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27
snippet: Included in today’s 2027 system updates from Apple are several new Screen Time and parental control features aimed at giving parents more control over how their kids use their devices. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Included in today’s 2027 system updates from Apple are several new Screen Time and parental control features aimed at giving parents more control over how their kids use their devices. Here are the details.

Today’s updates include important parental control improvements

Apple today released iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27 with what it describes as a “new suite of powerful, intuitive, and easy-to-use tools that helps parents create safer digital experiences for their kids,” many of which the company previewed in June, during the WWDC26 keynote.

In essence, the new features focus on four areas: what content kids can access, who they can communicate with, when they can use their devices, and how parents can manage those controls.

All of them fall under the protections and restrictions of Child Accounts, which Apple says are required for children under 13, or the equivalent minimum age in their country or region, and available for children up to 18.

With iOS 27, Apple has also simplified the setup process for new Child Accounts. Parents can start with a small set of essential apps, a recommended starter set, or choose exactly which Apple apps their child can access from the outset.

Once a parent sets up a Child Account, they can choose which apps and websites their child can access, as well as set age and content restrictions for movies, TV shows, music, books, and other media.

Parents can now also rely on Ask to Browse, a feature that lets kids request access to blocked websites in Safari across iPhone, iPad, and Mac, with parents approving requests in Messages. This is similar to Ask to Buy, which already requires parental approval before children can download apps or make in-app purchases.

Parents can also require kids to ask for approval before connecting with new contacts, set shared or individual daily limits for categories such as Entertainment, Games, and Social Media, and create schedules that determine which apps are available at different times of day. Those schedules can also vary depending on the day of the week.

Screen Time itself has also been redesigned, with a new architecture that Apple says makes parental controls sync more quickly across devices in a Family Sharing group. Parents can now see weekly usage summaries and their kids’ most-used apps at a glance, temporarily pause access to a device, open things back up for a limited period, and quickly switch between different schedules.

Communication Safety is also expanding beyond nudity detection. The feature can now block detected gore or violent content in shared images and videos, while displaying a warning and additional resources.

Time Allowances are also more flexible. Parents can create their own app categories, move apps between them, and assign a time allowance as soon as they approve a new app through Ask to Buy. Websites associated with an app can also automatically follow the same allowance.

Apple says its suggested Time Allowances are based on a child’s age and expert research. The company is also working with the American Academy of Pediatrics to adapt its Family Media Plan into guidance for parents using Apple products.

Finally, Apple notes that all devices in a Family Sharing group need to be running the version 27 software releases to use the new Screen Time experience.

title: 3 iPhone 18 Pro Upgrades That Will Make My Life as a Frequent Traveler Easier
snippet: Commentary: The iPhone 18 Pro seems to fix almost every gripe I’ve had with my iPhone 17 Pro Max — especially for how much I travel.
fullText:
I’ve traveled all over the world with the iPhone 17 Pro Max during the past year, but I think the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have made the right changes for someone like me who’s constantly on the go. The new Pro phones debuted last week at the company’s  “Surprise and Shine” event, and I think three new features in particular will solve the gripes I’ve had with my orange 17 Pro Max as a traveling companion.

While I am in awe of the Ceramic Shield 2 durability that impressively protected my screen, I wouldn’t call it the best travel phone. It gets warm to the touch in hot weather and doesn’t offer the same pleasing camera experience as Android heavyweights like the Vivo X300 Ultra, Xiaomi 17 Ultra or the Oppo Find X9 Ultra. That’s why I’m stoked for the camera upgrades on Apple’s new models.

But I’m most excited about two comparatively minor upgrades, too. The expanded Dynamic Island capabilities and a redesigned vapor chamber appeal to me as someone who is constantly on the move and needs glanceable information. Here’s why I think these upgrades might tempt me to upgrade to the 18 Pro Max.

More glanceable information in the Dynamic Island

The Dynamic Island is smaller on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max (right) than last year’s 17 Pro Max (left).Patrick Holland/CNET

When I’m on the go, I’m almost always jumping between multiple apps. One minute it is Flightly to track my flights, another minute I’m checking routes on Google Maps and then waiting for my Uber ride to arrive. On my iPhone 17 Pro Max, the Dynamic Island tracks two Live Activities, but I need to swipe between the three apps to multitask. Apple is changing this with its new Pro iPhones.

With the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the new Dynamic Island can expand to show up to three live activities simultaneously. It doesn’t stretch all the way to the screen edges. Instead, you get one main activity on the Dynamic Island with smaller circular icons on either side.

A preview of the three activities to be tracked by the Dynamic Island.Screenshot by CNET/Apple

This won’t change the way you use your iPhone, but I expect it to make multitasking easier with glanceable info right on top of your iPhone. The small icons likely won’t provide much information, but if I can get a navigation arrow alongside my Flighty updates and ETA for Uber rides, I’m sorted. The two icons also serve as shortcuts to open those apps, offering faster access than manually switching apps — which is common when I’m juggling my flight information while getting out of that rideshare vehicle.

A redesigned vapor chamber for better cooling

The iPhone 18 Pro has a larger vapor-cooling chamber.Screenshot by CNET/Apple

My iPhone 17 Pro Max gets warm to the touch when I’m navigating and using the camera app on my photo walks. It drains the battery faster than usual. That’s why I’m excited about the iPhone 18 Pro Max’s improved ability to keep itself cool during intensive periods like my constant photography.

The iPhone 18 Pro has a “next-generation” vapor chamber that’s three times the surface area of the one in the iPhone 17 Pro. Apple redesigned the phone’s interior so its A20 Pro processor can connect directly to the vapor chamber, which is claimed to continuously cycle deionized water throughout the system for “significant” improvements in cooling performance.

Theoretically, all of this could allow the A20 Pro chip to sustain higher performance for longer periods. I imagine it helping keep the phone cool on extended camera usage and navigation, and delivering longer battery life.

You can see the aperture physically open and close on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.Patrick Holland/CNET

Pro controls to take control of my photos

I’m not a professional photographer, but I love taking photos. I’m into street photography and portraits, and the iPhone 18 Pro’s new upgrades seem fantastic, at least on paper. While variable aperture would allow me to control the amount of light hitting the sensor, I’m more excited to try the Pro Controls.

So far, I’ve relied on third-party apps to take motion-blur photos, but I can finally do so within the iPhone 18 Pro’s Camera app itself. Apple is adding the ability to adjust the shutter speed from the viewfinder.

The new Pro controls will let you customize your camera and photo-taking experience by adding manual control options for changing the white balance, using a histogram to check exposure levels, changing the shutter speed and manually adjusting the aperture between four options (ƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8, and ƒ/4.0 f-stops). 

Pro controls on the iPhone 18 Pro can help capture more creative photos without needing any third-party apps.Screenshot by CNET/Apple

These Pro controls will allow me to take full control of how my image looks, rather than relying on Apple’s auto mode or processing to decide everything for me.

Sure, most Android phones have had this feature for years, which is why I carry an Ultra phone alongside my iPhone on9 every trip. However, the iPhone 18 Pro could finally make me ditch the second camera phone and carry just one device for my casual photography. 

These three upgrades have me stoked for the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. The redesigns that get me more glanceable information around the Dynamic Island, camera improvements that give me more control over my photography and improvements that will hopefully keep the phone from getting too warm will have an immediate impact on how I use the phone while running around the world.

title: MagSafe Monday: Vinich’s MagSafe wallet leans into a classic look
snippet: I’ve been on a spree of trying out new MagSafe wallets that look more like traditional wallets. Vinich’s MagSafe wallet is the latest one I’ve tried. It comes in 15+ colors, looks like a traditional foldable wallet built to sit on the back of a leather iPhone case without clashing with it. It’s designed to look more like an extension of your iPhone case. more…
fullText:
I’ve been on a spree of trying out new MagSafe wallets that look more like traditional wallets. Vinich’s MagSafe wallet is the latest one I’ve tried. It comes in 15+ colors, looks like a traditional foldable wallet built to sit on the back of a leather iPhone case without clashing with it. It’s designed to look more like an extension of your iPhone case.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Color options

The manufacturer clearly wanted to leave no stone unturned when it came to colors. They have options in black, green, brown, and even purple, all with a broken-in, aged look that goes well with a leather case rather than fighting it. They also have countless other colors as well. Vinich also offers Desert Titanium, which goes well with that color iPhone if you opt for a caseless look.

Wallet sotrage

Vinich lists three card slots and says you can realistically fit three to five cards, depending on their thickness. In day-to-day usage, that’s probably a driver’s license, a card or two, and a work access control card. There’s also room to fold a bill or two behind the cards, which I always appreciate in a wallet this size. I try to always keep $20 or so on me

The card compartment is lined with RFID-blocking material, and the interior is lined with microfiber so your cards aren’t rubbing against fabric all day. The magnets are strong enough here. I’ve had stronger ones, but I’ve also had much weaker ones.

Three things to know before you buy

First, this is synthetic leather, not actual real leather. It’s scratch-resistant with reinforced stitching, and at this price point, that’s exactly what you’d expect, but if you’re pairing it with a real leather case, you should know going in that the materials aren’t going to be an exact match. Vinich recommends conditioning it every three to six months

Second, it can slowly inch into the frame on wide-angle and macro shots. It sits below the camera on most iPhones, but for close-up photography, you’ll want to pull it off to make sure it’s not covering the lens at all

Finally, it does not work as a stand, even though it looks like it should. The flap is intentionally flexible to keep stress off the magnetic ring, so if you want a wallet that props your iPhone up for a call or video, this isn’t it.

Wrap up

Sub $25, the color range alone makes this worth a look if you’ve been running a nice leather case with a wallet that doesn’t match it. Most MagSafe wallets are built to disappear. This one is built to go with something, and it feels/looks more like a traditional wallet you’d even carry standalone as well. I’d love to see an option with Find Me integration in the future as well. 

You can buy the Vinich MagSafe wallet from Amazon or directly from Vinich.

It’s become common practice for Apple to ship smaller updates to its current OS version on the same day as major new releases debut.

The company typically presents iPhone users with two options. They can install the major new release, or stay on the current version and get additional security updates and bug fixes.

Today, iOS 26.7 is that second option. It doesn’t contain any new features, but it does ensure your iPhone stays up to date with the latest security patches.

The full list of security fixes has been published here. It’s an extensive list of patches, highlighting the importance of installing the update despite its lack of other improvements.

title: Samsung reportedly considers early ‘Galaxy Z TriFold 2’ release in wake of iPhone Duo
snippet: In the wake of iPhone Duo, Samsung is reportedly considering an early release for a Galaxy Z TriFold sequel. more…
fullText:
In the wake of iPhone Duo, Samsung is reportedly considering an early release for a Galaxy Z TriFold sequel.

The Galaxy Z TriFold delivered a wild new form factor to Samsung’s lineup late last year, but it didn’t stick around for long. The TriFold made its US debut in January for $2,900 and was discontinued barely three months later.

There have been rumors flying around a “Galaxy Z TriFold 2” coming in 2027 alongside another new form factor, a slideable, but it sounds like that might be moved up following Apple’s iPhone Duo reveal. 

Leaker Lanzuk says that Samsung is “considering” an early “Galaxy Z TriFold 2” release, with the slideable also being moved up. An exact timeline is unclear, and it’s likely enough that the 2027 timeline will remain.

	

The post also claims that the TriFold sequel will be “thinner, lighter, and more durable” compared to the first generation, with a goal of having the price be “nearly identical.” While $2,899 is still no small price to pay, it’d be impressive if Samsung were able to keep pricing unchanged given the market forces at play, not to mention rumors that the first TriFold was sold at a loss.

title: Googlebook pre-orders start on September 21
snippet: After previously teasing a fall timeframe, Google is set to open pre-orders for Googlebooks on Monday, September 21. more…

After previously teasing a fall timeframe, Google is set to open pre-orders for Googlebooks on Monday, September 21.

The email blast to users who signed up for updates on the Android-based platform went out this morning. On September 21 at 9 a.m. ET, you’ll be able to pre-order the first Googlebook devices.

You can expect devices from Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo, with several leaking in recent weeks. By that date, Google will presumably detail the full operating system, including sharing what the actual name is. In May, we only got a preview.

Today’s teaser highlights the Magic Pointer that allows you to access Gemini immediately. This animation transforms into the light bar that all Googlebooks are expected to feature as their marquee branding element. Google has yet to share what exactly it will do. Compared to Chromebooks, this will be the primary brand on the cover. “Googlebooks” only appears on the left palm rest just below the keyboard. 

	

It’s not clear what the gap between pre-orders and device shipments will be, but launching before the holiday shopping season seems likely.

title: Former Waymo CFO jumps to self-driving startup Wayve
snippet: Elisa de Martel, who left her position as chief financial officer at Alphabet's autonomous vehicle company Waymo in January, will be based out of Silicon Valley.
fullText:
Elisa de Martel, who was chief financial officer at Alphabet’s autonomous vehicle company Waymo, has been hired to the same position at buzzy self-driving vehicle startup Wayve. Outgoing CFO Max Warburton, who held the position at Wayve since 2024, is moving into a strategic advisory role supporting the company’s leadership team.

Her appointment as CFO comes as Wayve moves from development and testing to a company on the verge of deploying its automated driving technology on two fronts: robotaxis and passenger vehicles.

De Martel, who will be based out of Sunnyvale, California, has a history of working for tech companies, including as CFO at industrial-grade 3D printing company Carbon and an 11-year stint as manufacturing finance director at Apple. She was CFO at Waymo from 2022 to January 2026 — a critical period for the company as it began to commercially operate in several cities and raised $5.6 billion in a Series C fundraising round that was led by its parent company and pushed its valuation to more than $45 billion.

Wayve now sits in a similarly pivotal moment. The startup, which was founded  in 2017 and is now valued at about $8.5 billion, attracted investors and automotive customers for its self-learning approach to its automated driving software. The company developed a software layer using an end-to-end neural network that doesn’t rely on high-definition maps, custom hardware, or hand-coded rules and only uses data to teach the vehicle how to drive.

The company’s tech is the basis of two products: an “eyes on” assisted-driving system and an “eyes off” fully automated-driving system, which could be applied to robotaxis or consumer vehicles that can handle all of the driving in certain environments. 

Wayve’s pitch, and the agnostic nature of its technology, has resonated with automakers already locked into certain hardware. It’s also attracted investors — Wayve has raised $3.2 billion to date — and companies like Uber that want to use a more capable version of the self-driving tech to deploy robotaxis. 

Wayve CFO Elisa de MartelImage Credits:Wayve

While de Martel has a well-documented career in top financial posts, it was her connection to deep tech that was particularly attractive to Wayve’s leadership, including founder and CEO Alex Kendall, according to insiders who asked not to be named.

As CFO at Wayve, she will oversee financial strategy and planning, capital allocation, reporting, governance, treasury, and tax. The company said she will also work closely with Wayve’s executive team to support and advise on commercial, investor, and strategic partnership deals.

Wayve has locked in a number of partnerships with automakers, including Nissan and Stellantis. The company has also made progress on the automated vehicle driving systems for robotaxis; the company recently launched public rides in London — with a human safety operator on board — and Tokyo is expected to follow soon.

Now the company has to push past this historically precarious point of early and limited deployment and into a high-volume supplier to automotive.

title: Hear why Science Corp CEO Max Hodak says the screen era is ending at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
snippet: At this year's Disrupt, Science Corp CEO Max Hodak will present a vision for screen-free interfaces that can even offer medical help. Register before September 25 to save up to $200 on your pass.
fullText:
When you imagine working with a computer, you likely think of keyboards, clicks, or typing on your phone. Science Corporation CEO Max Hodak has spent the last several months advancing a different vision. His company has enlisted a top neurobiologist to lead the first U.S. human trials for its biohybrid brain-computer interface. Hodak shares what his company has discovered so far with the 10,000+ tech leaders, founders, and investors at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026.

At his Beyond Screens session on the Disrupt Stage, Hodak will make the case for why the next era of technology could be built upon a different kind of interface, one that adapts to us from brain-computer interactions to create new ways of engaging with machines.

Hodak’s career reads like a running bet that the interface between humans and machines has plenty of room for improvement. Having started programming at six years old, he studied biomedical engineering at Duke Pratt School of Engineering, and worked his way into Miguel Nicolelis’ brain-computer interface lab, interests that inform his work to this day.

He originally co-founded Transcriptic, a robotic cloud laboratory for the life sciences. But most famously, he co-founded Neuralink in 2016 and served as its initial president, helping build the company that put brain implants into the public imagination. title: I Tried Snap Specs: Really Big, but Also Like Nothing Else Out There
snippet: A business tool, or a theme park for my face? Right now I’m leaning toward the latter.
fullText:
Out in a courtyard at Snap’s Santa Monica, California, headquarters, I’m kicking a soccer ball around. I’m terrible at sports. But a glowing arrow stretching across the ground points me to a flashing target I’m supposed to dribble the ball to. I get there and get pointed somewhere else. I’m playing a virtual soccer game, but the ball is real. And the big Spec glasses I’m wearing are making it happen.

When Snap announced its $2,195 augmented reality glasses back in June at the Augmented World Expo conference in Long Beach, California, everyone mocked them. Absurdly large, crazy expensive. I was waiting to try them first, and now I have, for about an hour. I don’t think they’re all-day glasses, and neither does Snap CEO Evan Spiegel, whom I spoke with after my demos. “I’d still think of them today as a computer, and it’s going to be more session-based,” he tells me. “Almost like a pair of reading glasses you put on to get something done. But I don’t think we’re far away from lighter, less expensive and far more capable versions.”

I don’t think I’d want to use them all the time in my everyday life. But damn, I want to go to a museum or theme park or theater experience that uses them.

While most of the smart glasses that exist right now either serve up just audio and cameras and maybe a basic head-up 2D display, Snap Specs are more like a portable mixed reality device, something like a very pared-down Meta Quest but with see-through lenses. It’s another evolution of AR headsets going all the way back to Magic Leap and Microsoft HoloLens, but unlike those, Snap’s got all the pieces to fit into one arguably reasonably sized set of glasses.

Snap Specs are big. But there’s no extra battery pack or processing puck. Jesse Orall/CNET

Are these doorways to smaller glasses? A toolkit for AI? A way for Snap to try to get ahead of Apple, Google, Samsung and Meta while it can? Yes, possibly, but they also feel like the best-functioning prototype of an AR glasses idea that still isn’t mainstream for anyone yet. Snap’s also announced a charging case that doubles as a cellular hotspot with Verizon service in the US, a way to try to make this work standalone without a phone, that costs an extra $200 in a bundle with the glasses.

In my time with Specs, I felt like I was back in familiar AR experiences… but in the best current glasses-like form possible, given where tech is at. Which ends up being a state of existence unlike everyday glasses at all.

Specs are big even on me, and their lenses have a hazy look with the lens inserts added in.Scott Stein/CNET

Big, chunky, fine to wear, not normal glasses

First, the fit: Are the Snap Specs uncomfortable? Weirdly, no, not for a half hour at least. The very thick arms sort of rested against my temples, with a bit of pressure that didn’t bother me. My ears bent down a bit, but not in a way I noticed (till I felt them). The 4.7- to 4.8-ounce (132- to 136-gram) frames (depending on the size you get) are much heavier than other smart glasses, but they balance the weight well on the side of my head, though I sometimes felt them slipping down my nose.

But these are clearly not normal glasses, in any sense. Not just the design, which pushes at the very edges of “big eyewear.” The lenses are rainbowed because of their waveguide layer that shows 3D projections in AR. Unlike Meta’s Ray-Ban Displays, which hide most of the waveguide, these have a notable sheen.

The -8 lens inserts on Specs, snapped into the pair I was wearing.Scott Stein/CNET

Also, they don’t use standard installed prescription lenses. Instead, there are lens inserts that, well, snap in. Honestly, I prefer this. That makes the glasses look even chunkier, but it also means that if Snap were to use these devices at a theme park, a museum or some public space, demoing them would be a lot easier. I use snap-in lenses for VR headsets all the time. And finally, Snap at least makes inserts that go up to -8, which is basically where my heavy nearsightedness is at.

Seen from the side, Snap Specs show off their rainbow-tinged waveguide lens sheen.Scott Stein/CNET

Displays that are fine, but not always great

Specs have a limited field of view, far more limited than that of VR headsets (or even Xreal’s upcoming Aura pair of tethered AR glasses). It’s better than Snap’s previous Spectacles, and kind of close to or better than my memories of Magic Leap 2. The portrait-style vertical viewing area is tall but not that wide.

It’s wide enough, at least, to watch YouTube video highlights of the Jets-Titans game in a browser, which I call up by saying “Hey Snap” and asking the onboard AI. The display is bright enough indoors, but semi-transparent and ghostly like all AR glasses, and it can get washed out in bright light. That’s why these glasses also have transition lenses that become sunglasses outdoors.

I tried them outside and found the experience usable. But the resolution and the clarity are steps below what sharper micro OLED displays in glasses and headsets can do.

Me kicking a ball around through a 3D game called Football Trainer (captured on Specs).

A familiar set of experiences (for me)

I tried Snap’s developer Spectacles a bunch of times in the past, which showed a whole augmented reality OS that works with hand tracking and launches “Lens” apps, some 2D, some full 3D, that can map into the real world. A lot of those were back here, because Specs supports all the independent lenses and creator stuff that Snap’s been building out for a while. But I only got to try a handful of the new Specs during my demo.

I browsed YouTube in a window I called up, resizing the floating window as big as I could and pushing it back and forth with a cursor I’d control with my hands outstretched and pinching to tap. Some apps let you “touch” things directly or pinch them, but most involve aiming your outstretched hand and controlling an air cursor like a Jedi. When windows got far away or small, it became a little hard to aim and tap at times, but looking at your open palm brings up a button dashboard for recentering things, bringing up the home screen, or turning AI on or off. Windows can follow you if you want, as you walk around.

What the app dashboard looks like inside Specs. I didn’t get my own capture of it, but it’s accurate.Snap

I even wore Specs in a car: One demo put me in an SUV circling the parking lot while I kept watching Jets-Titans plays, testing how the built-in travel mode handled stability in motion. Pretty well, actually. The display stayed pinned and didn’t drift, and I didn’t get carsick. I enjoyed my Jets win while I could.

I tried connected experiences, one of Snap’s more intriguing features, sitting across from a Snap team member wearing a pair. We looked at each other to begin a shared session, and launched a dominoes game that was apparently co-developed with one of Snap’s celebrity ambassadors, NBA star Jimmy Butler. 

A capture from another pair of Specs showing the domino game we were both playing together.Snap

It was pretty basic: We laid virtual dominoes out one by one on the table in front of us, seeing the shared layout together. We could have just used real dominoes instead. But this idea, with other games I didn’t try – laser tag-like arena battles, virtual table tennis, or even larger group experiences that could support up to 30 people, according to Spiegel – could open some fascinating ideas. I like that these connect simply by looking at someone else wearing them.

Snap’s visualization of Navigation is exactly like what it felt like in-Specs when I tried.Snap

I tried a navigation app that hovered a 3D map in front of me, showing me how to walk to Santa Monica College. I shrank the layout down to a smaller directional arrow pointing the way.

And I tried working on Specs, launching Google Docs with a paired Bluetooth keyboard. That definitely wasn’t a great experience, mainly because of keyboard input lag in my session. But could you try to make this a portable work device? Snap is trying to prove it out.

Snap Specs have a set of quick-access buttons you can see when you look at your open hand.Scott Stein/CNET

I also tried live translation with a Snap employee who spoke Italian to me while I saw captions in English pop up in front of me – something I’ve done on other smart glasses, from Even Realities G2 to Meta Ray-Ban Displays to Google and Samsung’s upcoming glasses.

The most promising thing to me was kicking around a soccer ball outdoors using an app called Football Trainer. The training aspect wasn’t perfect, and I sometimes worried I’d try to finesse the ball to the virtual target and trip over myself in the process. But, I noticed that the glowing overlays had no occlusion, or a way of letting the ball or my legs look properly positioned over the graphics, something that exists on devices like Apple Vision Pro. Instead, the graphics overlapped the ball and my legs.

Snap Specs have thick arms that house the side projectors, but they feel solidly built. The arms don’t flex out, though.Scott Stein/CNET

But that real-world overlay showed me possibilities. I’ve tried Snap Specs with demos of overlaid virtual pets before, and tried theme park-like augmented reality experiences with other companies using hardware like the Quest 3 (DreamPark’s Mario Kart-like driving experience, where I rode a motorized unicorn along a virtual road). Snap Specs could do things like this if location-based experiences were built to support it. I saw an AR play in New York that used an older Magic Leap 2 to project virtual actors in front of a real audience. Snap Specs could do it better.

Snap promises its Intelligence AI agent will work across Mac, iPhone and Specs.Snap

AI ambitions with an agent called Snap Intelligence, too

Snap’s also betting hard on AI, to no one’s surprise. A newly announced agentic app called Snap Intelligence promises to work with Macs and iPhones and on Snap Specs glasses, tapping into your connected apps and information and providing recommendations and actions to help run your life.

The idea sounds like Meta’s recently launched AI agent Muse, which is likely to extend to Meta’s glasses hardware more expansively at next week’s Meta Connect conference. Snap’s getting ahead of that likely news here, but I wasn’t able to demo Snap Intelligence at all during my Specs briefing in Santa Monica. That’s all coming later this fall, per Snap, to time with the glasses launch.

“It actually installs on your Mac, so it can use your Mac for you,” Spiegel says to me about Snap Intelligence. “It can also log into services for you without accessing your credentials, because it can just use your keychain.” But he also promises the agent won’t act without your knowledge: “It just doesn’t do anything until you say it’s OK. It won’t change anything or send anything, or anything like that, until you say OK.”

Spiegel is bullish on lots of AI tools working in Specs beyond the company’s own Intelligence agent, from AI-infused AR experiences to running platforms like ChatGPT or agentic systems on the glasses. Snap’s also pushing promises of business partnerships for Specs with Amazon and Nvidia, among others, exploring how the chunky glasses could be worn in either offices or factory floors. Would they be safe and reliable enough to use? It’s unknown yet. But there aren’t any other current AR glasses with full world-tracking 3D and hand tracking in the size and form of Specs yet. Spiegel sees it as “get that big screen experience if you want it, but ultimately, hopefully, get the computer out of the way and just supervise agents who are getting things done on your behalf.”

The transitions lenses kicking in on Snap Specs. Would you know I was wearing smart glasses?Scott Stein/CNET

Privacy plans: Maybe being big and obvious is better?

Snap isn’t trying to hide what Specs are, something Spiegel seemed to celebrate as we chatted. Unlike Meta’s glasses, which can seem so normal that you wouldn’t notice the cameras in the corners, Specs are very much not standard-looking eyewear. Aas Spiegel said to me, you’d know if someone was wearing them. Will that help address growing privacy concerns on smart glasses that are increasing every month?

Recording photos and video clips, including captures that show your augmented-reality experiences overlaid, is done by pressing a side button on the glasses, which then lights up a big LED light. There’s also a clever new snapping gesture for taking photos, which is appropriately on-brand…and again a clearly visible gesture, although one people might not know was a photo-taking trigger.

Spiegel reflected on Snap’s own history of camera glasses, which extends way further back than Meta’s. He tried to make Snap’s Spectacles glasses look unique, even strange, to celebrate their distinct style…and also broadcast that they were different. It made me wonder if smart glasses should all be doing this, in the spirit of the at-the-time odd-looking, long-stemmed first-gen AirPods.

A cellular-enabled charging case for Specs could make these work away from phones.Scott Stein/CNET

Too ambitious, maybe, but these would be perfect for demos

Snap’s going for it all with these Specs, but I have concerns for sure. Battery life (promised as “up to four hours”), which I didn’t get to truly test during quick demos where I swapped pairs of Specs for different experiences. A not-perfect display. 3D experiences that sometimes looked good, sometimes a step below what a higher-powered VR headset could do. And would any of this really replace a phone at all? I doubt it.

But Snap is aiming to host demos for Specs at a new LA flagship store this fall, something I hope will expand to other locations. And installations and experiences. I’d gladly buy a ticket to a fun event where these Specs were used for a collective immersive experience, but I wouldn’t be compelled to buy a pair. Demos and experiences feel like the next step, and these Specs finally feel ready to be worn. Not all the time, but at least for a while. 

Snap Specs (left) next to my own thick glasses (right) for comparison. Scott Stein/CNET

Specs seem like part of a new wave of odd VR/AR devices pushing beyond their previous categories, trying to be more or to connect to other systems and services: Valve’s Steam Frame, Xreal Aura and Snap Specs. Specs are the closest living relative to the Meta Orion AR prototype glasses I demoed two years ago, but they’re still full of question marks. And yet, they’re also likely to be a place to prototype AR and AI ideas in outdoor spaces.

I want to see what else they can do, but that’ll have to wait until a review later in the fall. In the meantime, I appreciate they’re trying something no other hardware is doing yet…but also, there’s a reason others haven’t succeeded yet. Size and compromises to get to AR glasses are still a big challenge, but Snap’s Specs are the closest I’ve seen to making it work. It’s far from perfect, but it’s a start.

Editors’ note: Scott Stein’s travel costs were covered by Snap. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Scott Stein
						

						

							Editor at Large						
					

											

								

											I started with CNET reviewing laptops in 2009. Now I explore wearable tech, VR/AR, tablets, gaming and future/emerging trends in our changing world. Other obsessions include magic, immersive theater, puzzles, board games, cooking, improv and the New York Jets. My background includes an MFA in theater which I apply to thinking about immersive experiences of the future.
															
						See full bio

title: Judge scrutinizes Musk’s move to drop Apple from antitrust lawsuit involving OpenAI
snippet: Federal judge Mark Pittman wants details on any agreement that may have led Elon Musk’s companies to drop their antitrust claims against Apple. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Federal judge Mark Pittman wants details on any agreement that may have led Elon Musk’s companies to drop their antitrust claims against Apple. Here are the details.

Judge wants to see any Apple agreement

snippet: YouTube is starting its fourth season as the home of NFL Sunday Ticket and, ahead of Week 1 games, an overview of availability and pricing has been detailed, including a big discount for new customers. more…
fullText:
YouTube is starting its fourth season as the home of NFL Sunday Ticket and, ahead of Week 1 games, an overview of availability and pricing has been detailed, including a big discount for new customers.

For the 2026-2027 season, NFL Sunday Ticket on YouTube TV will start at $240/year.

That’s thanks to a big discount YouTube is running, but it’s only available for new subscribers. For those eligible, it’s a discount of up to 50%. For existing customers, the costs are $378/year through YouTube TV (in addition to monthly subscription costs) or $480/year through YouTube Primetime Channels.

You can sign up via YouTube’s Sunday Ticket website.

	

NFL Sunday Ticket packages at YouTube

On a support page and through a thread on Reddit, Google details what games are and are not available through NFL Sunday Ticket on YouTube this year, and where you can watch those other games.

It breaks down to:

Thursday Night Football: Not available on YouTube/YouTube TV

Sunday Afternoon Games: Out-of-market via Sunday Ticket, in-market via CBS or Fox on YouTube TV, in-market via Paramount+ or Fox One on YouTube

Sunday Night Football: NBC via YouTube TV, Peacock via YouTube

Monday Night Football: ABC/ESPN via YouTube TV, not available on YouTube

NFL Sunday Ticket also does not include preseason or postseason games, as well as some regular season games such as Thanksgiving Day games.

For Week 1 games being played on September 13, YouTube details what games will be broadcast via CBS and Fox and, as such, are not on Sunday Ticket if you live within the local region. So, as an example: If you live in Buffalo, NY, CBS will be broadcasting the Bills at Texans game, which will not be available via Sunday Ticket, but that game will be on Sunday Ticket if you live in Washington, DC.

title: GM just found the ‘sweet spot’ for supporting Android Auto & CarPlay [Gallery]
snippet: GM has been stubbornly standing by its decision to axe Android Auto and Apple CarPlay from many of its newer vehicles in recent years, despite loud and constant negative feedback from consumers. In its latest software update for two new trucks, GM has found the “sweet spot” for implementing Android Auto and CarPlay, but it’s unclear if that compromise will extend to other vehicles. more…
fullText:
GM has been stubbornly standing by its decision to axe Android Auto and Apple CarPlay from many of its newer vehicles in recent years, despite loud and constant negative feedback from consumers. In its latest software update for two new trucks, GM has found the “sweet spot” for implementing Android Auto and CarPlay, but it’s unclear if that compromise will extend to other vehicles. 

A new software experience – based on Android Automotive / Google built-in – debuting in the 2027 Chevrolet Silverado and 2027 GMC Sierra will see GM’s software not only get a nice new coat of paint, but also some welcome functionality. As detailed by CNBC, the update will “proactively surface relevant controls” such as call controls and even a garage door opener. Both vehicles have plenty of physical controls, too.

The biggest news here, though, is GM finding a new way to implement Android Auto and CarPlay integration.

GM announced in 2023 that it would remove phone projection systems from its vehicles while embracing Android Automotive and native functionality in its infotainment system, a decision that has not been positively embraced by customers. While GM has not backed down from this change on its electric vehicles, many of its vehicles still support both platforms. 

	

The change here is that the Silverado and Sierra will support Android Auto and CarPlay, but in a new windowed mode. The projection appears on a part of the display, with aspects of the native infotainment coming through around the sides so you can still easily control parts of the car that projection systems cannot without actually closing anything. 

Speaking to The Verge, GM group product manager for Google built-in, projection, and profiles Colin McCormick explained that this is the “sweet spot.”

I think we’re landing in a spot where… we don’t have a customer that has to decide, “Oh, I’m going to use projection, or, oh, I want to use the native system…” That’s our sweet spot.

That said, there’s no word here on whether or not GM will actually bring Android Auto and CarPlay back to more of its vehicles. Gas-powered vehicles remain with support for phone projection, but that’s still missing in its EVs, including the latest Chevy Bolt that launched earlier this year.

title: Google’s hyper-personalized ‘Dreambeans’ feed is now free to test [U]
snippet: Dreambeans is an experimental app from Google Labs that will “proactively dream up personalized daily stories.” After previously requiring a subscription, Dreambeans is now available for free Google Accounts in the US to test. more…
fullText:
Dreambeans is an experimental app from Google Labs that will “proactively dream up personalized daily stories.” After previously requiring a subscription, Dreambeans is now available for free Google Accounts in the US to test.

Update 9/10: Google officially announced the broader availability today.

Personalized topics: This could be everything from places to explore, shows to watch, or a reminder of upcoming events.

Connected apps: Distilled information from the Google apps you select, including Calendar, Gmail, Photos, Search, YouTube, and now Gemini.

Original 8/28: Dreambeans is very much like a hyper-personalized Google Now or Discover feed. Like the Gemini app and AI Mode, it uses Google’s Personal Intelligence system to learn your interests by looking at your Gmail, Google Photos, Calendar, Workspace, Search history, and YouTube. During setup, you can choose which apps Dreambeans can access.

Workspace supplies ground-truth transaction data like receipts and upcoming flights

Photos provides the visual memories and insights about you and the people in your life

YouTube identifies your active hobbies

Search detects your budding interests

By combining all these unique signals, Dreambeans can proactively generate rich and highly customized daily visual stories.

The app suggests topics to explore, things to try, places to visit, and interesting events. New stories arrive every morning.

	

Instead of using stock imagery, each Dreambeans story is accompanied by Nano Banana 2-generated artwork that uses an illustrated style. For example, if Dreambeans recommends a hike, you might see yourself and a group of friends at that location.

Tapping on a story lets you see a longer description. In the same example, you’ll get trail details, specific places to stop, what to wear, and timing recommendations. Dreambeans will link to trail guide content on the web. There’s also an “Ask anything” chat experience to get more information.

You can leave feedback by tapping the heart or downvoting, while the chat interface allows you to provide more details. “Tune your feed” lets you tell Dreambeans what you “want more stories about” and what it should never show.

The name combines two ideas at the heart of the app. The “dream” is how the app works overnight to find meaning in the content overload across your connected apps. It then distills what it finds into “beans” – a fresh collection of stories brewed for you each morning.

In June, it was just available for Google AI Ultra subscribers, with Google expanding to AI Pro earlier this month. The setup process “requires up to a day to build your first set of stories.” 

It remains to be seen how Dreambeans will graduate from Google Labs. The experience it offers today is largely standalone, with Daily Brief in the Gemini app possibly benefiting from a more visual experience. 

Dreambeans is available on Android and iOS in the US.

title: Tyrannosaurus Rex Was Warm-Blooded and Able to Live in the Arctic, Study Finds
snippet: It’s been 66 million years and science is still learning more about the most famous dinosaur.
fullText:
It was once widely believed that dinosaurs were all cold-blooded creatures, since they were classified as reptiles. But there is an increasing amount of evidence to the contrary, though scientists still don’t know the exact body temperatures of most dinosaurs. A domino in that discussion appears to have fallen, with a new study from researchers at UCLA that says the Tyrannosaurus rex had a similar body temperature to humans. 

The research, published Wednesday in Science Advances, was done in cooperation with the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, which provided teeth from Thomas the T. rex, a 34-foot-tall, 66-million-year-old specimen found in Montana in 2003 and one of the most complete in the world. 

Researchers from UCLA measured isotopic signatures on the tooth enamel to determine the giant predator’s body temperature.

According to Robert Eagle, co-author of the study and associate professor at UCLA’s Institute of the Environment and Sustainability, it’s possible to glean information from any bone in the body, but teeth are especially helpful because “tooth enamel has large crystalline structures that are extremely durable,” which helps them resist “chemical alteration” from being underground for eons. 

Based on that process, the team determined that the T. rex’s body temperature was likely around 36.3 degrees Celsius (about 97 degrees Fahrenheit). 

This puts the T. rex in the same general category as humans with our 98.6-degree bodies. It also puts them in the same neighborhood as Indian and African elephants, as well as large, flightless birds like ostriches and emus. 

“This is the first thermodynamically and relatively direct measure of body temperature,” Eagle told CNET in an email. 

UCLA created the process years ago and used it to determine that the megalodon was also a warm-blooded predator. However, the method destroys the samples, which led the National History Museum to deny UCLA the teeth until the process could be made more efficient, thereby sacrificing smaller parts of the teeth. 

“Nobody hands you a T. rex tooth unless you can show them you only need a few milligrams,” Aradhna Tripati, climate scientist, co-author of the study, and director of the Center for Diverse Leadership in Science, said in an email to CNET. “The instrument and method that my lab did is what made the science possible. It was over a decade of work involving senior scientists, like Rob, and technical staff like the lead author of this study.”

What this tells us about the Tyrannosaurus rex

Thomas the T. rex, one of the most complete T. rex specimens in the world, on display at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles, donated parts of three teeth for UCLA’s research.Zissoudisctrucker/Wikimedia

This sounds like a simple little thing, but it actually has some rather large implications. A prior study from 2022 suggested that, while reptiles are cold-blooded, evidence supported the idea that meat-eating dinosaurs had avian metabolisms, which would make them warm-blooded, whereas others, like the plant-eating Stegosaurus, were possibly cold-blooded. 

“It’s thought that many dinosaurs, but not necessarily all, were warm-blooded,” Eagle said. “However, even amongst warm-blooded (or endothermic) organisms there are questions of the degree — they can be warm-blooded like sloths or anteaters (low-level endothermy), modern large mammals, or avian endotherms, which typically have higher metabolic rates than mammals.”

At the time, researchers could only guess at the general temperature of many of these dinosaurs, so the study by UCLA not only backs up that the T. rex was warm-blooded, but it’s the first such study to produce precise measurements. 

“For an animal this famous, it is remarkable how little we actually knew,” Tripati said. “We had constraints on T. rex metabolism, mainly from bone and biomechanics, some of which has been controversial. We did not have a direct body temperature determination.”

Figuring out the core body temperature of the T. rex can give scientists all sorts of data about how they behaved and where they lived, and help explain some things humans already knew. For example, Tripati says that T. rex fossils have been found all the way up in Alberta and Saskatchewan and all the way down to Texas. No reptile alive today has that kind of range since they are cold-blooded and need to stick to warmer climates. 

“Thermal physiology drives behavior, range, energy budget and how a species responds to a changing climate,” Tripati said. “A warm-blooded T. rex could have gone almost anywhere on the continent, including the high Arctic. That is a very different animal from a sun-basking reptile.”

Eagle added that being warm-blooded means the T. rex likely had to hunt more often than originally thought to maintain its energy — and said it’s even possible that the T. rex migrated to find food, which may have led it into colder climates.

title: I Tested New Keurig Milk Pods for Instant Frothy Lattes
snippet: These new pods churn out frothy milk for coffee-house style drinks with the push of a push.
fullText:
I’d wager most American coffee-drinkers have sampled a Keurig brew. If you don’t already own one of the single-serve coffee makers, perhaps your aunt shared a cup during the holidays, or there’s one in the office break room. Intuitive to use, easy to maintain and long-lasting, the appliance offers terrific practicality. Simply pop in a pre-bought coffee pod, hit a button and watch a cup pour out.     

Courtesy of The Milk Pod, such easy extraction now extends to dairy, too. Compatible with Keurig brewers, these single-serve capsules produce rich-textured milk with a single push. Impressively, the pods are shelf-stable for 15 months and don’t even require refrigeration. Currently available in three classic coffee flavors — plain, vanilla and caramel—they’re made with milk powder and natural ingredients. Rather than just hot milk, the dairy’s composition turns out frothy, yielding a latte-like consistency. It’s an intriguing addition to Keurig’s already expansive pod selection.  

Coffee and milk, all at the press of a button

Milk Pods load in just like normal pods.Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Unlike a milk frother or steam wand, the pods require minimal instruction. They insert right into the K-Cup slot, no adjustment necessary. The Milk Pods entail no specialized setup; I was already sampling the dairy only minutes after opening the box.

As I brewed with Milk Pods one morning after the next, the initial ease continued. It’s recommended to brew the milk before the coffee, both to a six-ounce size, so the two liquids fit into a standard mug.  As long as I didn’t accidentally press the wrong volume (my Keurig offers 6-, 8- and 10-ounce settings), I couldn’t make any mistakes. 

Read more: I Brewed 50 K-Cups. These Are the 5 Best

Really, the only slight annoyance with the setup is the constant need to refill the water. My Keurig has a 30-ounce water tank, which means I need to top it up at half capacity. During only the second round of coffee, the brewer pinged me to take the reservoir to the sink, an upkeep that didn’t take much effort. Functionality-wise, the pods are remarkably easy. Pouring cold dairy out of the fridge is the easiest milk-integration technique. It’s hard to imagine a more consumer-friendly system.

Convenience is cool and all, but how do the pods taste?

Milk comes out hot and frothy, ready to be mixed with coffee.Nikita Ephanov/CNET

From dozens of seasonal K-Cups to various brand partnerships, Keurig capsules number in the hundreds. I sampled the Milk Pods with a generic brand of K-Cup from a local grocery store. Filled with dark-roasted coffee, the capsule brewed into a strong, lightly bitter-tasting brew – exactly the kind of flavor profile I’d dilute with milk. My chosen K-Cup wasn’t espresso-style, so the consistency resembled drip coffee.

Still, all three Milk Pods added a pleasant thickness to my Keurig coffee. The plain capsule lent the coffee a neutral creaminess, reminiscent of a latte, but nevertheless distinguishable from standard milk. The mouthfeel and taste reminded me of creamer, albeit with a more natural dairy character. Unlike the satisfying micro-bubbles in freshly steamed dairy, I picked up a smidge of powdery solids on my tongue. The cup wasn’t disappointing, but I still prefer the frothiness of fresh milk.

After you run a milk pod through the system, you simply load your coffee of choice.Nikita Ephanov/CNET

The bolder character of the flavored pods made the dehydrated downside less noticeable. I preferred the caramel of the two, which offered a complex nutty bitterness that paired well with my coffee. Sweet yet not saccharine, the pod reminded me of a well-made caramel candy. The vanilla capsule overpowered my coffee more, yielding a strong vanilla-syrup-like flavor. I could see this pod pairing better with other K-Cups, perhaps elevated even further in an iced latte. Overall, I found the Milk Pods pretty impressive for a shelf-stable product, but not quite cafe-quality.

In favor of shelf stability

Comparing the Milk Pods with fresh dairy reveals some differences, but you also have to consider convenience. The year-long durability, combined with no need for refrigeration, makes the pod worth stocking, even if it’s not a daily option.

Over several weeks of trialing the capsules, I left town and came back. The Milk Pods meant I didn’t need to worry about a carton left spoiling in the fridge. Plus, the morning after I returned, I didn’t need a bleary-eyed shopping run for my morning latte, either. I’d be happy to come across Milk Pods in a setting like an Airbnb or hotel. Given the self-contained ease of use, the pods align well with Keurig’s ecosystem. I could also see myself brewing the milk into a K-Cup of black tea or hot chocolate, making it a versatile Keurig option.

Milk Pods cost a dollar each, roughly the same as a coffee K-Cup. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Thinking about cost

Consumed day to day, coffee costs add up. A hot latte from a cafe averages well over $5, and even home-brewing can dent the grocery budget. A K-Cup capsule and a Milk Pod cost $1 each, for an affordable $2 drink. Especially since you can buy a Keurig K-Mini machine for as little as $50, switching to this setup can save you money on coffee out in under a month. Plus, a Keurig requires minimal expertise, so you won’t need to learn how to make coffee.

Still, with a bit more effort, you can find better-priced coffee and milk options. On average, a gallon of milk retails for $4.30, with 21 six-ounce servings of dairy — that’s just over 20 cents per cup. You will need to steam the milk yourself. Handily, though, Keurig sells a $9.50 frother for the task. Fresh milk takes more effort — but to my taste, the flavor and texture are better. Not to mention, warming fresh dairy yourself lets you try out alternative milks as well as milks with varied fat compositions. Want a touch of sweetness in your cup? You can always grab a bottle of syrup and mix in a pump or two.

I wouldn’t switch to Keurig brewers specifically for this milk product, but Milk Pods are a convenient option and may be worth buying if you already use a Keurig. They’d also be handy to have on hand when you’ve run out of milk but are too bleary-eyed to make a morning run to the market.

Rather than just hot milk, the dairy’s composition turns out frothy, yielding a latte-like consistency. It’s an intriguing addition to Keurig’s already expansive pod selection.

title: Apple Car Keys reportedly coming to three more automakers
snippet: Apple is reportedly preparing to extend Car Key support in Apple Wallet to three more automakers. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple is reportedly preparing to extend Car Key support in Apple Wallet to three more automakers. Here are the details.

Apple adds more automakers to its Car Key backend

As spotted by Aaron Perris on X, Apple has added three new automakers to its backend code for Apple Car Key: Lincoln, Freelander, and Lucid.

This does not mean, however, that support will be available right away. Backend changes are usually a good indication of upcoming Car Key integrations, but there is nothing in the code pointing to when they will actually launch. Apple has also yet to confirm which specific vehicles will support the feature⁠.

Today’s discovery follows a string of similar backend changes pointing to upcoming Car Key support from other automakers. In July, similar backend references appeared for GWM’s Tank vehicles, followed shortly after by Haval, another brand owned by the same Chinese automaker.

Apple had also previously announced that Lucid would adopt Car Key, alongside a list of brands that included Acura, Cadillac, Chevrolet, GMC, Porsche, Rivian, and others.

Announced at WWDC 2020, Apple Car Key allows drivers to use an iPhone or Apple Watch to lock, unlock, and start a compatible vehicle, with support varying by automaker and model.

It currently works with more than 50 vehicle models from brands including BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Hyundai, Kia, Genesis, Toyota, and Rivian.
