title: Roku adding new apps & subscription bundles, homescreen redesign expanding
snippet: Roku is rolling out a collection of updates, including a wider release of its homescreen redesign, new “Labs” features, and the ability to bundle streaming service subscriptions to save money. more…
fullText:
Roku is rolling out a collection of updates, including a wider release of its homescreen redesign, new “Labs” features, and the ability to bundle streaming service subscriptions to save money.

Available “soon,” Roku Labs is a new way for viewers to test experimental apps on their TV. This includes a new “Roku City Dash” game that was first announced earlier this year, as well as first-party Roku apps for Stocks, Weather, and a customizable “Backdrops Studio” with custom screensaver artwork.

Beyond Labs, Roku is also more widely rolling out its redesigned homescreen. Available first in the US back in May, the updated look is now heading to Brazil and Mexico with some regional tweaks. You can also use voice commands for more than just content, with new capabilities such as showing weather previews.

Roku is also making LT OS, the operating system for its remote, open-source.

	

Perhaps the biggest new addition, though, is being able to purchase streaming service subscription bundles from Roku. These bundles include “over 30 combinations” using services such as AMC+, Fox One, Starz, and more. Roku says you can save up to 30%.

Your favorite subscriptions are now available in convenient bundles with Premium Subscriptions on Roku in the U.S. and Mexico. With over 30 combinations in the U.S. from services like AMC+, FOX One, Hallmark+, Howdy®, and STARZ, each bundle offers savings of up to 30% compared to a la carte subscriptions. Like all Premium Subscriptions, bundles are discoverable across the Roku platform, including within the Subscriptions Destination, Streaming Store, Premium Subscriptions Home, and more. Subscription bundles are available in the US and Mexico.

title: I wore Snap’s $2,200 smart glasses
snippet: My favorite part of wearing the Specs, Snap's new augmented reality glasses, was playing dominoes. Sitting across the table from a Snap employee wearing the same pair of chunky glasses, I could select a virtual domino with a pinch and then move my hand to drop it in place, watching the tile snap down in front of us on a real table. It was unlike anything I've tried in other VR headsets or smart glasses - the ability to sit with another person and have a shared digital experience. Snap really believes in AR glasses. The company has spent more than half a decade developing the technology, producing two generations of glasses that only ever sh … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
My favorite part of wearing the Specs, Snap’s new augmented reality glasses, was playing dominoes. Sitting across the table from a Snap employee wearing the same pair of chunky glasses, I could select a virtual domino with a pinch and then move my hand to drop it in place, watching the tile snap down in front of us on a real table. It was unlike anything I’ve tried in other VR headsets or smart glasses — the ability to sit with another person and have a shared digital experience.

Snap really believes in AR glasses. The company has spent more than half a decade developing the technology, producing two generations of glasses that only ever shipped to a small number of developers. The company seems to want to untether itself from the limitations of being just one app in a big store and instead pioneer the next great platform.

Now, Snap is nearly ready to launch its first pair of AR glasses for consumers, the Specs, sometime this fall. That suggests Snap thinks these meet its vision well enough for regular people to enjoy using the $2,195 glasses. They’re certainly full of big ideas. But after an afternoon of testing at Snap’s offices this week, I’m skeptical of whether they’ll be fully ready for primetime.

Photo: Naohmi Monroe / The Verge

The Specs are big, black, bold glasses that come in two lens sizes, 47mm and 52mm. Part of why they’re so bold is almost certainly to make a statement — there’s no mistaking these for a regular pair of glasses, like you might with Meta’s Ray-Bans. (They’re a little too conspicuous for me personally; my glasses style is squarely “Elder Millennial Who Shops At Warby Parker.”) But they’re also so chunky because they house all the hardware necessary to let the Specs function as a standalone computer, meaning they don’t need to be tethered to a phone, compute puck, or external battery.

They may be chunky, but the Specs aren’t quite as heavy as they look. They’re heavier than my Warby Parker glasses, of course, which I can comfortably wear for most of the day. But the Specs didn’t drag on my face like a full-on VR headset. The Specs felt sturdy, too: I shook my head around and they didn’t fall off or even really slip. I wouldn’t suggest playing pickup basketball in these, but they’ll stay on your face while walking around. They made my ears sag just a little, though. And I wasn’t able to use the Specs enough to tell you if they’d start to feel uncomfortable over the course of a full four-hour battery cycle.

Actually using the Specs is kind of like using a hybrid of smart glasses and a VR headset. In front of your eyes, you can see menus, app windows, and elements of whatever app (“lens”) you’re using, like the digital dominoes. Those elements appear over whatever you’re looking at with your eyes through the lenses of the glasses, which have waveguide displays that can show “16 million colors” and “sharp, high-resolution visuals” (Snap hasn’t specified the exact resolution).

Thanks to hand-tracking tech in the Specs, you can pinch and drag to manipulate parts of the interface, such as resizing a window or moving a domino onto the game board, and Snap says you can even snap your fingers to take a picture in the Specs’ Snapchat app. Clever. You can also have windows follow along as you move your head, in case you want to keep a window in your vision no matter where you’re looking. You can access a home button, a Control Center-like menu, and status information like the time by holding up your palm in a setup that reminds me of the ill-fated Humane Pin.

In my limited testing, it was all rather finicky. I often had to pinch a few times or make sure my hand was placed in just the right spot to get something to work the way it should. I never quite nailed the two-part action of flipping my hand up and then using my other hand to press the home button. While standing in the sun, it was much harder to see the augmented reality graphics.

Snap has beaten competitors like Meta to shipping a pair of glasses with displays in both lenses, letting it deliver a true AR effect and not just another flat screen. But by putting the AR display dead center in your vision, the Specs’ 51-degree field of view becomes a major limitation. It meant that digital elements kept slipping out of sight during my demos, which ruined the illusion that they were actually in the real world. While watching Lanterns on HBO Max in a browser in a moving car, I had to shrink the window to make it easier to see in front of me. While playing dominoes, I had to keep physically turning my head to see my dominoes and the playing board and back again.

Because it’s 2026, the Specs also have a dedicated AI chatbot assistant, but in my limited experience it was slow and inconsistent. With a “Hey Specs” command, I asked it to show me funny cat videos on YouTube, as suggested by a Snap rep. I had to ask it twice because it didn’t pick up the command the first time. When the command worked, it then took about 15 seconds for the Specs to pull up a YouTube page with search results for funny cat videos.

Watching that video also revealed to me a bizarre social interaction that people will have to come to grips with if AR glasses gain any sort of traction. On that YouTube page, I picked some random cat video collection, and it played in the background while the Snap rep kept talking to me. Even though the Specs were playing audio through the onboard speakers, the Snap rep standing right next to me said they couldn’t hear anything.

That made me feel weird — these glasses theoretically let you watch and listen to a private video while staring somebody else straight in the eye. Even when I wasn’t watching the video, I found myself constantly distracted from the in-person conversations I was having during the demo because my eyes were caught up with what they were looking at while my hands were focused on arcane gestures for tasks that only I could see. I didn’t feel very present.

Like Meta glasses, which are currently grappling with a “pervert” glasses reputation, the Specs also let you take photos and record video. They too have a privacy indicator light, and it’s arguably more prominent than Meta’s take: Instead of a light that’s off to the side, the Specs’ light is right in the center of the glasses. But I don’t know if, given the growing pushback against Meta’s glasses, a blinking light is enough to deter concerns about potential unwanted recording.

That bar in the middle is the privacy indicator light.

In 2024, Snap CEO Evan Spiegel told The Verge that there is an opportunity for computers to evolve to “support the ways that humans have long interacted socially by looking at each other eye to eye with much more natural interaction.” Today, Snap has a simpler message: It says that its vision with Specs is to “make computing more human.” But even in my controlled demos, I found that Specs were actually more computer than other hardware; the glasses are unmissable on my head, and the digital content that only I could see was getting in the way of me interacting with the other people in the room.

Still, these headsets are coming. Meta is working on a pair, Google has a new glasses initiative, OpenAI has reportedly considered smart glasses, and Apple is apparently planning to announce Ray-Ban Meta-like smart glasses next year (and it’s worth noting that former Apple CEO Tim Cook has repeatedly praised AR in the past). It’s clear they all see the next frontier as glasses with tech like cameras and screens that sit on your head. Specs will be the first real test of what AR glasses can be. But even after Snap’s years of work, they still might be coming out too soon.

title: watchOS 27: Siri app lets you continue existing chats, though it’s a bit hidden
snippet: Apple Watch includes an all-new Siri app in watchOS 27. Unlike the iPhone and iPad versions, it’s a bit less intuitive to use in one way. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch includes an all-new Siri app in watchOS 27. Unlike the iPhone and iPad versions, it’s a bit less intuitive to use in one way.

Siri app comes to iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple Watch

Starting with Apple’s OS 27 software updates, Siri can save chat history for the first time.

This is useful for two reasons. First, you can easily reference something you looked up before without asking again. Second, you can actually resume a conversation with Siri without starting over from scratch. 

Having context in the chat thread changes how you need to communicate with Siri. Suddenly, you’re able to speak more naturally without explaining exactly what you mean each time. It’s a bit like sticking with one customer support agent instead of jumping around a phone tree.

Anyway, Siri apps for iPhone, iPad, and Mac make picking up the conversation intuitive and easy. It’s basically like using an iMessage chat thread.

Meanwhile, on the Apple Watch, it’s fair to determine that the Siri app just doesn’t support resuming chats. The chat threads are displayed, but there’s no obvious user interface for continuing the conversation from within the Siri app on Apple Watch.

How to continue Siri chats on Apple Watch 

Fortunately, there’s a way. The trick? Invoking Siri while the chat thread is open in the Siri app. This can be by holding the Digital Crown or by saying Siri/Hey Siri.

Again, it’s not really intuitive, but it works. Siri on watchOS will append whatever your input is to the chat thread in view. 

There’s probably a better way to do this that we’ll see in a future version of watchOS 27. For now, give it a shot.

watchOS 27 is officially available alongside iOS 27. Siri AI requires specific hardware, supported markets, and may be waitlisted before becoming available. 

Apple Watch Series 12 is currently available for pre-order from $399. Apple Watch Ultra 4 is available for pre-order from $799. Both models launch in one week on September 18.

title: iOS 27 adds new Phone app feature that’s an instant favorite
snippet: iOS 27 is packed with new features for apps like Notes, Wallet, Maps, Messages, and more. But one iOS 27 addition that’s especially impressed me is a new Phone feature: Call Context. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 is packed with new features for apps like Notes, Wallet, Maps, Messages, and more. But one iOS 27 addition that’s especially impressed me is a new Phone feature: Call Context.

iOS 27’s Call Context feature puts key info on-screen when you’re on the phone with a business

I’m not a big fan of phone calls, so the Phone app isn’t somewhere I spend much time. But last year in iOS 26, the app had two of my favorite new features: Call Screening and Hold Assist.

Now with iOS 27 this year, Apple has again impressed me with a new Phone app feature.

Call Context is an Apple Intelligence feature that automatically surfaces relevant info on the call screen when you’re on the phone with a business.

Per Apple’s website:

Get relevant information while on a call. Call Context can proactively surface relevant information from across your apps when calling a business — like a confirmation code from Mail when you call an airline.

I’ve had the chance to use Call Context a couple times during the iOS 27 beta. And I’ve very quickly concluded that this is the kind of no-brainer addition that should prove popular.

Recently I booked flights with Southwest Airlines, and later needed to call them about a change. 

When I called, my flight info was automatically put on the screen. My iPhone even offered to read the confirmation number out loud for me on the call.

iOS 27 was also smart enough to include details for another Southwest flight stacked underneath the foremost one. So if Call Context doesn’t show the most relevant info at first, in most cases it should be just a quick tap away.

Call Context is initially available only in English, and it’s limited to iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple Watch models that support Apple Intelligence.

title: iOS 27.2 gives Apple TV a new profiles feature on iPhone
snippet: iOS 27.2 beta 1 arrived today, and with it a key new feature for the Apple TV app on iPhone: user profiles. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 beta 1 arrived today, and with it a key new feature for the Apple TV app on iPhone: user profiles.

iOS 27.2 brings Apple TV profiles to iPhone, a great feature for parents

User profiles are a common feature in the streaming era, but Apple TV has been slow to adopt them.

You’ve been able to set up and switch between different profiles in tvOS for a few years now. But it was only last December with tvOS 26.2 that two key upgrades shipped:

the ability to create profiles for users without an Apple Account, like a young child

kid profiles being limited to age-appropriate content

Those were great changes that were long overdue. But they only worked on TV-based devices, not more personal products like the iPhone.

iOS 27.2 changes that though, bringing support for Apple TV user profiles to the iPhone.

When you launch the Apple TV app in iOS 27.2 beta 1, you’ll see a screen with existing profiles tied to your account. There’s also the option to add a profile.

And before you ask: there is also a button that reads, ‘Don’t Show This Again.’ So if you never want to use profiles on your iPhone, there’s an easy fix.

Like in tvOS, if you select a child’s profile on your iPhone, their TV app will be limited to only TV shows and movies that match the permitted content rating you’ve specified.

For users who ever hand a child their iPhone or iPad to watch TV, the addition of profiles not only ensures that your ‘Continue Watching’ won’t be cluttered by children’s content, it also provides a safer environment for them to only watch appropriate options.

title: Anthropic merging Claude Cowork with chat
snippet: Anthropic announced today that Claude Cowork is being merged with chat. This means Claude will drop from three to two modes: Claude Chat and Claude Code. more…
fullText:
Anthropic announced today that Claude Cowork is being merged with chat. This means Claude will drop from three to two modes: Claude Chat and Claude Code.

The company says the change will roll out over the next few weeks for Pro and Max subscribers. 

Here’s the announcement from Anthropic:

Starting today, Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude. Bring a quick question, or hand over a report due at noon, and Claude takes it from there, even after you’ve closed your laptop. It’s rolling out on Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks, with more plans to follow.

Additionally, Claude’s main view is adding or integrating these features as well:

Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new today, and Claude Design now works inside your conversations too. 

As for why the change is happening, here’s what the company says:

We built Cowork as a separate place for bigger work, and Design for visual work. People used both, and told us the frustrating part was deciding where a task belonged. What they’d started in one also didn’t carry into the other. So we stopped making you choose. Claude can now figure out what a task needs, so what Cowork and Design can do is available from any conversation, with the context, skills, and connectors you already have.

As mentioned, the change isn’t happening overnight. Instead, here’s what to expect:

This is rolling out to Pro and Max plans first, in the Claude app on web, desktop, and mobile over the coming weeks to existing and new users on these plans. There’s nothing to turn on. Team and Free plans will follow soon, and Enterprise admins will hear from us at least 30 days before anything changes for their organizations.

You can read the announcement in full here.

title: Federico Viticci on iOS 27: ‘It’s good to see Apple sweat the details again’
snippet: Federico Viticci’s annual iOS review is always a must-read over at MacStories, and this year is no different. Federico writes that, while iOS 27 isn’t as “flashy” as last year, the update shows that Apple is “still capable of delivering something new while caring about the old.” more…
fullText:
Federico Viticci’s annual iOS review is always a must-read over at MacStories, and this year is no different. 

Federico writes that, while iOS 27 isn’t as “flashy” as last year, the update shows that Apple is “still capable of delivering something new while caring about the old.” 

I value Federico’s opinion on AI, so I was especially keen to read his thoughts on Apple Intelligence and Siri AI in iOS 27. Here’s just one small excerpt: 

The new Siri is not an agentic product that is able to carry out long-running tasks to completion, and it would be downright absurd to compare Siri AI to the likes of ChatGPT Work, Claude Cowork, Grok Bot, Hermes Agent, or OpenClaw. I would love for Siri AI to become that kind of experience, and Apple seems to think it now has a foundation in place to enable agentic behavior at some point. But as things stand now, given my reliance on Notion, Slack, and Superhuman for work, and given the simpler, less intelligent nature of Siri AI, I can’t imagine using Apple’s assistant for productivity purposes.

Instead, I’ve come to appreciate Siri AI for what it is – a much better, smarter Siri that doesn’t aim to replace your favorite agent (yet) – without being upset that it’s not something more.

I’ve thoroughly enjoyed using Siri with Apple Notes, Reminders, HomeKit, and third-party apps such as AskPlay, Monologue, Alyx, MusicBox, and LookUp. I’ve found Siri AI to be best at quick, one-off interactions that perhaps involve a couple of follow-ups, but not anything much longer than that. If I realize that a question I have requires deeper research and more back-and-forth, that’s where I fall back to ChatGPT or the excellent Open Minis for iOS.

Federico’s review meticulously covers every detail of iOS 27, with his always-insightful commentary. You can read it over on the MacStories website. Also be sure to read the full MacStories review of macOS 27 Golden Gate and watchOS 27, both written by John Voorhees. Check out the Club MacStories membership program to unlock a whole bunch of extras.

And of course, read along with our coverage of iOS 27 here at 9to5Mac as well. We have roundups of new features, how-tos, guides, and much more.

title: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 needs battery banks that actually fit; iPhone Duo might help
snippet: Magnetic battery banks aren’t everyone’s cup of tea, but it’s hard to argue with the convenience factor they deliver. Samsung’s camera design already makes these difficult on Galaxy devices, but Galaxy Z Fold 8 only makes matters worse with a short form factor that leaves battery banks hanging way over the edge. iPhone Duo might help matters here, but the same old problem remains. more…
fullText:
Magnetic battery banks aren’t everyone’s cup of tea, but it’s hard to argue with the convenience factor they deliver. Samsung’s camera design already makes these difficult on Galaxy devices, but Galaxy Z Fold 8 only makes matters worse with a short form factor that leaves battery banks hanging way over the edge. iPhone Duo might help matters here, but the same old problem remains.

The Qi ring on Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 is very low on any already-short frame, which leaves magnetic wallets and battery banks well out of place on the foldable, hanging down below the bottom of the device. It’s a problem begging for a solution, and one that other wide foldables are also going to run into.

Is the iPhone Duo the solution to Samsung’s problem?

Not just yet. The iPhone Duo is bringing about a new wave of smaller Qi2 battery banks to fit the short and stout form factor. BMX just launched one of the first models with a solid-state battery specifically designed to fit the Duo. It has a kickstand ring and a little display to show battery percentage, with 5,000 mAh of power and a fit that doesn’t hang below the bottom edge of Apple’s first foldable.

	

I was hoping this would work on the Galaxy Z Fold 8, but BMX tells 9to5Google that this power bank won’t fit on Samsung’s device due to the camera. Foiled again!

Samsung’s camera design continues to be a problem here, which is why it’s nice that Samsung might be moving to something new on some of its Galaxy S27 devices. But, in the meantime, it remains a problem for existing users.

While BMX says the battery bank won’t fit perfectly on the Fold 8, it’s likely still a major improvement. The $80 power bank is available for purchase now, and it probably won’t be the last battery designed for the Duo and, in turn, a better fit for the Fold 8.

fullText:
Following some past leaks, another new report reveals basically everything about the upcoming “Lenovo Googlebook 15” including its full specs, but without a price tag.

Google said that the first wave of Googlebook laptops would have a premium focus, and the company wasn’t kidding based on this latest leak. Intel Core Ultra 5 325

16GB / 32GB LPDDR5x RAM

256GB / 512GB storage

15.3-inch, 2880 x 1800 OLED, 120hz, 16:10, touchscreen

fullText:
Trackers like Apple’s AirTag have been a great piece of added utility to the mobile ecosystem, and every option has a slightly different look and feel. Samsung’s Galaxy SmartTag 3 is rumored to be launching soon and, thanks to a pair of leaks, we know exactly what to expect.

SammyGuru and Dealabs have both obtained more details on the upcoming Galaxy SmartTag 3, starting with some official-looking images from the former.

These reveal that Samsung’s new design lacks any sort of built-in mounting mechanism. Instead, the squircle shape requires an add-on to be connected to a keychain, bag loop, or anything else. It does result in a smaller design from the looks of it, but it’s a pretty big departure.

As pictured below, both prior generations of Galaxy SmartTag have had some sort of built-in loop for mounting, and this is also commonplace among other third-party smarttrackers from the likes of Pebblebee, Chipolo, and more. Apple’s AirTag, Motorola’s Moto Tag, and Google’s upcoming Pixel Tag all lack built-in mounting options too, though.

	

Functionally, this leak also reveals that SmartTag 3 will have UWB and Bluetooth, as well as an IP67 rating and around 500 days of battery life. There’s no mention of what network it will use, but it’s almost certainly exclusive to Samsung’s network rather than using Google’s Find Hub network in any capacity.

The other report claims pricing will be unchanged at €39.99 ($29.99 US), though a 4-pack will go from €129.99 to $139.99 this time around.

title: India escalates Apple probe over alleged iOS 18 issues that incurred repair costs
snippet: India’s Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has reportedly escalated its probe into whether Apple should be held responsible for an iOS 18 update that allegedly caused display and microphone issues on some iPhones. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
India’s Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has reportedly escalated its probe into whether Apple should be held responsible for an iOS 18 update that allegedly caused display and microphone issues on some iPhones. Here are the details.

Apple faces yet another probe in India

As reported by Reuters, Apple is facing renewed regulatory scrutiny over the iOS 18 update, from 2024.

According to the country’s CCPA, the update allegedly “​led to screen display and microphone malfunctions among other issues, forcing customers to pay for related repairs, as no warranty is provided on software,” says Reuters.

Apple has denied the allegations, while also stressing that not offering a warranty for software issues is standard industry practice. Still, the CCPA is unconvinced and has recently escalated the matter to its investigation wing for a more detailed probe.

Here’s Reuters:

If found guilty, Apple may have to pay fines but more importantly could be ​forced to issue refunds or make changes to its business practices.

Reuters says the investigation covers complaints from users who reported green, pink, or white lines appearing on their iPhone displays after installing iOS 18.

Apple, meanwhile, says the case is based on just 75 complaints and that it found no systemic issues or safety concerns with iOS 18 in India. Apple further argues that requiring every software-related problem to be covered by warranty “would effectively ⁠convert any software provider into an insurer against all technological risk.”

The CCPA, however, argues that the issue goes beyond the number of individual complaints, accusing Apple of violating the rights of “consumers as a class.” The regulator also says that charging customers for repairs due to problems allegedly caused by Apple’s own software could amount to an unfair trade practice.

This probe is just one of several recent spats between Apple and Indian regulators, as the company is also fighting the Competition Commission of India (CCI) over an App Store antitrust case that could potentially result in a $38 billion fine.

Separately, Apple has repeatedly pushed back against Indian government orders requiring smartphone makers to pre-install a state-run app on devices sold in the country, while one of its major suppliers, Tata, recently faced scrutiny from local regulators over alleged wastewater contamination at an iPhone component plant.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 has subtle design change that Apple didn’t mention
snippet: Apple Watch Series 12 arrives this Friday (pre-order here), but some upgraders might be surprised by a subtle design change that Apple didn’t mention in its announcement: larger bezels around the display. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 arrives this Friday (pre-order here), but some upgraders might be surprised by a subtle design change that Apple didn’t mention in its announcement: larger bezels around the display.

Apple Watch Series 12 has slightly larger case size for increased bezels around display

If you track the history of Apple product design, one clear trend is that the company likes to reduce bezels around the display as much as possible.

Over time, the iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple Watch have all progressively shrunk the bezels for a design that puts all focus on the display.

But with Apple Watch Series 12, the reverse is happening as bezels increase slightly.

Per Apple’s website, here’s the breakdown of case sizes for Series 12 compared to the last two models:

Series 12

Series 11

Series 10

42mm

42mm by 37mm

42mm by 36mm

42mm by 36mm

46mm

46mm by 40mm

46mm by 39mm

46mm by 39mm

As you can see, while Apple Watch Series 12 has the same case height as its predecessors, the width is slightly larger. Per this comparison page though, all three models have the same display sizes. 

42mm: 374 by 446 pixels with 970 sq mm display area

46mm: 416 by 496 pixels with 1196 sq mm display area

What this means is that compared to previous models, Apple Watch Series 12’s display is slightly undersized for its larger case size. As a result, it has more noticeable bezels around the display.

Series 12 packs a ton of internal upgrades, like the new Health Sensing System and S11 chip. So it’s unsurprising that the case size would need to change some.

But if you’re upgrading from a recent Apple Watch model, just know that the design might look like a small step backwards rather than following the standard trend of shrinking bezels.

What do you think of Apple’s decision to increase bezel size on Apple Watch Series 12? Let us know in the comments.

title: Possible Google device at FCC could be Wear OS-powered fitness tracker
snippet: A new piece of hardware passed through FCC certification today, and the evidence points to it being a Wear OS-powered device made by Google. more…
fullText:
A new piece of hardware passed through FCC certification today, and the evidence points to it being a Wear OS-powered device made by Google.

This “Wireless Device” — as it’s officially labeled — comes from Goertek, which is already known for manufacturing various generations of Pixel Buds.

The “G8BL6” model name matches Google’s usual pattern for first-party hardware. Meanwhile, the e-label points to the existence of a screen, with the access method being Settings > System > Regulatory Information. That is identical to how you access the e-label on the Pixel Watch today. 

This would suggest the presence of Wear OS, with that possibility further bolstered by how the Android Debug Bridge (ADB) was leveraged during the testing process.

	

On the connectivity front, this device has Bluetooth LE and Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS), or GPS. The former uses a “Metal frame Antenna.”

Taken together, G8BL6 is most likely a Google fitness tracker powered by Wear OS, though the lack of Wi-Fi is curious. This would be a new form factor for the platform, raising questions about whether the OS is battery-efficient enough.

This filing comes as an unknown Google tracker was spotted in Pixel 11 advertising this August. We saw a vertical, pill-shaped display with a Pixel Watch-esque band. The watch face is very familiar, down to the existing Wear OS complications for fitness.

Following the Fitbit Air, this would make sense as a successor to the popular Fitbit Charge line, which is currently priced at $160 and last updated in 2023.

title: Google Wallet passes get fullscreen redesign on Android
snippet: Following the homepage revamp with search in May, Google Wallet is now rolling out a redesign of passes on Android. more…
fullText:
Following the homepage revamp with search in May, Google Wallet is now rolling out a redesign of passes on Android.

Instead of a small rectangular card against the Dynamic Color background, passes in Google Wallet now take up the entire screen. This includes theming the entire background of the page with the brand’s primary color. 

Scrolling down lets you access key actions like calling associated phone numbers and visiting the official website. Under “Settings,” you can edit the nickname and control how it’s used. These preferences were previously accessed from the three-dot overflow menu.

Old vs. new

	

Curiously, this redesign allows you to access the old look in its entirety by tapping the rewind icon in the top-right corner. 

This redesign applies to all loyalty cards and boarding passes, including manually created ones. Transit cards still use the old design. 

Visually, it’s absolutely a nicer experience, though some backgrounds can be quite bright, especially if you’re using passes at night.

As of today, we’re seeing this redesign widely rolled out.

title: The Google Pixel is fine and all, but still needs a ‘Ryzen moment’ [Video]
snippet: At what stage does “fine” feel like it’s doing heavy lifting for problems that might appear in the future? It’s something talked about around the Tensor chip in Pixel phones, but isn’t it about time we saw real-world performance gains? The truth is, we probably need a Ryzen moment for the Tensor chip. more…
fullText:
At what stage does “fine” feel like it’s doing heavy lifting for problems that might appear in the future? It’s something talked about around the Tensor chip in Pixel phones, but isn’t it about time we saw real-world performance gains? The truth is, we probably need a Ryzen moment for the Tensor chip.

For those who aren’t fully plugged into the history of desktop computing, AMD, or “Team Red,” long languished behind Intel when it came to desktop-tier performance CPUs. 

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

The Bulldozer architecture used on the FX series of chips was a bit of a disaster. Intel capitalized on this misstep completely, locking the consumer market into a complacent four-core monopoly for nearly a decade because it simply had no pressure to innovate.

	

With this percolating in the back of my mind, during a recent podcast episode, and spurred on by a Reddit comment I can no longer find over on /r/GooglePixel, there’s a strange sense of déjà vu applicable to Google’s smartphone lineup. There needs to be more than just incremental gains and AI being touted on a $1,000 phones best chip. 

Side note: if you are the original poster, please get in touch; you had me thinking about this more broadly and deserve credit for doing so.

While it’s hard not to laud the Pixel line for the brilliant software, extensive and unmatched feature drops, and mostly excellent camera processing, it’s the Google Tensor processor that is almost always the biggest caveat or talking point. 

Right now, the Tensor lineup has spent years echoing the systemic flaws of AMD’s Bulldozer era. Stumbling, faltering, and just about hanging in there. I think most of us can agree that Google doesn’t just need an incremental chip upgrade. To truly unlock the potential of the Pixel line, the company needs its very own “Ryzen moment.”

Back to Bulldozer for a second, because I’m not sure everyone is fully aware of chips built on this architecture. FX chips ran hot and throttled under load, were power-hungry, and, in many cases, lost to AMD’s own previous-generation Phenom II chips in terms of performance. They were able to cling to survival more because of very low prices than anything else.

Bulldozer was ditched in favor of the Zen project. Each successive architectural enhancement saw improvements, and in 2017, the first Ryzen 1000 series desktop processors blew everyone out of the water. Multi-threaded performance that rivaled $1,000+ chips from the market leader, Intel. Since then, AMD has been on a tear with Ryzen, beating a complacent Intel in practically all areas.

You can see the parallels between these mid-2010s AMD CPUs and the last few generations of Google’s Tensor chips, but this feels like the perfect blueprint.

It definitely feels that, like AMD in 2012, Google is sacrificing pure hardware efficiency in favor of trying to capture something less important, all while trying to lean into the key AI selling point. It’s a big, bold bet that makes less sense to true tech nerds, as most of the best off-the-shelf Qualcomm chips are, in many ways and metrics, better at AI processing right now than Tensor.

Some of the early Tensor problems fall at Samsung’s doorstep. Exynos chips have never had a great reputation, and relying on Samsung Foundry likely meant some limitations. You may also remember that Qualcomm briefly switched manufacturing to Samsung’s 4nm node for the Snapdragon 8 Gen 1. The chipmaker later moved production to TSMC for the follow-up Snapdragon 8+ Gen 1 chip due to poor manufacturing yields and efficiency issues with Samsung Foundry. This prompted substantial efficiency gains with heat reduction and sustained performance improvements.

Maybe Google eventually realized it needed a similar escape route and took similar steps. Alas, this hasn’t quite worked out to do what maybe we as nerds wanted. The pre-launch talk around the transition to TSMC manufacturing was probably spurred on more by hope than anything concrete – despite numerous leaks. 

I, like many others, expected a clean-slate architecture built on a superior node might finally deliver the performance gains that had been sorely missing for four generations. It’s frustrating and annoying that this hasn’t come to fruition.

Fast forward to the present day. We are now two generations into Google’s TSMC era, with the Tensor G5 and the current Tensor G6 powering the Pixel 11 lineup.

This transition has only eradicated some of the problems, but still leaves us with a now glaring performance gap. The year-over-year gains have been respectable increments, but they are not quite the massive generational “leaps” fans were hoping for before the switch.

I’m tempering my ire a little bit, though. We’ve not seen any major gains yet, but the groundwork is at the very least in place. That said, there’s only so long the company can allow Qualcomm to keep building an enormous performance gap.

A performance gap that, let’s be real, lots of people don’t care all that much about when using their phone. I’d put myself in that category, but I’d be lying if I said it wouldn’t be nice to have a Qualcomm-beating chip that can do everything a modern phone can without breaking a sweat.

While I might not be too disappointed, this matters to people buying phones, especially $1,000 phones. It helps market your product, selling on the promise of unrivaled performance. The Tensor platform is “fine” in that you likely won’t feel a major difference texting or looking at Instagram, and it’s true that Google tunes Android to feel as fluid as possible on a Pixel phone. Intensive things? It’s a bit of a mixed bag and a different story.

My question is, why make it harder for the engineers? A little extra breathing room would be more than welcome by practically everyone. By allowing Qualcomm and Apple to build an enormous, compounding performance gap year after year, Google is playing a dangerous game.

It limits what the phone can handle when pushed, whether that means recording extended 4K video clips without getting a thermal warning or processing heavy background tasks. That’s not to mention the things we’re missing out on, like local 8K video recording and many other video-centric functions that rival premium devices have shipped with for years.

More importantly, this performance gap directly threatens Google’s industry-leading promise of seven years of OS updates. 

I probably don’t need to tell you that a chip that feels just about “good enough” today will likely struggle under the weight of Android operating systems in the late 2020s and early 2030s. I’m still worried about the long-term longevity and thermal headroom required to ensure a Pixel actually lasts through its promised support window. 

7 years is a long time, and with prices ballooning and no sign of coming down any time soon, there are people who will be keeping their phones longer into that support lifecycle than ever before. Using a phone for 5 years without switching is likely to become the norm.

Apple is another parallel that Google has to keep in mind, and they show exactly where the broader computing landscape is going.

Look at what Cupertino did earlier this year with the MacBook Neo. They took the A18 Pro, which is a smartphone chip, and threw it straight into a fanless, entry-level laptop running a full, desktop-grade operating system. They didn’t need to strip macOS down or compromise the user experience to make it happen. The silicon is simply so efficient and so inherently powerful that it treats a desktop workflow like a walk in the park.

This laptop paradigm is precisely why Google desperately needs a high-performance breakthrough. It isn’t just about making the Pixel 11 feel snappy because there’s a bigger ecosystem picture that needs to be considered. The company has spent the last couple of years laying the foundation for full desktop windowing in Android. It’s clear that the company wants devices to function as actual desktop machines the second you hook them up to an external monitor.

Imagine a future first-party Googlebook, or a pro-tier Android productivity tablet that docks into a mouse and keyboard setup, running entirely off the custom silicon in your pocket. I’m still surprised it hasn’t taken off, given how futuristic it seems to my millennial brain, but if there is any life in this vision, it completely lives and dies by the quality of the processor. Which is likely why most people are happy to stick to a dedicated laptop plus mobile in most cases.

If Google wants Android to transition from a mobile OS into a genuine productivity system that spans phones, laptops, and potentially desktops, Tensor cannot just be an “okay” component for scrolling social media. It needs the raw architectural grunt to act as a proper desktop computer without turning into a pocket-warmer.

When AMD launched Ryzen in 2017, the initial 1000-series chips didn’t instantly obliterate Intel in pure single-core speed. It took time, patience, and consecutive generational refinements with Zen 2 and Zen 3 to achieve complete, undeniable dominance, especially in the gaming space.

Moving to TSMC hasn’t instantly gifted Google the mobile performance crown with the Tensor G5 or G6; it at least feels like the company has finally established a stable, thermally efficient base to iterate on. The iterating is definitely tiny right now, but I’m desperately hoping a breakthrough might come with the next version.

	

For years, Google’s Android engineers have been performing optimization miracles, almost shoehorning what I would consider the best mobile software to glide smoothly over what some might call “compromised” hardware.

What kind of funny is that despite this, Pixel phones do often age better as a result, but engineering shouldn’t be an endless exercise in potential damage control. Hand-waving the Pixel 11 performance as good enough sometimes feels reductive, and there’s only so many times it can be deemed acceptable. We need chipset performance gains, not just more AI papering over cracks. To weaken my argument somewhat, I don’t doubt they will come with more time.

If we get a true Ryzen moment with their custom TSMC architecture in the coming generations, Google can finally market the Pixel ecosystem on the promise of unrivaled, unthrottled performance across phones, tablets, and heck, maybe even desktops if Android works on the form factor. The foundation is poured, and the blueprints are drawn. It is time for Google to stop compromising and finally unleash its inner Team Red.

title: Here’s everything new for Apple Wallet in iOS 27
snippet: iOS 27 launched today for iPhone, here’s what’s new for the Apple Wallet app in the latest major software update. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 launched today for iPhone, here’s what’s new for the Apple Wallet app in the latest major software update.

Create a Pass

Apple Wallet is always improving, including several recent updates in iOS 26. But iOS 27 brings even more new features to Wallet users.

Create a Pass is a new feature you’ll find when you hit the + button inside iOS 27’s Wallet app.

It enables you to create a pass in one of two ways: 

Scan a physical pass to import it using your iPhone’s camera and visual intelligence

Create a pass manually from scratch

The former requires the next-gen Apple Intelligence capabilities. Creating a pass manually, meanwhile, provides you with three options: Standard, Membership, and Event.

The goal is that Apple wants to make the Wallet app your go-to hub for all kinds of passes, whether they’re digital or physical.

Split Bill with Apple Cash

Split Bill with Apple Cash is another iOS 27 addition to Wallet.

When using the new Siri mode in the Camera app to scan a receipt, you’ll see the option to Split Bill with Apple Cash.

From here, the Wallet app opens and you’ll be presented with options to ‘Request’ payment from others or ‘Pay Your Share.’ It’s quick, easy, and offers another reason to use Apple Cash.

Recurring transactions for Apple Card

If you use Apple Card, there’s a convenient new hub in iOS 27 for all your recurring transactions.

Behind the three-dot icon in the top-right corner of the Apple Card screen, there’s a new ‘Recurring’ option.

This shows you all upcoming recurring transactions. You can see them on a calendar month view, or listed out.

Essentially, this new section provides an easy way to track current subscriptions and anticipate upcoming charges.

Hotel Key upgrades

Beyond some small UI updates and a refreshed app icon, the last noteworthy iOS 27 feature for Apple Wallet involves hotel keys.

Per a press release, here’s what Apple says is coming to hotel keys soon:

With iOS 27, Apple Wallet will offer an enhanced key experience for participating hotels and resorts. Today’s key experience allows guests to seamlessly unlock their rooms and hotel amenities using their iPhone or Apple Watch. And with the new enhanced key experience, they will also be able to view even more details about their trips, receive timely updates about booked activities, access services available during their stay, and more — all in one place in Apple Wallet.

iOS 27 also adds an ‘Insights’ feature to Wallet for users in select territories. It lets you track spending across multiple cards. But in the US at least, that feature isn’t available despite being present in some iOS 27 betas.

title: Google rolls out Motion Assist bubbles to Pixel, Samsung
snippet: After announcing earlier this month, Google has rolled out Motion Assist to Pixel and Samsung phones running Android 17. more…
fullText:
After announcing earlier this month, Google has rolled out Motion Assist to Pixel and Samsung phones running Android 17.

The aim is to reduce motion sickness when you’re in a car, bus, or other moving vehicle with an onscreen bubbles overlay that adjusts to the device’s motion.

To enable, search for “motion assist” in the Settings app or open the Quick Settings editor and scroll down to “From system apps” (on Pixel). The long route is Settings app > Google > All services tab > Personal & device safety > Motion assist. Part of Google Play services, it appears alongside Advanced Protection and Theft protection.

This menu lets you have Motion Assist automatically “Start in a moving vehicle,” but Google also recommends adding a Quick Settings Tile to manually enable and disable “from any screen.” Once active, there’s also a silent system notification that lets you disable with a tap. On most phones, you get two columns of shapes on the left and right edges.

	

The Customize menu lets you adjust:

Color: Based on system (Dynamic Color), Red, Yellow, Green, Blue

Shape: Circle, Square, Pentagon, Diamond

Opacity: Slider

Randomization: “Color and shape change every few seconds”

As of today, Motion Assist has widely rolled out on all our Google Pixel and Samsung Galaxy (Fold 8 series) devices running Android 17. Be sure to restart your phone if it’s not yet live. We’re seeing the bubbles with version 26.33.32 of Google Play services.

title: Battery draining faster after updating to iOS 27? Don’t panic …
snippet: If you’ve just updated your iPhone to iOS 27, you may have felt concerned after seeing your battery draining faster than usual, as well as your device getting hot in normal use. If so, there’s no cause for panic. While both effects may be very real, they are only temporary … more…
fullText:
If you’ve just updated your iPhone to iOS 27, you may have felt concerned after seeing your battery draining faster than usual, as well as your device getting hot in normal use.

If so, there’s no cause for panic. While both effects may be very real, they are only temporary … 

Any time you update to a new version of iOS, there will be some things going on in the background for some time afterwards. This is particularly true for major updates.

These CPU-intensive background processes will often see your iPhone getting hotter than usual, and consuming significantly more battery power. Apple specifically warns about this.

Immediately after completing an update, particularly a major release, you might notice a temporary impact on battery life and thermal performance. This is normal, because your device needs time to complete the setup process in the background, including indexing data and files for search, downloading new assets, and updating apps.

The impact of iOS 27 is bigger than usual, thanks to the need to completely re-index your device for use with Siri AI. This process may last several days.

The good news is that once all of the background processing has completed, your device will return to normal. Indeed, the efficiency of iOS 27 means that you may find that battery life is improved once the update has finished all of the under-the-hood work.

fullText:
Andrew Webster

 

is an entertainment editor covering streaming, virtual worlds, and every single Pokémon video game. Andrew joined The Verge in 2012, writing over 4,000 stories.

After teasing a music-related reveal a few days ago, Rockstar has officially announced the soundtrack for Grand Theft Auto VI. Called Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album, the soundtrack will feature 34 songs, which Rockstar describes as “brand-new, original tracks.” Based on the first six singles, which are available today, it seems that the collection will span a pretty wide range of genres, with everyone from Keith Richards to Travis Scott contributing.

Here’s what’s been confirmed so far:

Yung Lean - “That’s It” (feat. Future & Metro Boomin)

Travis Scott - “RHYNO” (prod. by Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo)

CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso, PinkPantheress, Fred again.. & Etienne de Crécy - “Sexy Magic”

Morgan Wallen - “Last Thing You Need”

Rauw Alejandro - “Macacoa 2000”

Keith Richards - “Bright Lights, Big City”

The soundtrack will be coming to all major streaming services, and Rockstar says that it’ll be available on both CD and vinyl. It’ll be launching on November 19th, the same day as the game.

The reveal of the album is just the latest Rockstar announcement as GTA VI approaches it’s long-awaited and oft-delayed launch. Last month the studio debuted a lengthy first-look at gameplay, which premiered on Netflix before being released on YouTube. The anticipation around the game is so big that almost every major game publisher — with the notable exception of Nintendo — has gotten out of its way.

title: Hands-on: Dbrand’s MNML Pixel 11 Pro cases are simply good, and that’s the point [Gallery]
snippet: Dbrand is definitely best-known for its flashy skins and bombastic personality, but the company is now launching a more subtle brand in “MNML,” aiming to offer dead-simple cases that are comfortable and have good quality. These are available for the latest Pixel 11 Pro phones and, in person, they certainly get the job done. more…
fullText:
Dbrand is definitely best-known for its flashy skins and bombastic personality, but the company is now launching a more subtle brand in “MNML,” aiming to offer dead-simple cases that are comfortable and have good quality. These are available for the latest Pixel 11 Pro phones and, in person, they certainly get the job done.

Available in four colors – black, navy, tan, and burgundy – MNML cases are true to their (shortened) name. The case lacks any notable branding outside of the four letters off to the side. The buttons have a metallic finish, while the case itself is a polymer material with a rough texture.

In the hand, it’s grippy without being too grippy – looking at you, Google and Samsung – while not being overly thick either. Over the past couple of years, I’ve been going caseless more and more often, but this is exactly the sort of case I would want to use, as it’s not adding a ton of unnecessary bulk. 

On Pixel 11 Pro XL, the cutouts and fit are both absolutely perfect – it helps that there’s no SIM tray to worry about, which I recently found out dbrand bafflingly leaves inaccessible in its full-coverage skins (this is dumb). The buttons are clicky, though the chunky shape and size feels a little weird to the touch. I wish the power button had a different texture so as to stand out.

	

The built-in magnets are very strong too, perhaps even more so than the array already found in Pixel 11 Pro.

These are dead simple cases, and in a way an upgraded version of the infamous Spigen Thin Fit. It feels better than the Thin Fit usually does while having 10% more personality in its colors. 

At $40 a pop (discounted if you buy multiple), it’s not cheap. But it’s a good case across the board, so you won’t regret picking one up.

title: The streamers are fighting over Halloween
snippet: The Toronto International Film Festival is a place to go to see the future of film, but this year it also provided a glimpse at what is coming very soon in the realm of streaming. Four different streamers - Peacock, Netflix, Amazon, and AMC - all premiered early looks at upcoming horror-adjacent series that are dropping very soon. And by doing it at TIFF, they showed just how important the month of October has become in the realm of streaming. Perhaps the most high-profile is Carrie, which is coming to Prime Video. An adaptation of the classic Stephen King novel, which has already been turned into no fewer than three feature films, this ver … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
The Toronto International Film Festival is a place to go to see the future of film, but this year it also provided a glimpse at what is coming very soon in the realm of streaming. Four different streamers — Peacock, Netflix, Amazon, and AMC — all premiered early looks at upcoming horror-adjacent series that are dropping very soon. And by doing it at TIFF, they showed just how important the month of October has become in the realm of streaming.

Perhaps the most high-profile is Carrie, which is coming to Prime Video. An adaptation of the classic Stephen King novel, which has already been turned into no fewer than three feature films, this version of Carrie is notable in particular because of who is helming it. Mike Flanagan has done a handful of King adaptations in the past — including Doctor Sleep and The Life of Chuck — but the director is perhaps best-known for his work on limited series for Netflix. That includes the likes of The Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass, and The Fall of the House of Usher. Those series came out on a near-annual basis between 2018 and 2023, making Flanagan’s particular blend of dramatic horror a staple of Netflix in October.

Then, in 2022, Amazon poached Flanagan to work on projects for Prime Video. The first of these is Carrie, which starts streaming on October 7th. It still tells largely the same story as its predecessors — a young girl’s destructive psychic powers awaken after getting bullied in high school — but it updates it in a few ways. For starters, the story has been thoroughly modernized, with much of the bullying happening in cyberspace. But since it’s a series instead of a movie, Carrie also stretches out the story, which gives it the space to explore the teen drama a little, and also adds plenty of opportunities for Flanagan’s trademark lengthy monologues. I’ve only seen the premiere episode so far, but early on it’s a combination of flavors that work really well together.

Netflix, meanwhile, has filled in the gap with a new series called Below, which premieres on October 8th, just a day after Carrie starts streaming. I saw the first two episodes earlier this week — there will be six in total — and while it’s a different kind of story compared to the likes of Hill House, it has a similarly dark and mysterious energy. Below is about what seems to be an ancient sea creature that begins terrorizing a small fishing village in Newfoundland, on the east coast of Canada. From what I’ve seen, the show does a great job of steadily building the terror of the creature’s reveal, while also mixing the scares with a healthy dose of family drama, led by Josh Hartnett as a struggling fisher who is struggling to keep his family together.

Then there’s Peacock, which is joining the fray with a prequel series. Fans of Friday the 13th will know that Jason’s mom plays a pivotal role in the very first film, and the new show Crystal Lake explores how she got to that point. It stars Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees, a single mother who is thrown into a pit of despair and disbelief when her young son drowns to death.

I went into the show thinking that I didn’t really need to know much more about the backstory of Jason’s mother, but the first two episodes that premiered at TIFF — and Cardellini’s performance in particular — have me second-guessing that. Crystal Lake is surprisingly tense and dramatic, but, given its connection to Friday the 13th, it also has slasher-movie levels of gore and gross-out deaths, ones that are so brutal they approach comedy. If nothing else, it gets off to a very strong start. All episodes of Crystal Lake hit Peacock on October 15th.

Rounding out the list is Yaga, a supernatural detective series that’s coming to AMC Plus on October 23rd. Unfortunately I wasn’t able to catch the premiere screening for the show, but it does seem promising, with a cast that includes Carrie-Anne Moss and Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams, and a very intriguing trailer:

What has become abundantly clear in 2026 is that horror is big business. The likes of Backrooms and Obsession have exploded at the box office, while Widow’s Bay had a dominating night at the Emmys. So it only makes sense that streamers are continuing to capitalize on the trend, and using TIFF as a showcase event. October is going to be a very busy month for horror fans.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 review: More personal than ever before
snippet: The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 are all about what’s happening underneath. Headlined by a new Health Sensing System, they bring some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years. I’ve spent the last week with the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Here’s everything you need to know. Buy Apple Watch Series 12 from $390 (Reg. $399) Buy Apple Watch Ultra 4 Black from $780 (Reg. $799) more…
fullText:
The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 are all about what’s happening underneath. Headlined by a new Health Sensing System, they bring some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years.

I’ve spent the last week with the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Here’s everything you need to know.

Buy Apple Watch Series 12 from $390 (Reg. $399)

Buy Apple Watch Ultra 4 Black from $780 (Reg. $799)

Design

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 look the same as their predecessors. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes in the same two titanium finishes as before: Natural and Black. My review unit is the Natural finish.

For the Apple Watch Series 12, the real design story is in the colors and finishes.

First, there are some very minor changes in the dimensions of the Apple Watch Series 12. Apple’s tech specs page details that the display area is about 2% smaller than the Series 10 and Series 11. The overall pixel count, however, hasn’t changed. With that slight reduction in display area, the casing is about 1mm wider on the Apple Watch Series 12.

In practice, none of this is noticeable in the real world. The Apple Watch’s display still stretches near the edge of the casing. When you think about the revamped health sensing system (more on that below), it’s especially impressive Apple has maintained that design.

The Apple Watch Series 12 is available in three materials: aluminum, titanium, and ceramic.

Aluminum comes in four finishes: Dark Bronze, Light Gold, Black, and Space Gray. The aluminum version also switches from Ion-X to Ceramic Shield 2 for the front glass.

My Apple Watch Series 12 review unit is the black aluminum finish. Unlike last year’s Jet Black aluminum case, the black Apple Watch Series 12 is a matte finish. I think I’m partial to the Jet Black look personally, but I understand Apple switches things up on a year-to-year basis and it could return at some point in the future.

Space Gray
Light Gold
Dark Bronze

In my hands-on time with all the Apple Watch Series 12 aluminum colors last week, Dark Bronze stood out most. It’s an elegant finish that is unlike any previous aluminum Apple Watch. The Light Gold is also a really nice color for fans of gold. The Apple Watch Series 12 isn’t available in silver aluminum, but the space gray is light enough that I think it will tick that box for most people.

Titanium in Radiant Gold

The Apple Watch Series 12 in titanium is available in two finishes: Radiant Gold and Natural. In comparison, the titanium Apple Watch Series 11 came in Natural, Gold, and Slate.

The Radiant Gold is striking. Based on the appearance and how it differs from last year’s color, I think Apple’s goal is clear: to make the titanium Apple Watch Series 12 look as much like real gold as possible, but without actually using real gold. People have a lot of strong opinions about what “real gold” actually looks like, but to my eye Apple has done a great job with the Radiant Gold titanium on the Series 12.

Pearl white ceramic

Saving the best for last, the Apple Watch Series 12 in ceramic is available in two finishes: Night Blue and Pearl White. The last time Apple released a ceramic watch was with the Series 5 in 2019, and it quickly became a fan favorite.

I only spent a few minutes with the ceramic Apple Watch Series 12 at last week’s Apple event. The Night Blue is nice, but I immediately gravitated towards the Pearl White. It’s not quite as white as the Series 5, with a very soft off-white glow to it depending on the lighting.

Health tracking

The big change to the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the new Health Sensing System, which brings what I think is the biggest upgrade to the Apple Watch’s health suite in years.

This starts with a new design for sensing hardware. Apple outlines three aspects to this:

Electrodes get more contact area without the sensor growing. This enables better skin contact during ECG readings.

The photodiodes have been redesigned and are now arranged in a ring to capture more reflected light.

The green LEDs are larger, for more reliable readings while you’re moving, and more power efficient.

This enables the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 to take more accurate and more frequent background heart rate measurements. That is, more heart rate readings when not doing a workout.

Previous Apple Watch models attempted to capture your background heart rate every five minutes when you were mostly stationary.

Apple says the new Health Sensing System delivers “the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” In a study of more than 1,000 participants, Apple says the Series 12 achieved statistically better overall accuracy than every competing wearable it tested across workouts and daily activities.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 offer a big improvement. They will capture your heart rate every five seconds, regardless of whether you’re moving or stationary. Having such frequent and accurate heart rate readings unlocks new levels of data and insight.

When measuring your heart rate once every five minutes while stationary, previous Apple Watch models had an inherent blind spot. They either didn’t capture moments where your heart rate increased while not working out, or they captured one or two arbitrary readings somewhere in the middle of those moments.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 not only take more readings, they take readings while you’re in motion. You can see how things like hauling groceries, doing yard work, and shoveling snow impact your heart rate.

Apple has also added several new ways to view your heart rate data. First, the Heart Rate app on Apple Watch has been redesigned, so you can now see your heart rate and a graph of readings from the last two minutes.

There are also two new heart rate complications for your watch face that show your heart rate at a glance.

In my one week with the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, I’ve found that added data very insightful. I’m learning more about how little things I do throughout the day impact my heart rate. For example, I can visualize the impact of a late afternoon cup of coffee, or the impact of a stressful moment at work.

Beyond simply giving you more raw data, Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 proactively use the more frequent heart rate readings to enable new features and improvements.

First, Apple says the data enables improved calorie estimates. I haven’t noticed much change in my data here, but it might become clearer once I’ve worn the new Apple Watch for more than a week.

One thing I had hoped to see was the more frequent heart rate measurements would improve automatic workout detection. At least in my testing so far, that doesn’t seem to be the case. 

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 also now sample heart rate variability (HRV) at a higher rate than before. Previously, it captured HRV once every two hours, but the new Apple Watch models enable measurements as often as once every five minutes while at rest.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 also now track recovery HRV, which is best at recognizing daily signals of stress and fatigue. The new Apple Watch models also continue to measure overall HRV, best at identifying broader health signals, as they have done for years.

Furthermore, Apple is integrating recovery HRV measurements into overnight vitals.

Vitals

Speaking of Vitals, Apple is making several changes to the broader Vitals experience with the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. First, there’s a new daytime view for Vitals.

Previously, Vitals was an overnight-only report that you would see in the morning. The daytime view shows you your daytime heart rate and HRV, with the idea being you can see if something is out of whack without waiting for your overnight vitals report.

Vitals also now shows you four different categories for your metrics: notably off, slightly off, typical, or favorable. This gives you more granularity than the old two-tier system, which just categorized your metrics as typical or outlier.

I’m a big fan of the Vitals app on Apple Watch, and I’m glad to see Apple making meaningful improvements with the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4. It has routinely caught signs of a looming sickness before I actually felt anything.

The new daytime view will require some additional testing to know just how useful it is, given that it’s limited to just two metrics. Still, there are some really nice improvements to Vitals that tap into the more frequent heart rate and HRV measurements enabled by the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.

Readiness

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 offer a new readiness score that aims to distill all of the data your Apple Watch has on you into a single score.

Apple says that readiness factors in your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score. Your readiness score also updates throughout the day based on naps, activity, and daytime heart rate, so it’s dynamic based on new data that comes in.

You can view your readiness score in the Readiness app on Apple Watch, as well as in the Fitness app on iPhone. It’s also available in the redesigned version of the Health app, which is currently available in beta testing.

The biggest Apple Watch competitors have offered similar scores for years, including Whoop (Whoop Recovery) and Oura (Readiness Score). Apple’s addition of its own readiness feature for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 is its most direct response yet to those other wearables.

I’ve worn an Oura Ring for the past year, primarily for its Readiness Score. I appreciate that number distilling multiple different metrics into a single number I can glance at each morning. It’s felt like a huge gap in the Apple Watch’s software experience, and I’m glad Apple is taking a similar approach now.

Apple Watch’s Readiness score requires one week of sleep data, and I’ve only had my review units for a week. This means I’ve only gotten one Readiness score thus far, so it’s too early to make a determination on how useful Apple’s version of the feature is.

I’m optimistic given the type of data Apple is taking into account for readiness. I also think Apple is making the right call by using a 0-10 scale, unlike Oura’s 0-100 scale. Here are Apple’s readiness ranges:

0-1: Recover

2-4: Pace Yourself

5-7: Ready

8-10: Go For It

These strike me as straightforward enough, and potentially more actionable than the scores and patronizing (or passive aggressive) recommendations offered by Oura. I look forward to testing it more and comparing the scores directly to Oura in the coming weeks.

For comparison, on a day where my Apple Watch’s readiness score was an 8/10, my Oura Ring’s was an 85/100. 

I also like how Readiness shows which factor pushed your number up or down, whether that’s sleep, activity, or your overnight vitals, and you can tap through to that app for the details.

Performance

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Apple Watch Series 12 are both powered by Apple’s new S11 chip, which the company describes as its “most powerful wearable chip.”

This is the first meaningfully new chip for the Apple Watch since the S9 debuted in the Apple Watch Series 9 in 2023. The Apple Watch Series 10’s S10 chip was the same design in a thinner package, and last year’s models didn’t get a new chip at all.

Apple touts that the new S11 chip includes CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine components derived from the A20 Pro chip used in the iPhone 18 Pro. It also reportedly doubles the Apple Watch’s RAM from 2GB to 4GB.

There’s another aspect to the S11 chip: a new always-on processor that can handle complex workloads without tapping into the main chip. Inside it is a secure exclave, a hardware-isolated compartment to keep microphone data for Audio Intelligence private and secure.

In practice, Apple says the S11 chip, combined with the always-on processor, plays a role in multiple Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 features:

It works in conjunction with the new Health Sensing System to provide the higher-frequency heart rate readings.

It helps power the Audio Intelligence features like Siri Recap (more on that below).

It runs the redesigned pedometer model that Apple says is more accurate, including when your arms are stationary (like pushing a stroller).

In comparison to my Apple Watch Ultra 3, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Apple Watch Series 12 feel quicker when launching new apps, scrolling through menus, and doing basic interactions with Siri AI. To me, however, it shines by playing such a vital role in powering the aforementioned new health features.

Battery life

The Apple Watch Series 12 features a slightly larger battery, combined with the improved power efficiency of the Health Sensing System and S11 chip. Here are Apple’s battery claims for Apple Watch Series 12:

24 hrs normal use (unchanged from Series 11)

38 hrs Low Power Mode (unchanged from Series 11)

10 hrs outdoor workout, up 2 hrs

Apple also touts faster charging in select scenarios:

Up to 10 hours of sleep tracking with a 5-minute fast charge

Up to 12 hours of battery life with a 15-minute fast charge

Up to 80 percent battery charge in about 30 minutes (unchanged)

Those top two line items stood out to me in my testing of the Apple Watch Series 12. With Apple Watch’s increasing focus on sleep tracking, having a way to quickly top up before bed is very important.

For Apple Watch Ultra 4, which also has a larger battery, Apple says:

50 hours normal use, up from 42 on Ultra 3

84 hours Low Power Mode, up from 72 on Ultra 3

Workouts: 18 hours standard (up from 14), 25 hrs Extended (up from 20), and 45 hours Max Extended

Up to 18 hours of battery life with a 15-min fast charge, up from 12 hours on Ultra 3

In my testing, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 lives up to Apple’s battery life claims. In my real-world test, I charged it to 100% around 8 p.m. on Sunday and didn’t put it back on the charger until 8 p.m. on Tuesday. That’s 48 hours on a single charge, including 90 minutes of workout tracking, three hours away from my iPhone, and two nights of sleep tracking.

Odds and ends

There’s a new Steps complication for your watch face that updates your step count in real-time. I love it.

Apple has redesigned the Ocean Band for the Apple Watch Ultra. It’s now made from a translucent silicone material and comes in translucent gray, translucent kelp, and translucent black. In addition to the different appearance, the new Ocean Band style also feels lighter on my wrist.

There’s a new Siri Modular watch face, which is also backwards compatible. Zac covered it in detail here.

More to come

This is really only the start of what to expect from Apple Watch this year.

First, Apple is working on a completely redesigned version of the Health app, with a new Longevity tab and metrics like Health Age. I’m eager to try the new Health app. Apple says it’s coming in a software update later this year, and it’s available in beta as of Wednesday afternoon.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 will also add new Audio Intelligence features later this year, including Live Rewind and Siri Recap. 

Live Rewind lets you recall what was just said in the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet by double-pressing the Digital Crown. Siri Recap, meanwhile, creates high-level summaries of conversations that you can review later. Both of these features will launch in beta later this year, Apple says. The company has outlined a thorough privacy strategy around these features, too. 

Combined with the launch of Siri AI, Siri Recap and Live Rewind are the biggest steps yet toward Apple turning the Apple Watch into a full-fledged AI wearable — something I’m really excited to see play out.

9to5Mac’s Take

Who should upgrade to the Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4? I think this is one of the most substantial upgrades we’ve seen in recent years. If you’re in the Series 9 or Ultra 2 crowd (or earlier), I’d seriously consider making the jump. If you have a newer Apple Watch, it really boils down to how much you care about the new health features.

On the surface, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 seem like small updates. They don’t reinvent the form factor (although the new colors and material options are fantastic).

Instead, it’s what’s happening underneath that makes the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 so interesting. Apple has focused on making the watch considerably more capable at what it already does best: serving as an always-on companion that can monitor your heart, sleep, and activity. Oh, and it keeps you connected to friends, family, and the rest of the outside world.

The new Health Sensing System is the foundation for all of this. It fundamentally changes how much your Apple Watch knows about you throughout the day.

Crucially, Apple didn’t just increase the frequency of heart rate readings and put the burden on you to decipher all that added data. The new hardware ties together with watchOS 27 to provide meaningful insight into your daily life, including the promising Readiness app and a more capable Vitals app.

The story is even more exciting when you factor in the Siri Recap and Live Rewind features coming later this year. Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 not only know more about you now than ever before, but they will also help you keep up with the world around you.

Taken as a whole, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 offer the clearest indication yet of what the future holds for Apple’s most important wearable.
